Regarding the preface to the carving of the Combined Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra:
tracing back to Tiantai and extending down to Ouyi, those who have provided commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are not few; each has opened [the text] for themselves...
This new work differs from others in that it establishes its own positions while refuting those of others.

Having only recently begun my study, I read it three or four times without fully comprehending it until I encountered the *He lun* (Combined Treatise) by the Stone Gate Yuanming Chan Master, which explains his own realizations regarding points previously left unexplained.
Mr. Yin then intended to carve woodblocks to disseminate it; I nodded in approval, saying, "This is sufficient for lecturing on the scriptures."
I have added Chinese characters as annotations alongside these points for the benefit of those who apply the eye-salve;

however, due to being afflicted by illness in recent years, my spirit has grown weak and I have been unable to engage in detailed examination or cross-verification. I do not presume to deliberate upon whether this merits blame or praise;
I merely venture to inform all quarters and hope that you will kindly apply the brush. When the carving was completed in the year of Renwu, I returned from the capital to the East.
Spring of the second year of Ōei.
Written by the bhikṣu Shōtoku Ryūhō at the foot of the Chijaku Wheel in Raku, together with his lifelong mentor,
as the first fascicle of the *Combined Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*.
Sūtra translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Treatise composed by the Song Dynasty Chan Master Baojue Yuanming, Huìhóng (Appendix).
Preface written by the Song Dynasty Prime Minister and Layman Wújìn, Zhāng Shāngyīng.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* states:
"The subtle and wondrous nature of the mind cannot be fully described by the discrimination of language. Is it then ultimately invisible? It is said:
'Only by employing skillful means (upāya) to establish images can its meaning be conveyed, so as to enable the student to realize it.'"

To seek it for oneself and obtain it is what can be seen; this is the manner of the Dharma-giving of the Tathāgatas of the three periods, and the cause for the entry into awakening of Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions.
That which is difficult for sentient beings to see is their own mind, while that which they habitually see is the lotus flower.

By pointing to the lotus flower as the symbol of what they habitually see, it reveals the subtlety of that which is difficult to see; therefore, the sutra is titled "The Subtle Dharma" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
The lotus is the essence of tranquil extinction and enlightened awareness; its function is a vast and radiant illumination.
According to the measure of what is known, it is embodied in the text of seven fascicles and the meaning of twenty-eight chapters.

Responding to capacities and expounding in accordance with nature, there is neither detail nor brevity, neither coarseness nor subtlety—all are manifestations of the image. Even as the lotus is just beginning to open, it already contains the seed.

Within the seed, the pericarp already exists; these three phases are simultaneous. By observing one's own mind through this, one knows that past, present, and future are perfected within a single thought-moment.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going.
Since the lotus seeds have already been distributed, they are also gathered therein. By observing the faculties and their objects through this, one knows the subject and the object.
To be divided yet uninterrupted—as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*—is because it is "non-dual, without duality, without distinction, and uninterrupted.
Judging from this, that which is perfected in a single thought-moment throughout past and present is the lotus of the three periods of time;
that which is divided between subject and object yet remains uninterrupted is the lotus of the ten directions. This extends even to the Buddha’s manifestation of the broad and long tongue.
He emitted countless rays of light, and the sound of his coughing and snapping his fingers shook the three thousandfold world-system.
As he stroked the heads of the Bodhisattvas with his hand—beings who had entered parinirvāṇa long ago—the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna suddenly appeared.

The pure lands of the ten directions were each transformed three times, and the emanation Buddhas from all quarters assembled. Following the voice of the Buddha’s words, Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust surged forth from the earth.
Emerging from [the earth] and appearing everywhere where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is being preached, the jeweled stupa manifests;

that one shall see me, along with Prabhūtaratna and the Buddhas of the emanated bodies, is not merely a supernatural manifestation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), but rather the constant manifestation of the divisions of one’s own mind—this is the intended meaning.
Is this seen only in this sutra? It is also found in the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the case of the Rishi Vimala.
As soon as he took the hand of the youth Sudhana, Sudhana himself saw his own body travel to worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields,
arriving at the abodes of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields; he beheld those buddha-fields and their assemblies,
and the various adornments of the marks and signs of those Buddhas, continuing even for hundreds of thousands of billions of eons.
For as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, until at that time the seer released Sudhana’s hand,
whereupon Sudhana saw his own body returned to its original place; yet he also saw himself before Buddhas numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields,
for the ten directions were not separated by distance, even though it might have taken hundreds of thousands of billions of years [to travel].
It may be said that even across kalpas as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field, the three periods of time do not shift.

If a student can perceive the subtle mystery herein that is not transmitted, they are said to have repaid the Buddha’s kindness. The *Sūtra* is like warp threads and the *Vyākaraṇa* (Exegesis) is like woof threads;

while the *Sūtra* provides the constant warp, the *Vyākaraṇa* provides the changing woof. What is spoken of in the *Sūtra* serves merely as the warp, whereas what is accomplished through the woof is that which the *Sūtra* alone cannot express.
The Lotus Sutra of the Marvelous Dharma, Chapter One: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

The commentary states: the Liang dynasty monk Paramārtha of the Western Regions said that, according to the *Sūkṣma-vinaya*, Ānanda should ascend the seat and perform the formal recitation of the precepts (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
At the time of compiling the Dharma-piṭaka, his body was like that of a Buddha, complete with the primary and secondary marks; when the great assembly looked up at him, three doubts arose:

the doubt whether he had arisen from nirvāṇa to preach the Dharma for sentient beings again, the doubt whether a Buddha from another direction had come here to preach the Dharma, or the doubt whether Ānanda had attained Buddhahood to preach the Dharma for the assembly. To eliminate these three doubts, Ānanda...
"Thus have I heard at one time" is the statement that immediately resolves the three doubts.

"Residing on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha" indicates the place where this sutra was preached. King Ajātaśatru of Magadha built a palace on that site, and thus the city was named Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).
Gṛdhrakūṭa means "Vulture Peak"; the mountain is so named because its shape resembles that of a vulture. As for the mountain...
To the south of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus... [who have] attained mastery over their minds.

The commentary states: "Bhikṣu" means one who seeks alms purely; it means one who has destroyed the afflictions (*kleśa*); it means one who is able to maintain the precepts; it means one who is able to...

"Bhaya-bhañjana" (Terrifier of Māra), "Arhat," "Dasyu-pramathin" (Destroyer of Thieves), "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings), and "Anutpāda" (Non-arising)—all these terms contain multiple meanings within a single name.

Here, he is called a "Bhikṣu" (Monk) and designated as "Great" because he is a singular hero among all assemblies, revered by gods and humans alike, and capable of prevailing over the debates of the ninety-six types of heterodox schools; thus, his taints are... [exhausted].
The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of form (*rūpa-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) exist because of the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*);

thus, there are afflictions (*kleśa*). One who is able to cultivate the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and realize untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) possesses a spirit without fissures, such that afflictions cannot enter.

When the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) flow forth, one undergoes restraint and bondage; for views, entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), and so forth are all afflictions, as they are firmly bound and difficult to exhaust.

Therefore, these are called "fetters. If there are no causes for the three outflows (*āsrava*), there will be no effects of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*); "three realms of existence" is a specific designation for the three worlds.
When *śrāvakas* have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s merit of benefiting others, they achieve only their own benefit.
That which was difficult to exhaust, once exhausted, leads to the liberation of the mind and its mastery; thereafter, there are no further afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thus, having destroyed the thieves and attained their own benefit, they have become worthy of offerings and have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), so that they shall not be born again.

This is a general account of what the twelve thousand members of the assembly have realized; as for those who were preeminent and outstanding among them, their names are specifically designated and will follow in the subsequent text.
Their names were Ājñāta- (up to) ... together with their retinues. The commentary states:
*Ājñāta* means "one who understands the meaning," which is his name; *Kauṇḍinya* means "fire-vessel," which is his clan name.
Because he served the fire-god (*Agni*) in worldly affairs, he took it as his surname. *Mahākāśyapa* means "Great Turtle."
Regarding their clan: their ancestors were blessed with the auspicious sign of the state of Kauravya;
furthermore, because they were superior in both virtue and seniority among all the Kāśyapas, they were distinguished by this title.
"Uruvilvā" means "Pumpkin Grove," "Gayā" means "City," and "Nadī" means "River. These three Kāśyapa brothers resided in these respective locations.
"Forest," "City," and "River. Śāriputra means "Son of Śārī"; because his mother’s physical appearance was beautiful, people in the world named him after her.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana means "Great Maudgalya"; Maudgalya is his clan name, derived from what his ancestors used to eat.
Mahākātyāyana means "Great Kātyāyana"; Kātyāyana is his clan name, referring to his literary refinement.
Aniruddha means "Free from Poverty" and also "Wish-Fulfilling. Kapphiṇa means "Kappa Star";
his parents prayed to this star at his birth, and thus it became his name. Gavāmpati means "Ox-Like. Revata means "Revatī Star.
Piṇḍola-bharadvāja means "Remaining Habits"; he had the habit of pride.
Bakkula means "of good appearance"; Mahākoṭṭhila means "great-knee"; Nanda means "joy";
Sundarananda means "beautiful joy"; Pūrṇa means "full," which refers to his father;
Maitrāyaṇī means "compassion," which refers to his mother; he is named after both his parents.
Subhūti, this means that at the time of his birth, the granaries, vessels, and utensils of his household were all empty.
Ānanda, this means "Joyful One. Rāhula, this means "Obstruction";

he is able to devour the moon, for my Dharma is like the moon, and this child was able to obstruct me in life after life, preventing me from leaving the home-life, thus hindering me throughout successive generations. I [am] the world...
The world is able to renounce. Now, those called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*) are those whose outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted and who remain on the stage of training;
those "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) are the Arhats. Those who occupy this same station but whose secret practices and subtle functions are not known by the multitude are described separately:
Mahāprajāpatī, which means "Great Path of Compassion" (*Mahāmaitrī*).
*Ni* (尼) means "woman"; she was the Buddha’s maternal aunt who nursed him. *Yaśodharā* (耶輸陀羅) means "Flower-Color" (*Puṣpavarṇā*).
As described above, there are errors and omissions in the transliteration of these names; for example, *Ājñātakauṇḍinya* (阿若憍陳如) is fully rendered as *Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya*.
*Kauṇḍinya* means "male. He was the first to attain realization when the Buddha attained enlightenment.
Because this clan has many women, he is called "male" (nara) to distinguish him from them; it is also translated as "Already Known" (*jñāta*), which is a corruption of the meaning.

For example, *Revata* is fully called *Hyalivada*; it is also translated as "Fictitious Combination," for when its meaning is compared with that of the constellation Śatabhiṣaj, they are vastly different.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "This bhikṣu takes the empty sky as his meditative object."
When Ding saw two ghosts contending over a corpse, he realized that the body is but a provisional combination; thus, Shi Xing’s translation [of the name] may be considered questionable.
For instance, Kātyāyana is fully called Mahākātyāyana, which means "Great One of the Kaṭa-śreṇya Clan.

This likely refers to his ancestors who were skilled at using knives and shears, and thus took it as their surname. To translate it simply as "Ornamented" (Wénshì) would be far too abbreviated. As for...
Śāriputra is also called Śāriputtra, Śāradvatīputra, or Śakuntaka;
he is so named because his mother’s eyes were beautiful and charming. While she was pregnant with him, her eloquence and wisdom already surpassed those of her maternal uncle, Kauṣṭhila.
Kauṣṭhila said, "Once this child is born, he will surely surpass me; I must exert myself in study lest he cut me down."
This refers to those who find leisure even amidst their fingernails.
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, numbering as many as eighty thousand, were present.
The commentary states: *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment."
*Dhāraṇī* means "total retention" (*saṃdhāraṇa*). Regarding the Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment, it is said that they all "do not regress.
Regarding total retention, up to the turning of the non-regressing wheel, it is said that they have "all attained" it.
What is meant by "all attaining non-retrogression" is like gold extracted from ore that never again becomes ore, or like wood turned to ash that never again becomes wood.
Regarding the tree reaching the stage of making offerings to all Buddhas, it is said: "It plants the roots of all virtues. The term "plants" (*zhi*) means to nourish and cultivate.
Regarding the skillful entry into the Buddha-wisdom, it is said: "One cultivates the body with compassion. The term "cultivates" (*xiu*) means to augment and increase.
Through this nourishment and augmentation, the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages nurture great loving-kindness and great compassion.
This is the language of praise used by all Buddhas; however, it is highly incorrect for Bodhisattva Asaṅga to divide this into ten types of meanings regarding non-retrogression.
Since the Buddhas have already offered their praise, they ought to demonstrate [the path] through wisdom, compassion, and the six pāramitās;
thus it is said: "To penetrate great wisdom and reach the other shore. This, in essence, refers to...
Great wisdom is conjoined with compassion; "the other shore" (*pāra*) is conjoined with the six *pāramitās*.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All classes of sentient beings, even unto my leading them all into *nirvāṇa* without remainder"—this is compassion.
Yet, while thus delivering immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in reality there are no sentient beings [to be delivered].
To attain extinction (nirvāṇa) is wisdom. A bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon. Giving is called *dāna-pāramitā*;
this *dāna-pāramitā* encompasses all six perfections. Vasubandhu Bodhisattva explains: "The meaning of *dāna* subsumes the six [perfections]: material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma.
Among these, the first, second, and third are termed the "abodes of cultivation" (*caryā-vihāra*). By this it is known.
If a bodhisattva wishes to deliver all sentient beings through skillful means across the stream of birth and death to the shore of nirvana, they must first possess compassion and wisdom;
if they wish to fulfill the myriad practices and adorn the ground of wisdom, they must first rely upon the six pāramitās.
Therefore, eighteen great bodhisattvas are cited to substantiate the preceding meaning: Mañjuśrī represents wisdom, Avalokiteśvara... [represents compassion].
Out of compassion, by the power of his knowledge and vision, he shakes the palaces of Māra; therefore, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Because in every thought-moment his mind does not conjoin with the worldly mind, he is named Nityodyukta (Ever-Exerted). Since even if space were to perish, he would never grow weary or exhausted, he is named Anikṣiptadhura (One Who Never Lays Down the Burden).
By these three stages, his diligence is established and proven. Seeing that they lack the means for sustenance, he provides them with the necessities of life.

Because he bestows gifts, he is named Ratnapāṇi (Jewel-Palmed); because he sees the suffering caused by the conditions of illness and bestows the gift of fearlessness, he is named Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King);

because he sees the suffering of saṃsāra and bestows the gift of Dharma, he is named Sūradatta (Courageous Giver). By these three stages, he realizes and perfects the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

Because he purifies the *vinaya* like the first appearance of the moon, he is named Ratnacandra (Jewel Moon); because he accords with desirelessness, he cultivates the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

Just as the light of the moon is entirely the substance of the moon and is therefore called "moonlight," so too are morality, concentration, wisdom, and even lust, anger, and delusion all part of the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*).
Because they illuminate without discriminating between the foul and the pure, it is called the "Full Moon.

By means of these three stages, the perfection of morality (*śīla-pāramitā*) is realized. Because one is free from sinking and agitation, one attains the concentration of transformation (*nirmāṇa-samādhi*), and is therefore called "Great Power" (*mahābala*).

Because he dwells in the maintenance of the adornment of light within samādhi, he is named "Immeasurable Power" (*Anantabala*); by these two stages, the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is established.
Because he has completely exhausted the mind of the world, he is named "Transcending the Three Realms" (*Trailokyasamatikrānta*);
because he skillfully guards the city of the mind, he is named "Bhadrapāla"; *Bhadrapāla* means "skillful guardian. By these two stages, [the perfection of ethical discipline] is established.
The Perfection of Patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Initially ascending to the stage of "Fulfillment of Enlightenment" (*pūrṇabodhi*), it is still termed the "Phase of Wisdom" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*);

thus he is named Maitreya. Because this phase of wisdom causes one not to abide [in fixed states], he is named Ratnākara. By uniting these two dharmas to rescue all sentient beings, he is named Śāstṛ (the Teacher).

Through these three stages, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is realized and established. Now, regarding the description of the six [perfections] in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

If one must necessarily proceed from the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) through to the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), why is this alone not the case? It is said:
The Sūtra reveals the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*) so that ordinary beings may realize it in reality;
since such realization must rely on the power of diligence (*vīrya*), diligence is placed at the head of the six perfections to convey this intent.
At that time, Śakra [up to] two thousand devaputras were present together.
The Commentary says: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that when a trichiliocosm first forms, the palaces of the various devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are formed first;
next, the dwelling places of humans and other sentient beings are formed; and finally, those of the Four Heavenly Kings (*cāturmahārājika*).
The gods who neighbor the sun and moon dwell upon the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the ocean.
The sun and moon revolve before their palaces to illuminate the four continents;
from that point upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is another forty-two thousand *yojanas*, which is the abode of Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
At the summit of the mountain, there are thirty-two heavens in its four corners, all of which are presided over by Śakra.
The Sūtra says "Śakradevendra," which means "one who is capable of acting"; that is, he is capable of acting as the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
This is the very Śakra mentioned in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. As for the three sons of heaven named Candraprabha, Samantagandha, and Ratnaprabha, they are [the attendants of] Śakra.
The ministers [of the gods] are like the world’s high officials and the Four Heavenly Kings; the retinue of Śakra is like the world’s military generals.

The two devaputras, Maheśvara and Īśvara, refer to the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*) and the Heaven of Mastery over Others’ Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This account describes the assembly coming from the desire realm; as for those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are [described in] the *Yogācāra* [treatises].
The treatise says: There are eighteen abodes, namely: the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya), the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita), and the Heaven of Mahābrahmā.
These three arise from having repeatedly cultivated the first dhyāna with medium and superior degrees of intensity.
As the Sūtra states, "The Lord of the Sahā World, the Great Brahmā Śikhin," this refers to the preeminent stream of these [deities]. "Sahā" means "endurance" (kṣamaṇa); "Brahmā" means...
The phrase "desire-free Śikhin" refers to the *śikhā* (topknot). This describes those who have come from the first dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Minor Light, Immeasurable Light, and Utmost Pure Light"—these three arise because one has repeatedly cultivated the second pure dhyāna (*viśuddha-dhyāna*) through the medium and superior grades of the fire-like [meditative heat].
The Sūtra’s mention of "Mahābrahmā of Radiant Light" and so forth refers to this superior outflow (*niṣyanda*). This is the description.
Question: Why is it that among the assemblies coming from the Second Dhyāna, those of the Tuṣita and Yāma heavens are not specifically mentioned? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Because the lands where the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven reside are near to the Buddha, they constantly come to make offerings to the Buddha during his birth, his period of ascetic practice, his attainment of the Way, and his turning of the Wheel of Dharma; this is not the case for the palaces of the other four heavens."
The gods of the Heaven of Free Abiding in Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana) do not come because their attachment to the subtle pleasures of the five desires is so deep.
Although the Tuṣita heaven possesses sharp faculties and its own Bodhisattvas in the stage of succession to Buddhahood preach the Dharma there, they likewise do not come.

Although the Brahma heavens are distant, because they are free from desire and their longing for the Dharma is profound, they have requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma; thus they have come. One knows this by observing this sutra through the discourse of the Prajñāpāramitā.

The harm wrought by the five desires is extreme; even the devas, encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world, are obstructed by them and fail to hear the Dharma, let alone the ordinary beings of the six realms of existence after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
There were eight dragon kings (up to) accompanied by their retinues of hundreds of thousands.
The commentary says: The eight dragons each receive their names based on where they dwell; how could this burden their names?

Some are named for their virtue, some for their majesty, some for the sea, and some for the pond. Nanda means "Joy"; Upananda— *Note: The original text fragment ends with "跋難陀" (Bananada), which corresponds to the Sanskrit Upananda.*
These names refer to the two dragon brothers, Sunanda and Nandaka.
Because their spiritual power causes wind and rain to fall in due season, bringing joy to the hearts of people, they are so named. Sāgara means "Salt Ocean.
Vāsuki means "Many-Headed. Takṣaka means "Manifesting Poison. Anavatapta means "Without Heat or Affliction."
The Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage act as the Mānasas; this means they possess a compassionate mind.

When rain is about to fall, the clouds gather for seven days while they wait for the affairs of sentient beings to be completed, and only then do they let it rain. The *utpala*—translated here as "dark-colored lotus"—is like the joy of a compassionate mind:
when it dwells in virtue, many heads appear; when it manifests its power, it displays its majesty without the heat of affliction.
The dark-colored lotus is situated in the pond, while Sāgara is situated in the ocean; yet, since dragons have no ears, how could they hear the Dharma?
It is said: when a human takes on a dragon form, they are able to do so. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Mañjuśrī transformed himself and entered the human realm, and at the site of the Great Stupa to the east of the city of Kapilavastu, he turned and preached this sūtra, titled 'Universal' (*Samantabhadra*)."
In the great ocean, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nāgas came to the place where the *Dharmadhātu-prakāśa-sūtra* was being taught;
having heard the Dharma, they developed a profound weariness with their nāga existence and attained the mind of great bodhi, reaching the stage of non-retrogression.
It is sufficient to say that immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nāgas came to that place; it must surely be said that at this great shrine, the wheel [of Dharma] was turned.
Why is this sutra preached? It is said: because the stūpas and shrines are in a state of quiescent extinction, it is preached that there is nothing preached;
because the nāgas have no ears, they hear that there is nothing heard.
There were four kiṃnaras (up to) accompanied by hundreds of thousands of attendants.
The treatise says: There is worldly happiness and there is supramundane happiness. Supramundane happiness is the happiness of the Dharma;
the four *kiṃnaras* are an example of this. Worldly happiness is that of the four *gandharvas*.
*Kiṃnara* means "neither human nor non-human," also called "doubtful person" (*śaṅkāpuruṣa*), because when one sees them with their horns, one doubts whether they are human.
Is he a human being or is he not a human being? He is a deity of the Dharma-music of the Heavenly Lord who relies on melody to perform the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, it is called "Dharma Performance. He performs the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; therefore, it is called "Performance of the Sublime Dharma.
He performs the Dharma of the Six Pāramitās; therefore, he is called "Upholder of the Dharma. A Gandharva—this term means "seeking fragrance"—refers to one who, by means of...

Those who take fragrance as their food and pleasure are like those who perform on bamboo poles and other such acrobatic feats; those who delight in the sounds of drums, cymbals, strings, and pipes are like those who possess beautiful, radiant concubines and exquisite dances;
and those who find beauty in clear singing are like those with bright teeth and pure voices.

An ancient saying holds that "strings are not equal to bamboo, and bamboo is not equal to the voice," because these latter approaches gradually approach the natural state. Although all four are referred to by the title of "King," regarding the mastery of music and the understanding of its arts, [the voice is supreme].
Regarding the distinction between male and female, Kumārajīva said: "The Kinnara King and the Heavenly Emperor play worldly music;
how could the gods ever perform the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, or the Six Pāramitās and still call it 'worldly'?
Although Kumārajīva was widely learned, he was unable to refute [the opponent] with reason, and his errors were many.
There were four asuras who... [and so on] ... withdrew to sit at one side.
The commentary states: "Asura" means "no wine. They constantly gather flowers to ferment them in the ocean to make wine;
however, because of the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the flavor cannot change [into wine]. At this, they became greatly enraged and vowed never to drink it again. "Bāzhi" is its name.
Bound as the Lord of Devas, he was tied around the neck with five objects:
Khara-karṇa (meaning "Broad Shoulders," who was also broad and courageous, skilled at leaping over the ocean); Vimalacitta (meaning "Pure Mind");
Uccaiḥśravas (meaning "Loud-Sounding from the Sea"), the kinsman of Śakra; and Rāhu (meaning "Obstructing Holder"), who obstructs the sun with his hand.

Regarding the "Lunar Beings" (*candras*), the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states there are five classes: first, those who are extremely weak and dwell among humans in mountain forests, or in great, deep caves within the mountains of the West;
they possess palaces that are not of the devas—these are translated as *asura*, which means "non-deva.
Second, twenty-one thousand *yojanas* beneath the great ocean to the north of Mount Sumeru, there are the *rākṣasa*...
Twenty-one thousand yojanas below is the palace of Huhu; twenty-one thousand yojanas further down is the palace of Śauṇḍa;
twenty-one thousand yojanas further down is the palace of Mālādhāra—“Mālādhāra” here refers to one who adorns his body with variegated paintings and garlands;
and twenty-one thousand yojanas further down is the palace of Vemacitrin.
There are eighty-four thousand [yojanas] deeper than Mount Sumeru. The Kālaṃgas—here translated as "Golden-Winged Bird"—have wings that are golden in color;
when spread, they extend for three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand li.
When the life of a dragon dwelling in the ocean is about to end, he splits the sea with his wings to seize and devour it, using his awesome power to terrify the various classes of nāgas.
He is named Mahātejas (Great Splendor). Because his body is larger than that of his peers, he is called Mahākāya (Great Body).
Because his hunger is satisfied by eating nāgas, he is called Mahāpūrṇa (Great Fulfillment). Because there is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) upon his neck, he is called Cintāmaṇi.
Vaidehī means "one who reflects"; she is the mother of King Ajātaśatru. Ajātaśatru means "unborn."
The enemy was the King of Magadha; because he named his son after his mother, he was called the Son of Vaidehī.
At that time, the World-Honored One—[reaching] until—"his body and mind remained unmoved.
The Commentary states: The rise and fall, the pauses and cadences of the sūtra text are divided into two sections, yet their expressions appear interchangeably as one.

What do you think? Since it is said that immeasurable meanings are taught to instruct the bodhisattvas, and since these meanings are expressed through immeasurable words, how could one say "this sutra has been preached" at the very moment of the assembly?
Furthermore, it is said that [the Buddha] entered the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings;
yet if meaning has no real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), how can there be a "place"? This is indeed questionable. — Huayan [Sutra].
The *Yan lun* states: When the Buddha was in the country of Magadha, at the Bodhimanda of the Aranya-dharma, he first attained perfect enlightenment.
In the Hall of Universal Radiance, he entered the Samādhi of the Limit of the Kṣaṇa;

taking the Dharma-realm body as the essence of meditative concentration because it lacks the nature of the three periods of time, [he manifested] from his descent from Tuṣita Heaven until his entry into Nirvāṇa—these seven.
In the nineteenth year, he dwelt in the world and turned all wheels of Dharma; in total, this did not transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
Because this samādhi is perfectly pervasive from beginning to end, it is neither of the three periods of time nor of antiquity or modernity.

Comparing this sūtra with other treatises, his dwelling in the world for seventy-nine years and turning all wheels of Dharma likewise did not transcend the limit of a single kṣaṇa; thus, the assembly gathered.
Recently, while discussing the duration of time, it was established that the body of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-kāya) is the essential substance of meditative concentration;
because it lacks the nature of the three periods of time, its immeasurable meaning is not a quantity of many or countless numbers. Students should contemplate this deeply.
At that time, it rained from heaven... [until] they single-mindedly contemplated the Buddha.
The Commentary says: *Mahā* means "great"; *Mandārava* means "pleasing to the mind"; *Mañjūṣaka* means "soft.
This refers to celestial flowers that are soft and supple, delighting the minds of men. [The earth] surged up in the east and subsided in the west; it surged up in the south...

When the north subsides and the center surges while the edges subside—such as when the earth quakes and trembles—it is merely to cause one to realize that the characteristics of dharmas are empty and deceptive.
While the Buddha and the great assembly remain solemnly and silently abiding, heaven and earth undergo such transformations; thus one knows that all dharmas are themselves the Truth.
Therefore, there is no distinction between the sentient and the insentient. As the *Zhaolun* says: "The profound Way lies in wondrous awakening."
Sublime awakening consists in realizing that which is identical to the truth; when one realizes this identity with the truth, things and self are viewed as the same.
When things and self are viewed as the same, "the other" and "self" are no longer dualities. Thus, heaven and earth share the same root as I, and all phenomena constitute a single body with me.
This scripture intends to explain this meaning at length, but here it merely reveals its initial traces. Upāsaka—this term means a layman who attends to religious affairs.
*Upāsikā* means "female lay practitioner" (*upāsikā*). *Yakṣa* means "swift and agile. *Mahoraga* refers to the class of beings that are great pythons or belly-crawlers.
The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) states: "When Bodhisattvas of the ten wholesome paths develop the Great Mind, they forever part from the ocean of the suffering wheel of the three realms.
Those of the lower grade of goodness become minor kings (*kṣudrarāja*), while those of the upper grade of the ten wholesome paths become [rulers of] the Iron [Circlet]."
The Wheel-Turning Kings (cakravartin) of the *śikṣā-bīja* [stage] possess a copper wheel over two continents; those of the *rūpa-bīja* [stage] possess a silver wheel over three continents;
and the Wheel-Turning Kings of the *dharmatā-bīja* and *dṛḍha-guṇa* [stages] possess the seven treasures and golden light over the four continents.
When the Sūtras speak of "lesser kings, wheel-turning holy kings," and so forth, this is not intended as an abbreviation for all lesser kings.
At that time, the Buddha emitted [light]... (until) he caused seven-jeweled stupas to arise.

The commentary says: from the eighteen thousand worlds of the eastern direction, downward to the Avīci Hell—*Avīci* meaning "uninterrupted"—and upward to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—*Akaniṣṭha* meaning "the ultimate limit of obstruction."
Since there is nothing that is not universally pervaded, this world is likewise vast; yet it is manifested within the light of a single pore of a hair.
From the various beings of the six realms, according to the goodness or evil of their karmic conditions, to the beauty or ugliness of the retributions they receive;
from bhikṣus and bodhisattvas practicing the Way up to the attainment of Buddhahood; and from the preaching of the Dharma by all Buddhas to their entry into nirvāṇa—all are contained therein.
From the time the stūpas were erected until now, many years have passed; yet how could this be seen as occurring within the span of a single thought-moment?

The meaning of the Sūtra is as clear as the sun and stars, yet the masters of letters have provided commentaries and exegeses, whereupon names and characteristics proliferate like fine hairs, and the pursuit of principles arises in a chaotic clamor, like clouds rising, smoke gathering, thunder rolling, and lightning flashing.
It is lamentable that scholars run hither and thither, shifting their positions so that morning and evening cannot be distinguished.

To possess a light between the eyebrows like a finger—showing it to one who is thirsty as a sign of where water is located—and instead of doing so, to take pride in the elegance of its railings and the craftsmanship of its paving stones to boast of to others: how could this possibly quench one's thirst?
The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* says: "At the limit of a single kṣaṇa, the three periods of time interpenetrate;
even unto an ocean of immeasurable kalpas, they abide according to the present without shifting for even a moment. All sages and worthies know this and thereby attain the Way.

Those whose thoughts and perceptions are deluded and who view the three periods of time as real do not understand that wisdom is the precursor; thus they are unable to know it. Observing by means of this principle, one finds that...
The vessel-worlds of the ten directions are all sustained by perversion; the root-bodies of the three periods of time are all perceived through emotional and conceptual thought.
That which is called the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment—pervading the ten directions, giving birth to Tathāgatas, and being of the same substance as all phenomena—remains eternally as it is.
Through the light of expedient means, the Buddha illuminates one expedient, knowing that the ten directions are likewise entirely so.

Thus, just as one knows the flavor of the entire cauldron by tasting a single morsel without needing to eat from the whole cauldron, so too, by mentioning only the eastern direction in the Sūtra, one can know all other directions;
this demonstrates the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*). By mentioning the vessel-world, one can know the sense-faculties and the body (*indriya-ātman*);
those who wish to study should observe these two aspects in relation to one another and clarify them for themselves. The old commentary states: "The Western Regions..."
Taking the East as the superior direction, this scripture is intended for those with the Mahayana capacity for Buddha-nature, not for those with the capacities of other vehicles;
just as the rising sun first illuminates the high plateaus, the Buddha first delivers those of superior faculties. That they have lost the essential meaning of this scripture is indeed lamentable.
At that time, Maitreya (up to) asked in verse.
The Commentary says: Mañjuśrī is the past Buddha, Ratnakarandakaniṣṭha;
Maitreya Bodhisattva is the future Buddha who will succeed Śākyamuni Buddha. Thus it is said of Mañjuśrī and...
In the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, on Vulture Peak, Śākyamuni emits light and manifests auspicious omens;

Maitreya poses questions to resolve doubts; and Mañjuśrī explains according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This scripture presents the image of the past, future, and present being simultaneous and mutually interpenetrating, as described in the preceding text;
it thus represents the sudden vision of pure and impure lands, wherein one contemplates the kalpas.

Recently, when it came to the verses, he became even more detailed; yet Maitreya’s profound compassion desired that sentient beings would be sharply awakened, much like Han’s Fan Zeng’s affection for Xiang Yu.
When Zeng urged Yu to kill the Lord of Pei at the Banquet of the Red Bird Pass, he repeatedly signaled Yu with his eyes and raised the jade pendant he wore three times to show him.
Xiang Yu remained silent and did not respond. Maitreya’s verses recounting what he had seen and heard are repressed and repetitive, spanning over a thousand words;
yet from time to time they leak out the Buddha’s secret mechanisms, much like Fan Zeng’s repeated pointing toward the jade pendant.
One should see this for oneself upon reading the text.
Mañjuśrī, I shall now briefly explain. The Treatise says:
Maitreya stated that among the things I have seen within a single ray of light, there are a thousand billion;
I have now set these forth in verse, yet this is merely a brief summary. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The youth Sudhana..."
The son saw that within each step of the four surrounding walls of Maitreya’s pavilion,
all manner of precious jewels served as adornments; within every single jewel, there appeared Maitreya practicing the bodhisattva path in past kalpas—
sometimes giving away his head or eyes, sometimes giving away his hands, feet, lips, tongue, teeth, ears, nose, flesh, blood, skin, or bones.
Flesh, and even down to nails and hair—all such things he is able to relinquish;
wives, concubines, sons, daughters, cities, towns, villages, kingdoms, and royal thrones—he gives them all away entirely according to whatever is required.
He causes those in prison to be released and those who are bound to be set free; for those who are ill, he provides medical treatment. Entering...
For those on wrong paths, he shows them the right way; or he acts as a boatman to ferry them across the great ocean;

or he acts as a horse-king to rescue them from all calamities; or he acts as a great seer to skillfully expound sublime discourses; or he acts as a wheel-turning monarch to exhort them to cultivate the ten wholesome actions;
or he acts as a king of physicians to skillfully treat all manner of illnesses; or he is filial and obedient toward his parents; or he draws near to virtuous teachers.
Sometimes appearing as śrāvakas, sometimes as pratyekabuddhas, sometimes as bodhisattvas, and sometimes as tathāgatas,

they teach and discipline all sentient beings; even the various forms of Maitreya Bodhisattva practicing the perfections for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas—
all these images [were seen] by Sudhana within the assembly of jewels in the pavilion.
Within each and every adorned object, one sees these as well as other immeasurable and inconceivable realms of sovereign mastery;
thus, even the manifestation of eighteen thousand lands within a single hair-pore between the eyebrows is merely a demonstration shown according to the capacity of what they know.
Although such descriptions are numerous, I shall now briefly state them by way of illustration.
This is one instance of the jade pendant.
"I saw that land" (up to) "to seek the Buddha-way. The commentary states:
The previous mention of such sights and sounds, as well as the thousands of billions of matters, was intended to describe their vastness; this present statement...
The phrase "concentrating the mind in mountain forests for hundreds of millions of years" describes its duration;

the underlying meaning suggests that a space as small as a single hair-tip should not be able to contain such vast matters, and a moment as brief as a single thought should not be able to encompass such a long period of time.
These words are extensive and profound, yet their intent is subtly revealed, much like holding up a jade pendant.
Second: The *Shenxian zhuan* records that in the first year of the Shenjue era of the Han dynasty, at Mount Jinhua in Eastern Wu, there was a widespread tradition that many immortals practiced there.
A woodcutter named Muke was gathering firewood in the mountains when he saw two men wearing yellow caps playing chess beneath a pine tree.
Muke sat in a corner to observe them; the men in yellow caps continued their game with composure. After a long while, they yawned and appeared ready to depart, but suddenly vanished.

Wherever he went wearing his yellow cap, he found the remnants of a chessboard left on the ground, yet not yet cleared away. Picking up an axe from his hand, he saw that its handle was already rotted and broken;
greatly startled, he hurried out of the mountains, only to find that the hills and valleys had changed and the towns and villages were no longer as they were before.
Asking a passerby what time it was now, he was told: "It is the thirteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. Upon this, he [realized]...

This wood-gatherer sighed deeply and subsequently hid within the mountains. Furthermore, the *Record of the Western Regions* states that in Central India there was a hermit who could transform gold into rubble;
he further sought the art of levitation and after a long time attained it.

To employ this method, he had a man of noble character stand beside the altar clutching a sword, holding his breath and remaining silent; then, throughout one night, the hermit himself recited secret mantras.
Thereafter, he ascended as an immortal. Later, a certain heroic man was found; [the master] bestowed his full attention upon him with ritual courtesy.
As they were about to perform the rite, [the master] said to him, "Can you remain silent for one night for my sake? He replied, "If you honor me so deeply, I would not decline even death;
how could remaining silent for one night be difficult? Thereupon, he was made to perform it according to the ritual. As dawn was approaching, the hero—
The official let out a cry, and fire descended from the sky. The hermit hurriedly led him into the water to take shelter.
The official apologized, saying, "I warned you not to speak; why did you call out so recklessly?
He replied, "Since receiving my new life, I have dreamed that my former master rebuked me for remaining silent and subsequently killed me. I have been reborn as a great Brahmin in South India."
The family reflected upon their profound kindness and remained silent until, suddenly, a son was born.
His wife said, "If you do not speak now, I shall kill this child," and she raised her blade to strike him. She stopped him in haste, and before she realized it, his speech had emerged.
While the game of chess was not yet finished, the wood-dweller sat through four changing reigns; from night until dawn, the man of integrity passed through two lifetimes in a dream.

Although waking and dreaming differ, they do not transcend a single thought-moment; that which is difficult to believe is verified by means of that which is trustworthy, just as the taste of honey is uniform from its center to its edges.
Or, having seen a Bodhisattva [approach], what does he preach for them?
The Commentary states: The grandeur of these verses and the richness of their analogies are like opening a military armory where myriad treasures lie scattered;
yet, toward the end, two verses repeatedly mention the emission of light, saying, "The Buddha emits one ray of light" and "emits one pure ray of light.
Why is such great emphasis placed on speaking of light? It is because he [the author] intends—
The scholar’s urgency to awaken is like raising a jade pendant three times to show it;
yet the scholar ultimately fails to awaken, remaining as silent as Xiang Yu, because their calculations are deeply attached to language and writing.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "One should not grasp at or become attached to what is said; those who seek the truth are free from words."
Therefore, Mahāmati, it is like a foolish person who, when pointed at an object by means of a finger, looks only at the finger and does not grasp the actual reality.
In this same way, such fools follow the finger of verbal expression, grasping and clinging to it until the very end without relinquishing it, and thus they are unable to attain the ultimate,
true reality that transcends the finger of verbal expression.
At that time, Mañjuśrī... [up to] the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Humans.
The commentary states: The name of the Buddha in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is Vairocana, which means "Universal Radiance.
The name of the assembly in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* is the "Great Radiant Treasury of Supernatural Powers. Now, as for the term "Universal Radiance," it cannot...
If one seeks the words through their locus, they are the Great Luminous Treasury of Spiritual Powers (*abhijñā-mahā-āloka-garbha*), which cannot be sought through time;
being without locus and without time, this is the samādhi of all Buddhas at the limit of a single *kṣaṇa*. Thus, this sutra speaks simultaneously of "without locus" and "without time.
*Asaṃkhyeya* here refers to incalculable eons (*kalpa*); this refers to the divisions of time. The sutra says: "In the past, immeasurable and..."
The "inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas at the limit" refers to a realm beyond the reach of thought, a time that is no time;
it is a place where the sun illuminates the day, the moon illuminates the night, and lamps illuminate the darkness—a land of pervasive radiance that is yet no place.
Nevertheless, rather than speaking directly as in the *Avataṃsaka* or the *Awakening of Faith*, one must speak of "non-existence."
Regarding the mention of "numerous kalpas," "days and months," and "lamps," the sutra uses these metaphors solely to convey its intended meaning.
It does not stop at this alone. As for the statement that when one intends to preach the Great Dharma, rain falls: the rain symbolizes all-pervasive universality;

the conch shell symbolizes the horizontal extension across the ten directions; and the drum symbolizes the vertical exhaustion of the three periods of time. This is because when a conch is blown, it must necessarily be struck horizontally.
The drum must be held upright. The Buddha is named Sun-Moon-Lamp because he is fully endowed with the ten titles.
Because he has come by way of the path of reality as it truly is, he is called the Tathāgata. Because the merit he has performed deserves all offerings, he is called the Arhat.

Because all dharmas are immovable and indestructible, he is the Samyaksaṃbuddha (the Perfectly Awakened One). Because he knows one dharma and two dharmas, he is called the Sarvajña (the All-Knowing One).

Because he has fully realized all phenomena, he is called the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha). Because he is endowed with both merit and wisdom, he is called the "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna).

Because he goes wherever he intends like the two wheels of a chariot, he is called the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata). Because he knows the world, knows the end of the world, and knows the path leading to the end of the world, he is called the "Knower of the World" (Lokavid).
Because he is supreme among all teachers, he is called the "Unsurpassed One" (Anuttara).
He is a "Sthavira" (Elder) because he trains men as masters; he is called the "Teacher of Gods and Men" because he teaches and transforms sentient beings through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles;

he is called a "Buddha" because he is able to awaken himself from the sleep of afflictions of all worlds and awaken others; and he is called the "World-Honored One" because he dwells in the most supreme state.
[He] expounds the true Dharma (up to) the characteristics of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

The treatise states: within the Sūtras, there is the meaning of explaining the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) by means of unimpaired conventional designations (*prajñapti*), which refers to the three dharmas that are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
However, these three phrases must necessarily be connected in order to fully comprehend their meaning; taking the excellence of the beginning as [the starting point...]
The designation "good in the middle" is established as the true meaning because "good in the end" is also a designation;
thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Prajñāpāramitā is indeed not Prajñāpāramitā; it is called 'Prajñāpāramitā.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga’s commentary explains: "It is like a vajra held by a naked deity, which has two ends."
Because its center is wide and its ends are narrow, that which is wide is empty and that which is narrow is substantial.
Thus, what is called "prajñāpāramitā" is a provisional name; that which is "not prajñāpāramitā" is the true mark (dharmatā).
That which is designated as "prajñāpāramitā" is likewise a provisional name. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: First, it is "good in the beginning," meaning at the time of hearing.
It is "good in the beginning" because it gives rise to joy; "good in the middle" refers to the time of practice, as it is free from hardship and avoids the two extremes by relying on the Middle Way;

and "good in the end" means it is ultimately free from all defilements, as it culminates in the ultimate transcendence of desire and the attainment of the fruit through the perfection of practice, for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is inherently free from stain.
Because it is free from defilement; that which is called "free from defilement" is a provisional designation, for it is itself subject to contamination. An old commentary states:
"To say that the Dharma of the Śrāvakas is 'good in the beginning,' the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas is 'good in the middle,' and the Mahāyāna Dharma is 'good in the end' is an error."
"For the sake of seeking the Śrāvaka [vehicle] up to the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).
The Commentary says: This describes how when the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa appeared in the world in the past, he likewise did not immediately reveal the Single Buddha Vehicle (ekabuddhayāna);
rather, employing skillful means (*upāya*) according to the capacities of his audience, he taught the Three Vehicles. "Now that I have attained the Way, I reflect upon..."
The ancient precedents for the gift of Dharma should likewise be honored and expounded upon.

When the elder thought of his son, he was moved by a poignant and sorrowful longing as if he could actually see him; he rejoiced greatly at the prospect of his return, and seeing him from afar, he sent someone to call out urgently while another pulled him forward.
His son threw himself prostrate on the ground, crying out in grievance and lamentation: "I..."

Why was he seized for his offenses? The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging, whenever he saw people, would intentionally go to them to prostrate and praise them, saying, "I do not disparage you; you shall all become Buddhas.
Yet he repeatedly encountered those who struck him with tiles, stones, staves, and clubs, and drove him away, saying, "We do not accept your false prediction! O Householder!
The love a mother has for her child and the love of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta) for his followers can be called ultimate;

nothing could surpass it. Yet, the means by which he caused them to strike themselves, the complaints they voiced, and his chasing, beating, and hurling of them were, in fact, expedient methods of conversion and words of proclamation.
From this, one knows the [teachings of the] Three Vehicles.
The expounding of the Dharma is the immutable standard of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, regarding the Buddha [from "next there is again a Buddha" to] "good in the beginning, middle, and end," the treatise states:
When the first Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows to illuminate the eastern direction, it was by means of the six sense faculties of the root-body (*indriya-kāya*).

Because all [the worlds] move their brows while this alone remains still, and because the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) in the ten directions is all still while this alone moves, light is emitted from within the stillness to reach the moving places.
Thus one knows that although the root-body (indriya-kāya) and the vessel-world are divided into subject and object, there is no distinction between the sentient and the insentient.
In this context, the root-body is described by means of the Buddha; the Buddha is named "Sun and Moon."
The text mentions "Lamp-Light" twice, saying: "Next there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa; next there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Why is this? It is because it seeks to demonstrate that once the sense-faculties and the physical body are complete, they necessarily span the three periods of time.
To be exhaustive, it states that twenty thousand Buddhas all share the same name and the same surname.
The single family name is Bharadvāja; "Bharadvāja" means one of sharp faculties and understanding.

If the sutra speaks of a thousand Buddhas in one direction, it implies ten thousand Buddhas in the ten directions, because this sutra demonstrates that the light shines universally throughout the ten directions.

Thus, it mentions ten thousand Buddhas—the first and the last—meaning that these twenty thousand are not only identical in name, but their characters are also the same. It is not merely that the names are identical.
The "specific name" (zì) is the same, and furthermore, the clan name (xìng) is the same. Those with the same clan name share the same ancestral lineage;
those with the same specific name share the same meaning; those with the same personal name (míng) share the same substance.

When these three are identical, the ten titles are fully realized, and it is impossible for the teaching—excellent in its beginning, middle, and end—not to be identical as well. However, regarding the vessel-world (the physical realm), the Buddha merely manifests...
While the light of the eastern direction is merely an example, as it pertains to the root-body (*mūla-kāya*), it manifests illumination throughout all places.

After forty-odd years of maturing his disciples, he then gathered at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa an assembly of arhats— both those still in training and those beyond it—
as well as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, nāgas, and other holy beings, and emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows the light of the Middle Way.
The light shone forth, revealing eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was being preached.
The characteristics of all phenomena have been eternally quiescent from the very beginning; they cannot be expressed in words.
"Sublime" (*miao*) means supremely sublime and inconceivable. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust its meaning, just like the *udumbara* flower.
The *udumbara* flower appears but once in an aeon; it is an auspicious lotus. This flower is as difficult to encounter as it is to meet a Buddha.

That which is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma) is not like the "lotuses" found in other sutras, which either take the blooming above the water as their metaphor or signify the simultaneity of cause and effect.
It refers rather to the Middle Way within the light of the mark between the eyebrows.
This is the light [of the Buddha]. To represent the appearance of the Buddha illuminating the East: "East" signifies the beginning of the sun and the initial birth of all things;
it serves to symbolize that this assembly marks the beginning of the preaching of the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). As for the eighteen thousand worlds:
having practiced through cultivation over kalpas across these eighteen realms, the Buddha-light finally manifests here; therefore, the East is used to represent this.
There were also twelve thousand bhikṣus, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
two thousand bhikṣuṇīs led by Mahāprajāpatī with their retinue of six thousand;

and eighty thousand great bodhisattvas—whether twenty thousand, two thousand, six thousand, or eighty thousand—to represent the two vehicles, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the six [perfections].

He has attained the eight liberations. As for why he does not designate a leader, it is because this assembly of mine consists purely of the true and real, without further branches or leaves—just as the twenty thousand Buddhas of the Sun-Moon-Lamp Brightness were of the same name and the same clan.
Wherever the Buddha’s light shines, there is nowhere it does not pervade; yet only those who have attained the Way perceive it, while the sentient beings of the six realms do not.
Within the light, they were not even aware of it themselves. This sutra brings the three vehicles together to return to the One Vehicle.
Maitreya is the Buddha of the future, and Mañjuśrī is the teacher of Buddhas; therefore, these two serve as the primary figures who pose the questions and provide the answers.
Śāriputra receives the prediction of enlightenment to open the beginning, and Samantabhadra exhorts and inspires to bring it to its conclusion. Mañjuśrī...
He proclaimed that when the past Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he emitted light and manifested auspicious signs no different from those of the present;
this demonstrates that there is no difference in the Dharma between former Buddhas and later Buddhas. The Buddha is the father of all sentient beings;
when the eight princes heard that their father had left the household life, they followed him to practice the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), whereby their eight consciousnesses were transformed.
To practice the pure and holy life (*brahmacarya*), he remained on this seat for sixty minor *kalpas* without rising;
thus he fulfilled the six *pāramitās* without leaving that place. This sutra is called the *Svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*, the *Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means of the Dharma-Sound*.
"Svādhiṣṭhāna" (Svada) means revolving and mutually encompassing so as to return to one; "skillful means" means attaining the meaning while forgetting the words.
Speech does not become obstructed by the traces of names, marks, calculations, or enumerations.
Once these two dhāraṇīs are attained, the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra will manifest with brilliant clarity. The "Introductory Chapter" concludes.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Two: The Expedient Means.
At that time, the World-Honored One... [up to] ...that which cannot be known.
The Commentary says: The Buddha, because the wisdom of all Buddhas is inconceivable, manifested the white tuft of hair through wondrous skillful means.
The marks of this radiance enter the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings; thus, all practitioners seek it and attain it themselves, which is called the "Gate of Wisdom.
Yet, as this is the realm of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), how could those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) lineage be able to enter it?
When Vimalakīrti heard that to the east, beyond lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers, there was a world...
The world-system was named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa, and its Buddha was named Sumeru-dīpa-rāja.
That Buddha was eighty-four thousand yojanas tall, and his lion throne was eighty-four thousand yojanas high, being the most exquisitely adorned of all.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti manifested his supernatural powers, and immediately that Buddha dispatched twenty-two thousand lion thrones.

The high, wide, magnificent, and pure seats entered the room of Vimalakīrti—seats such as the great bodhisattvas, the great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and others had never seen before. Śāriputra said, "It is unprecedented!
How can such a small room contain these high and wide seats without obstructing the chamber of Vaiśālī? Śāriputra stood there in amazement.
He reflected that the obstruction had arisen spontaneously within himself, and was not the fault of the chamber in Vaiśālī.
When the youth Sudhana arrived before Maitreya’s tower, through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Maitreya,
as well as by means of the inconceivable power of illusory wisdom and his ability to know all phenomena through illusory wisdom, he attained the sovereign mastery of all bodhisattvas.
By the power [of his supernatural faculties], he saw within the pavilion all the majestic and sovereign realms of adornment.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva withdrew his supernatural power, entered the pavilion, snapped his fingers to make a sound, and addressed Sudhana, saying:
"Son of good family, arise! Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). This is the causal condition for a bodhisattva’s wisdom that knows all dharmas."
The characteristics manifested by the aggregates are such that their intrinsic nature is like an illusion, a dream, a shadow, and an image;
none of them are established. At that time, Sudhana heard the sound of a finger-snap and arose from samādhi, seeing various realms.
This realization of accomplishment by Sudhana occurred in the mere instant of a finger-snap through his own self-awareness, and was not due to the power of Maitreya’s tower.
To discuss this, the gateway to the wisdom of all Buddhas is inherently difficult to understand and difficult to enter;
it is certainly not something that śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can know.
Why is this? (Up to: so as to cause them to be free from all attachments.
The Treatise says: Because all sentient beings possess a nature of awakening that is itself without self-nature, they are unable to know this lack of self-nature for themselves;
this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). If one knows this lack of self-nature, ignorance is immediately extinguished and the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*) is perfected.

Although it is said that this awakening does not depend on another, it nevertheless must rely upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) as a condition. Therefore, when the Buddha was about to preach the Dharma, he first spoke these words:
Though one draws near to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, such meditative concentration and contemplative insight are merely expedient means for drawing near;
though one possesses the myriad practices of the six perfections, these are for the purpose of nurturing and bringing to fulfillment.

All of this is for the sake of accord and compliance, rather than being the actual cultivation and realization. Therefore, it is further said: "To exhaustively practice the immeasurable path-dharmas of all Buddhas with courageous vigor."
At the beginning, in the Deer Park, the Venerable Vīra first taught the Hīnayāna for those of inferior faculties, clarifying that both the mind and its objects exist.
Next, he taught the Dharmalakṣaṇa Mahāyāna for those of middling faculties, clarifying that while objects are empty, the mind exists, according to the principle of Vijñaptimātra;
because their faculties were still inferior, they were unable to fully enter the equality of true emptiness, so he made such statements. Thereafter, he [taught] for those of superior faculties...

The *Mūlamadhyamaka-śāstra* states that the Mahāyāna is characterized by signlessness (*animitta*), wherein both object and mind are realized as empty, equal, and of a single flavor; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

It is like a person splitting wood: one first uses a fine wedge and subsequently a coarse wedge. Therefore, it is further said: "That which is taught according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand in its underlying intention (*abhiprāya*)."
"Why is this so? (up to) "The Buddha has fully accomplished [them].
The Commentary states: The scriptural phrase "Why is this so? is an expression that reiterates the meaning of the preceding section of the sūtra. There are three aspects to the meaning of the sūtra:
namely, the Tathāgata’s *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means), *jñāna* (knowledge), and *darśana* (insight) *pāramitā*, which refers to what is taught according to what is appropriate for each occasion.

That which is difficult to understand through intention is this: what is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—vast, profound, immeasurable, and unimpeded—is precisely the manifestation of light from the ūrṇā-kośa (the hair-treasure) to reveal the lands of both ordinary beings and sages.

What is called the powers, the fearlessnesses, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the samādhis that penetrate the boundless is precisely entering the locus of the Immeasurable Meaning.
It is this: the body and mind are unmoving in samādhi. All unprecedented dharmas are accomplished by means of these three kinds;
how much more so when there are immeasurable and boundless [dharmas], all of which are fully accomplished.
Therefore it is said, "Śāriputra, to speak in brief. "In brief" is a term used to provide a general summary.
"Cease, Śāriputra... [until] the ultimate equality of beginning and end.
The Commentary says: When the Buddha knew the time had come for him to speak, he said, "Cease; there is no need to speak further. These words were indirect while his intention was direct;
he provoked them with words of exhortation. If they did not exert themselves and rouse their spirits, they would be unable to deeply contemplate all phenomena.
The Dharma is the true mark (*dharmatā*). Regarding the true mark of all phenomena, to say it has "such a mark" refers to the mark of arising while being non-arising.
Since there is no arising and yet no non-arising, there is nothing by which to name it; one can only say "it is thus" (*tathatā*).
While it is appropriate to speak of its "mark" as being "thus," it is further elaborated that its nature, essence, function, activity, causes, conditions, and karmic retributions are all likewise.
What is meant by this name? It is said: these nine kinds of meanings arise necessarily at the same time; within a single *kṣaṇa*, there is no sequence of before or after.
Therefore, the conclusion of the passage states: "The beginning and the end are ultimately equal. The term "equal" (*pingdeng*) means "simultaneous. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"I teach the meaning of *kṣaṇa* as the non-arising of all phenomena; that which is about to arise already exists."
I do not preach this cessation to the foolish; rather, through these verses, one contemplates nine meanings.
If these accord like the joining of two tally-sticks, then the non-arising of all phenomena is suchness in its nature (*svabhāva*) and suchness in its essence (*ātman*).

When I speak of the meaning of *kṣaṇa* (moment), it refers to suchness in its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), suchness in its powers (*bala*), and suchness in its activities (*karman*). Question: Is there a scriptural basis for these three meanings being identical within a single *kṣaṇa*? Answer: [Yes].

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) abide for only a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), how much less could there be such things as 'activity' (*kāritra*) or an 'agent' (*kartṛ*)?
To speak of their arising as activity or as the exertion of an agent is impossible.

Indeed, when the characteristics of arising in a single moment and its activity and agency are fully present, it is clear that these three meanings exist within a single moment; thus, they must arise simultaneously.
That which exists ceases; thus it has such causes, such conditions, such fruits, and such retributions.
Only when that which is about to arise ceases can it be said that the beginning and the end are equal.

This is not taught for the sake of the foolish, for it is a most rare and extraordinary Dharma that only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaustively realize. Therefore, the verse in the following text says:
The term "World Hero" (Lokavīra) is immeasurable; it is precisely because the assemblies of the Three Vehicles, as well as devas and humans, all submit in awe before him.
That the Sui monk Zhiyi explained it through nine meanings and the Tang monk Kuiji further condensed them into five phrases is not at all surprising.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
