attached to play and sport, they may fall and be consumed by fire. As the subsequent passage states:
"Sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress, and are thus burned by the fires of the triple world."

As for what burns this dwelling, how can it be explained? It is because of this: they do not know suffering, they do not know the origin of suffering, and they do not know the cause by which the life of wisdom is lost.
Though they pass through birth and death, or even encounter the age of a Buddha, they do not know or hear the Dharma;
therefore, it is said that they likewise do not know what is fire and what is [the dwelling].
To take "shelter" means what? It refers to the loss of one's direction, running about to play while merely looking toward one's father, as stated in the subsequent passage:
"In these three realms, one runs hither and thither; though encountering great suffering, one does not regard it as a calamity.

Because one turns one's back on light and casts oneself into darkness, it is called "hither and thither"; because the cycle of birth and death proceeds with such rapidity, it is called "running about. And thus...
Because he gives rise to views and attachment within [the world], it is called "playful" (*līlā*).
At that time, the householder (until: "all shall be given to you").
The Commentary says: The Buddha appears in the triple world in order to deliver sentient beings; if he were to abandon skillful means (*upāya*), then the One Great Matter would [not be accomplished].
The causal conditions were also nearly exhausted, and thus both father and sons would have perished;
therefore, he said, "I and my sons will surely be burned," and so first ordered them out of the suffering before preaching the true Way.
Thus it is said that one should employ skillful means to enable the sons to escape this harm, as stated in the subsequent text: "Although [the father] possesses strength and has nothing to fear..."
It is not that he does not use them; rather, it is through wisdom and skillful means that he delivers sentient beings from the burning house.

Knowing that the minds of all sentient beings have various desires, he speaks according to what is appropriate for them; therefore it is said: "The father knows the former inclinations of his sons, each having their own preferences...
[he says] 'Come out quickly as soon as possible, and I shall give you everything according to whatever you desire.'"
As the subsequent text states: "He preaches for them the Śrāvaka-yāna, Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and Buddha-yāna, praising the three vehicles to entice them toward liberation from suffering.
It further says: "You must not dwell with complacency within the triple world; do not crave coarse and inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
Quickly emerge from the triple world, and you shall attain the three vehicles. These three vehicles are all praised by the noble ones."
This refers to the "exclamations" and so forth.
At that time, the sons [were filled with] joy and leaped for gladness.

The Commentary states: regarding the distinctions in the modes of cultivation and realization within this treatise, [it concerns] diligence and laxity, transcendence and ascent, and their respective sequences.
Therefore, it is said that their minds are each courageous and sharp, pushing one another along the common path of the Eightfold Noble Path;

because there are differences in speed, it is said they "vie with one another to gallop and run" as they strive to exit the burning house. To drive like a chariot is called "galloping" (che-chi), while to walk on foot is called "running" (zou).
By means of this, they escape the burning house of the triple world; hence the following passage says: "They seek nirvana for themselves."
Seeking natural wisdom and seeking all-knowledge—this refers to those named Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those of the Buddha-vehicle who have emerged from the burning house.
Indeed, having emerged from the perilous path of the triple world at the place where the three vehicles converge, they observe and reflect upon themselves through the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, it is said they are "in the midst of a four-way crossroads. Although their delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) have been eliminated, [their delusions of] cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)...
He remains as he is and is not called "in the open air" because his contemplation of the three realms has already been exhausted;
he is said to be "in the open air" because he dwells in the fruit of the path and does not advance further; he is said to be "serene" because he is no longer constrained by views or afflictions;
and he is said to be "joyful" because he gives rise to the perception of peace and security within *nirvāṇa*. As the text below states: "The Tathāgata acts for the sake of all sentient beings."
It is when the father sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings emerging from the suffering, fear, and perilous paths of the triple world through the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching,
attaining the bliss of nirvana;
at that time, the sons and others arrive to attend and protect him.
The treatise says: The two carts of the sheep and the deer are small rather than large, while the ox, sheep, and deer are large rather than identical.
Now, since there are neither the two carts of the sheep and the deer, nor the three carts of the sheep, the deer, and the ox, it is said that they are given only one great cart.
Śāriputra, having already doubted whether the Buddha would deliver [beings] solely by means of the Lesser Vehicle, [conceived of] the Buddha as being singular.

Furthermore, there are those who harbor doubts that outside of this vehicle there are two other distinct vehicles, or that we have likewise entered the *dharmatā* [the nature of phenomena] under the notion that within the One Buddha Vehicle there are three distinct vehicles. Now, none of these exist; there is only the One Buddha Vehicle.
Because this vehicle is supreme and boundless, it is said that its carriage is high and wide; because it is adorned by the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*), it is said to be magnificent.
Because it is protected and shielded by the *dhāraṇīs* adorned with jewels, it is said to have "surrounding railings.

Because it transforms beings through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), it is said to have "bells suspended on all four sides. Because it universally covers all with compassion and mercy, it is said to have "canopies spread above";
furthermore, because these acts of compassion and mercy are adorned with manifold virtues, it is said to be "also [adorned] with various rare and precious jewels."

It is further adorned and made firm through the four vows of compassion; thus it is said that jeweled cords are interlaced, using the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to harmonize and gladden them like flowers.
It is like a necklace (*hāra*) because supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are used to startle and move them;

thus it is said that various flower necklaces hang down. Because of the softness of the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), it is said that a layered, elegant seat is spread out for the sake of stability.
Because his body is the ultimate security of the primary truth (*paramārtha*), it is said that he is "placed upon a vermilion pillow"; the pillow is used to support his head.
In the Western Regions, pillows are stuffed with cotton inside and covered with red leather on the outside; thus they are called "vermilion pillows.
Because he is pure, tamed, and fully endowed with both merit and wisdom, it is said that he is "drawn by white oxen" whose skin and color are full and clean.
Because his countenance is withered yet his bones are firm, he is capable of great undertakings; therefore it is said that his physical form is beautiful and he possesses great strength.

Because he attains *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) swiftly through concentration (*samādhi*) of wisdom and insight (*prajñā*), it is said that his gait is level and upright, as swift as the wind, such that all Māras and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are merely at his command. Therefore it is said that he has many servants who attend and protect him.

As the subsequent text states: "All the requisites for the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and enjoyments of all Buddhas are of a single characteristic and a single kind;
they are praised by the noble ones and are able to produce the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss. This is it.
Why is this so? (Up to: ...and provide them with great chariots. The treatise says:

Because the adornments of concentration and wisdom are equal, and because [the goal] is equal, it is therefore said that there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*) to cause all to become Buddhas;
hence it is said: "I have such seven-jeweled great chariots, their number being immeasurable; you should regard them with an impartial mind."
It is not appropriate to treat them differently from one another, as the following passage states:
"I possess an immeasurable and boundless treasury of the Buddha-dharma consisting of the power of wisdom and fearlessness; all these sentient beings are my children.
Thus, he bestows the Mahāyāna equally upon them so that no one shall attain extinction alone. Even if, at first, there were no skillful means, directly...
The preservation of one's entire life is more important than mere playthings;

thus, even when one has already obtained such playthings, they are not considered wasted, let alone when one employs original expedient means to pull others out of the burning house—how could that be in vain?

This uses the rescue from hardship through expedient means as an illustration; how much more so the case of directly preserving one's entire life? Therefore, it is said that having escaped the disaster of fire, one preserves its—
How could my life and body not be free from falsehood? Why is this? If I had merely preserved my own life and body, I would already have obtained objects of pleasure;

how much more so when, through skillful means, I rescue others from that burning house! Even if one possessed sufficient wealth and impartial affection, yet used skillful means only to extricate them from distress, it would still not be false;
how much less so when, with abundant wealth and equal desire to benefit them, one acts in this way?

How could there be any falsehood? Therefore it is said that he knows for himself his wealth is immeasurable, and wishing to benefit his sons, he provides them with great carts, as stated in the following passage: "The Tathāgata is likewise; he is without falsehood.
He guides sentient beings and subsequently delivers them by means of the Great Vehicle alone. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses the immeasurable..."
It is this treasury of all dharmas, characterized by the power of wisdom and fearlessness.
The Buddha told Śāriputra (up to) "distinguishingly teaching the three.
The commentary says: Seeking natural wisdom that is not obtained from others is superior to that of the śrāvakas; however, it is [only] when one delights in solitary excellence [that one attains it].

If one’s tranquility cannot simultaneously encompass goodness, one is inferior to a bodhisattva; for a pratyekabuddha deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena, which is why this is called the dharma of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, they do not receive it from others and delight in solitary goodness, like a deer that does not rely on others, yet their power is less than that of an ox.
A Buddha universally knows all phenomena; this omniscience is precisely the wisdom of a Buddha.
The term "self-enlightened" (svayambhū) refers to the Buddha’s wisdom, which is self-arisen wisdom;
self-arisen wisdom is teacherless wisdom, and teacherless wisdom is the wisdom of one who has no teacher—this is the sequential explanation of the terms.

Pratyekabuddhas are also called self-enlightened, yet they lack omniscience (sarvajñatā) and possess only wisdom (*prajñā*). To use an analogy of oxen: it is because their strength is greater than that of sheep or deer.

Furthermore, although the Mahāyāna is obtained from others, because this Dharma abides in its own station and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant, one need not harbor resentment toward those upon whom it depends.
Yet, before emerging from the burning house, even the Mahāyāna was categorized alongside the sheep and deer vehicles as three;
once they have attained equality, there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. This is why it is [so designated].

Nevertheless, the Sūtra states: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, believe and accept it, and diligently cultivate it with vigor, seeking all-knowledge, the Buddha-knowledge, self-existent knowledge, teacherless knowledge, and the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, powers, and fearlessnesses—then even ordinary persons can realize these through direct experience. From this, we know that the Buddha-vehicle is inconceivable.

The *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states: "It is just as when the chick of the king of birds, the kalaviṅka, is still within its egg and its beak has not yet emerged, it already utters the exquisite song of the kalaviṅka;

likewise, those bodhisattvas within the egg of the Buddha-dharma, though they have not yet destroyed the view of self and have not yet emerged from the triple world, are nonetheless able to produce the exquisite sound of the Buddha-dharma."
The Buddha, wishing to proclaim this again, [described] the manifestations of transformation as being thus.
The commentary states: The prose of the sūtra summarizes the general meaning and is therefore concise; the verses, however, recount the specific events in detail.
Nevertheless, the characteristics of the three realms do not transcend the three poisons of ignorance and the ten proclivities of varying sharpness and dullness.

Malign views, defilements, inverted perceptions, and subtle delusions—within the vessel-world they cause the turmoil of the five turbidities, and within the root-body they bind one with the eight sufferings.
Generally, these are illustrated by the metaphor of various kinds of malign views;
as the sutra says, "the house is ancient and moreover suddenly dilapidated," meaning that transformation occurs through secret shifting, such that one is unaware of impermanence.
When the foundation is pressed down and the steps collapse, ignorance serves as the foundation and the remaining conditions serve as the steps;

the foundation is the base of the hall and the steps are the tiers of the stairway. Because they arise from one's own consciousness through successive stages of conditional dependence, they are called "steps.
Because they ultimately undergo transformation and extinction, they are called "collapsing. When the walls crumble and split apart, this refers to the four great elements.
The mud and mire that have been left behind represent the emaciation of the skin; the thatch and straw that have fallen into disorder represent the discarded hair;
the rafters and eaves that have cracked and detached represent the decayed and missing teeth;

and the surrounding walls that are crooked and filled with all manner of filth represent the thirty-six constituent parts of the body—the hundred members and nine apertures—where dust and impurities intermingle such that not a single part remains pure.

Is it not because sentient beings are so deeply attached to the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that [the Buddha] speaks of this in detail, to show that all phenomena are illusory and deceptive, and cannot be relied upon as stable or enduring?

As for the five hundred people dwelling therein, they are those comprised within the five destinies (*pañcagati*) who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The owls, crows, eagles, vultures, ravens, magpies, and pigeons...

The pigeon represents the poison of greed; its extreme form is procreation and mating, while its mild form is seizing and plundering. The transmission of saliva and the movement of the eyes represent the poison of hatred;
this includes vipers, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes. The chameleon, the centipede, the weasel, the wildcat, and the mole represent the poison of delusion.
If a chameleon eats seven *jin* of cinnabar and grinds it to apply to its body, the poison will be extinguished upon contact with a hundred [others].
The "feet" refer to the millipede, which has many feet yet moves slowly; the "weasels and rats" refer to the flying squirrel (*pūyīyóu*), which possesses five skills yet fails in them all.
The phrase about various evil insects running to and fro in crosswise fashion summarizes the preceding arguments.
As for the foul-smelling places of excrement and urine where filth overflows and dung beetles and other insects swarm upon them, it is because...

The preceding [passage] clarifies that anger and delusion arise from greed; this [passage] clarifies that greed and craving exist because of delusion. Because one cannot distinguish between the pure and the impure, it is delusion;
because one takes pleasure in attachment and does not relinquish it, it is greed. As for the foxes, wolves, and jackals chewing and trampling [the corpse]:
the fox is greedy yet suspicious, the wolf is greedy yet fierce, and the jackal is greedy yet deluded. Suspicion is a form of delusion.
To distinguish the wolf is to resent it; this refers to distinguishing the mixed characteristics of the three poisons (*trivisa*).
To chew and trample upon it refers to being attached to impure objects (*aśubha-viṣaya*) without weariness, and treading upon them without separation.

To gnaw at corpses until bones and flesh are scattered in disorder refers to calculating and clinging to the impermanent body (*anitya-śarīra*) without relinquishing it, remaining in turmoil and failing to restrain oneself. It is for these reasons that...
When a pack of dogs competes to seize and snatch food, they fight and struggle over it out of greed;

when they tear at one another, snarling and barking, they do so out of hatred. Since they thus pursue and contend for such impure objects within this impermanent body, this is the characteristic of delusion.
These constitute the characteristics of the three poisons in equal measure, as well as the various fetters and afflictions.
Even up to the eighty-four thousand afflictions, all arise from the specific characteristics and the combined characteristics of the three poisons;
the phrase "the house is thus terrifying and transformed" is also a term used for such a state.
"In every place there are [immeasurable terrors]. The Commentary states:
"The first ten verses primarily describe the five dull afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), namely greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt;

whereas these ten [subsequent] verses primarily describe the five sharp afflictions (*anuśaya*), namely the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of [clinging to] views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*)."

"Taking precepts" refers to the fetter of attachment to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Because the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇakleśa*) universally take the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) as their objects, it is said that they exist everywhere.
However, ghosts and spirits (*yakṣa-rākṣasa*) are used as a metaphor because they possess supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and intelligence (*prajñā*);

whereas birds and beasts are used as a metaphor for the dull afflictions (*mṛdukleśa*) because they lack both supernatural powers and intelligence. As for "chi-mei-wang-liang," *chi* means "to separate," and *mei*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
The terms "mei" (obscure) and "wangliang" (phantoms/spirits) both refer generally to all ghostly entities; they share the same dharma-nature.
All arise from departing [from reality] and failing to maintain it, being obscure and lacking clarity, appearing as phantoms without emerging [into truth], and being dualistic rather than unitary.
Because they rely on various views, they possess the sixty-two [wrong] views. Thus, the yakṣas—swift-moving spirits who eat human flesh—deny [the existence of] the [Three Jewels].
Regarding those who hold that virtuous causes and effects exist, they maintain that eating harmful insects constitutes a negative karmic cause;

whereas those who deny evil causes and effects, such as the non-Buddhist Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, claim that all phenomena are of a nature of annihilation and emptiness, and thus there is no retribution for birth and death.
As for the production of offspring through conception and lactation, these are worldly phenomena that arise from causes of their own kind, producing effects of their own kind.
"Self-concealment and protection" refers to the "concealment" (garbha) of the effect within the cause and the "protection" (rakṣā) of its inevitable non-loss.
This statement clarifies that the causality of good and evil is as clear as the light of day for the benefit of living beings; it exposes the evil of the heterodox paths and their false views.
Possessing these false views in full, they are satiated by them; with these false views spreading like creeping vines, they blaze forth, creating contentious arguments to trap people in [suffering].
The miserable realms are as terrifying as the sound of battle; the kumbhāṇḍas are fearsome, yet those who are victorious through their tainted virtues are able to be born in superior places.
Among the six heavens of the desire realm, at their highest point, there is the appearance of earthen mounds where these spirits crouch and squat;
sometimes they rise one or two feet above the ground, and this is their form.

The realm refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). To roam about, wander, and indulge in wanton play means to come and go within the three realms, ascending or descending, remaining attached and failing to emerge from them, finding entertainment without satiety.
To seize a dog by its two hind legs and strike it until it loses its voice is to slander [the truth that] suffering and its origin do not exist.
To place one’s foot upon the dog’s neck and take pleasure in terrifying it is to slander [the truth that] cessation does not exist.

The Way is like that of the non-Buddhist Vairaṭīputra Viśvāmitra, who claimed that the Way need not be sought, but that once the kalpas of birth-and-death have passed, suffering will naturally be exhausted.
He used the analogy of a dog to illustrate suffering, whereby one perceives suffering and abandons its origin, just as two feet are mutually dependent.
Now, however, by asserting that the Way need not be sought, he renders the teaching of suffering and its origin ineffective.

It is like seizing someone by both feet and throwing them down until they lose their voice. To cultivate the Path and subsequently realize cessation is like the head being above and the feet being below.

Now, however, to believe that the exhaustion of suffering constitutes the attainment of the Path, and to use this as a pretext for weariness with suffering so as to indulge in self-indulgence, is like placing one's feet upon one's own neck to frighten a dog while seeking one's own pleasure.

Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large; they reckon the three periods of time vertically as "self," which is called "tall," and they reckon the five aggregates horizontally as "self," which is called "large.
Because they wear the garment of shamelessness, they are said to be "naked"; because they lack the dharma of purity, they are said to be "black";
because they lack the substance of merit, they are said to be "emaciated"; and because they stubbornly cling to their own views, they are so described.

Because they have never for a moment abandoned their views, it is said that they dwell eternally therein; they raise their voices to proclaim [their doctrines], regarding evil as the fruit they hope to attain and seeking only sustenance.
Their throats are like needles, so that while their breath is but a thread, their lives remain precarious yet prolonged.
These are those who perceive the non-perception (asaṃjñin) as impermanent, yet reckon it to be Nirvāṇa. Those whose heads are like the head of an ox are severed.
"Constantly" refers to the two horns of a cow, representing the two extremes. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"People of the borderlands who have human bodies but oxen's heads—those who calculate [reality] through nihilism do not cultivate wholesome causes, like eating human flesh; those who calculate [reality] through eternalism do not seek the cessation of suffering, like eating dog meat.
Because they rely on various views, they are in a state of chaotic disorder and unable to manage themselves; therefore, they are called 'heads'."

The disheveled hair represents the breaking of permanence by means of impermanence, and the breaking of impermanence by means of permanence; thus it is said that they are cruel, violent, and devoid of wisdom.

Because they nourish themselves with food and drink, they are said to be oppressed by hunger and thirst. Because of the back-and-forth of contentious debate, they are said to be shrieking and running about.
Such are the characteristics of the afflictions of the desire realm, all of which are of a nature associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because they constantly lack the flavor of the Way and are deeply attached to false views such that they cannot emerge from them on their own, it is said that they are "in urgent hunger,
looking out through the windows in all four directions. The phrase "such immeasurable perils and fears" is a concluding statement that summarizes the preceding meaning.
"This dilapidated old house" (up to) "raising one's voice and crying out.
The Commentary says: Now, the triple world is that which the Buddha manifests through his transformations;

because he first resolved his mind on the vow to deliver all sentient beings, he said, "This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person," [referring to] myself at the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
The Buddha has constantly instructed you all that you must subdue the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

Because I have responded to conditions in other realms and the spiritual capacity for your response has been exhausted, the five turbidities have now arisen; hence it is said that "those people have recently emerged.
As stated in the text below, "frequently manifesting nirvana" is precisely the meaning of "leaving the house. That the flames on all four sides simultaneously blaze up together signifies this.

Because the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena arise as the four perversions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings, which continue to increase in succession, it is said that they are "blazing together.
Because the life-force has been severed and the sense faculties naturally decay, it is said that "the rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars crack and split with a roar;
the breath is extinguished and the body dissolves. Because [the aggregates] are crushed and fall away, it is said that "the walls collapse and the foundations crumble."
At that time, as various views were in turmoil and could not be stilled, it is said that they raised their voices and cried out loudly.
From the vultures and eagles to the various birds, there were many such hardships and difficulties.
The Commentary says: This demonstrates the signs of the fire arising in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). The *kumbhāṇḍas* and others were terrified and panicked.

The "terrified" refers to the *kumbhāṇḍas* who hold evil views; because they are bound by the light flight of craving and attached to these evil views, it is said they cannot emerge from them on their own.
As for the "wild beasts and venomous insects hiding in holes," the meditative concentration of the four dhyānas is like a hole;
those who are burned—such as those who have not reached the state beyond the gate—are not overtaken by the fierce flames, just as one in meditative concentration is not.
Within this [state], the coarse and debased evils of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are not seen.

Although the piśāca demons also dwell therein, and though there is no fierce flame within these cavities, there is still the affliction of heat; so too, although the fourth dhyāna lacks the evils of the desire realm, it possesses the subtle suffering of attachment to its flavor (*āsvāda*).
Thus, because craving and [the object] mutually oppress one another, as if they were drinking and devouring each other, it is said: [as follows].

To harm one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, refers to the arising of various views within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which prevents the production of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*);

remaining silent like one who drinks blood and being attached to the joy of the five factors (*pañcāṅga-prīti*) like eating flesh—these characteristics of the jackal and its kind represent craving (*rāga*).
Since craving for the desire realm has already been severed by the concentration of the future stage (*anāgāmya*), it is said that both are simultaneously abandoned.

The various great, evil beasts that previously died and now compete to devour [the body], with foul-smelling smoke billowing and filling the four quarters, represent those who have lightly abandoned greed but whose heavy attachments have not yet departed—like evil beasts devouring a jackal.
The circling of evil perceptions is like the foul-smelling smoke that fills [the space]. Herein, he further demonstrates the appearance of fire arising in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, having become weary of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they emerge from it and turn toward the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Through the contemplation of weariness, they perceive the coarse objects of the form realm as being like centipedes or venomous snakes that have been driven out of their holes by fire; thus, they desire to contemplate the dharmas of the formless realm.

Because one who attains concentration in the formless realm must necessarily extinguish the conditions of the form realm, it is said that they "follow what they take as food. Moreover, as for the various hungry ghosts (*preta*) with heads...

Regarding those who ascend to the realm of the "Blazing Fire" (Ābhāsvara): although they are formless and non-percipient and dwell at the very pinnacle [of existence], they still undergo arising and ceasing without cessation;

thus, they have not yet transcended all suffering. Why is this? Because their minds involve diverse thoughts, it is called the suffering of birth (*jāti-duḥkha*); because every thought-moment does not abide, it is called the suffering of aging (*jarā-duḥkha*);

because their activities are agitated and obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called the suffering of illness (*vyādhi-duḥkha*); and because they fall back from concentration for these reasons, it is called the suffering of death (*maraṇa-duḥkha*). Thus they seek...
If one cannot attain meditative concentration, this is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; if it necessarily becomes an obstacle, this is the suffering of encountering those one hates;

the four aggregates are the suffering of the proliferation of the five aggregates; and because one is attached to this concentration and cannot bear to leave it, this is the suffering of separation from the beloved.
Because there is no wine of the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), one speaks of hunger and thirst; because one has not yet escaped saṃsāra, one speaks of wandering about in distress. Its...
"The house is thus exceedingly terrifying; the harms of poison, fire, and various calamities are not one"—this is the phrase used to describe its bonds.
At that time, the master of the house [remained there] playing and sporting without ceasing.
The Treatise says: "Because I have safely emerged from this gate that was being burned, it is said that 'I am standing outside the gate and hear the calamity of the burning house.

This expresses the intention of how one is to be saved. Since the preceding text already stated, 'I, with the Buddha-eye, observe the suffering of sentient beings in the six realms,' why is it now said, 'I hear someone say'? It is replied: [This is a rhetorical question introducing the following explanation.]
This is a parable. As for the statement in the parable that "someone was heard," it is merely an introductory phrase intended to lead into what follows.
If it were said that the Buddha’s eye perceives the six realms of existence, that would be a description of the reality as taught by the Dharma.
The prior mention of entering this house while playing refers to how the characteristics of the three realms arise from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Because of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there is birth and death. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "From ultimate non-existence, one establishes ultimate existence.
Thus, the Buddha sighed with great compassion and spoke; he uttered words of admonition and instruction because [beings] were startled into [the realization of suffering].
Therefore, the calamities and difficulties described—such as malevolent spirits and ghosts—are truly terrifying. The house is [in peril] because of the fire.

Regarding the statement that the calamitous fire spreads like creeping vines: since suffering arises from delusion and the house [of existence] has already been destroyed, one must therefore repair the house;

thus, it is said that the various sufferings proceed in succession. Furthermore, within dependent origination, ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth, thereby forming an accumulation of the three types of suffering;
hence, it is said that they continue without interruption. This refers to what are called the venomous snakes, vipers, and adders.
The various yakṣas and all their evil views, as well as the manifestations of the three poisons, arose again in chaotic profusion; thus,

although the Buddha used skillful means to entice and instruct them, they ultimately did not believe or accept his teachings, and so it is said that they still delight in and cling to play and sport without ceasing.
At that time, the elder... [leading them] to ultimate extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

The Treatise says: Those who were previously learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), each thinking they had already attained *nirvāṇa* by means of their own detachment from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the views of existence and non-existence (*astitva-nāstitva-dṛṣṭi*)—how could they have known the secret treasury of the Great *Nirvāṇa*, the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*)?

The treatise says: As stated in the *Māṇḍatya-sūtra*, the World-Honored One said: "If nirvāṇa were a self-existent entity, I, who now possess keen intelligence and sharp wisdom, would not fail to see it.

[The interlocutor asks: "The Buddha said that nirvāṇa truly exists; why then do you not see it? [The Master replies: "Because you have not yet attained the non-conceptual noble wisdom (*avikalpa-āryajñāna*), you are unable to see it.
Because it is subtle, it is not an object obtainable through the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); it is [attained] through the [wisdom of] reality (*bhūtārtha*)."
Because it is real, it cannot be attained through the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

If even the subtleties of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom of reflection cannot attain it, how could that which is merely called "liberation" by virtue of being free from delusion possibly attain it? Question:

When the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) are taught, one speaks only of the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). Are the Four Noble Truths complete within each of the Three Vehicles? Answer: Regarding the Four Noble Truths...
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these are called the Four Noble Truths, which are the common teaching for the three vehicles; they differ only according to the depth or shallowness of what is realized.

A Pratyekabuddha contemplates from ignorance up to old age and death as suffering and its origin, and contemplates from the exhaustion of ignorance up to the exhaustion of old age and death as cessation and the path. When a Bodhisattva contemplates the Four Truths, it is thus...
This is because there are differences between the sudden and gradual approaches regarding this single truth.
"I am the Dharma King" (up to) "...is not within the scope of one's own wisdom.
The treatise says: There are two kinds of faith: first, the faith that penetrates through wisdom; second, the faith that relies upon supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Wisdom...

Regarding those who have faith in its penetration—namely, that the wisdom of all-knowledge, the teacherless wisdom, and the spontaneous wisdom have all been fully accomplished—one has faith that the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, his preaching of the Dharma, his saving of sentient beings, and his entry into parinirvāṇa, from beginning to end, do not transcend the single limit of a kṣaṇa.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, you have entered this sūtra through faith; this is wisdom."
This is the faith of "penetrating through" (tō). That which relies on the faith of penetrating through is so called because it is an intellectual understanding based on emotion;

thus, the net of doubt is not removed. Furthermore, because one trusts the Buddha’s words, the Sūtra says: "The remaining śrāvakas, because they trust the Buddha’s words, follow this sūtra, as it is beyond the scope of their own wisdom.
This is the faith of penetrating through. Wang Xizhi of the Jin dynasty was renowned in the world for his skill in calligraphy.
His disciples all took his brushwork as their model. When Wang Xizhi was about to set his brush to paper, his hand forgot the brush and the brush forgot the technique;
his mind merged with the spirit, so that wherever his strokes and dots reached, their aesthetic expression was naturally complete.

Those who modeled themselves on his brushwork did not let their hands forget the brush nor their minds forget the characters. If they were unimpeded, they moved forward; if not, they stopped. All of this is called "calligraphy," just as it was for Xizhi.
Those who "follow" this represent the faith of penetrating through wisdom; those who "take it as their teacher" represent the faith of relying upon penetration. An old commentary states:
"This is because those of the two vehicles with indeterminate nature are now just beginning to accord with and give rise to faith.
Thus, even one of superior faculties like Śāriputra must first believe my words before gradually attaining realization—how much more so for other śrāvakas of indeterminate nature? This is an error.
Furthermore, from "Moreover, Śāriputra" to "The Lotus Sutra.
The commentary states: From "Moreover, Śāriputra" to "Do not preach this sutra," there are thirty-six verses in detail explaining the retribution obtained by those who slander the sutra.
What is called "this sutra" does not refer to words, chapters, titles, paper, ink, or script.

The "character" (word) is the very mind of all sentient beings. For those who receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and expound it—whether walking, sitting, lying down, bending, turning, looking up, or looking down—they do not allow other thoughts to dare interrupt it.
Therefore, to slander it by saying one does not believe it is to distrust that which is most intimate—the mind—and instead to trust material things; this is called being deluded.
Because those who are inverted and perverted must inevitably undergo transmigration, the Buddha spoke at length regarding its causes:

having been born in the hells, they experience all manner of suffering; yet when their karma for that realm is exhausted, they are born among the animals, where they again experience all manner of suffering.

Once the karma for that state is exhausted, they are born into the human realm; however, due to the karma that follows them, they remain muddled, ignorant, base, and dark, as is the nature of the world.
It is only natural that they harbor hatred and envy. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Ānanda, these sentient beings—having failed to maintain the rules of discipline, violated the bodhisattva precepts, and destroyed the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, as well as other sinful karmas—shall undergo burning for kalpas until their offenses are exhausted.
Thereafter, they receive the forms of various ghosts. Even when their karmic retribution as ghosts is finally spent, both their emotions and their perceptions..."
Only when they have attained emptiness do they encounter their original creditors in the world;

taking birth as animals, they repay those karmic debts from former lives. While they are thus repaying their prior debts as animals, if the creditor exceeds what was owed, these sentient beings will return to being human and reclaim that surplus.
This refers to those who slander the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Since the retribution for such offenses is thus, the *nirvāṇa* of the Buddhas and the self-mind of sentient beings are not two distinct things.

The Inexhaustible Layman’s Discourse says: "Once Śāriputra had realized the meaning of the skillful means of the Three Vehicles, his doubts and regrets were forever exhausted, and he knew with certainty that he would become a Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed him with words of secret protection before the devas, humans, brahmins, and the great assembly."

Within the assembly, he revealed his past lives, causing them to remember their original vows, and bestowed upon them the prediction that in a future age they would become buddhas named Padmaprabha, in an eon called Mahāratnavyūha.
As for what is meant by "great jewels," it is because in that land, bodhisattvas constitute the great jewels.
These bodhisattvas have all long planted the roots of virtue throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands [of eons].

Having purified and cultivated the Brahma-conduct in the presence of ten billion Buddhas is just like the present Maitreya Bodhisattva currently teaching and transforming the multitudes of those reborn in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven;
the matter is identical to his receiving the prediction of future descent to be born at the Dragon Flower tree.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli to symbolize pure radiance, and there are eight intersecting roads to symbolize the Eightfold Noble Path.
The paths demarcated by golden cords represent the essence of the precepts; the rows of trees made of the seven treasures represent the seven factors of enlightenment;
the lotus flowers supporting their feet represent the treading upon them; and the various colored flowers and fruits represent the pure karma of practice and understanding.

Such is the case with these external environments as well. Having received this prediction, Śāriputra and the twelve hundred who had attained mastery over their minds heard what they had never heard before.
Upon hearing this, everyone fell into doubt and perplexity. Śāriputra requested that the Buddha explain the underlying causes and conditions. The Buddha said:
"In the past, I have used parables and skillful means in my discourse on the Dharma, all for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas.
However, I shall now further clarify this meaning through another parable. There was once an elder whose years had declined; he represents the Buddha who is about to enter nirvana."
Panya’s house was vast and spacious, yet it had only a single door; this signifies that the Buddha-vehicle of the ten directions is non-dual and non-triple.
That five hundred people dwell within it signifies the sentient beings of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

That the halls and pavilions are decayed and ruined signifies there is nothing to behold. That the walls and partitions have collapsed signifies there is nothing to hear. That the bases of the pillars are rotten signifies—
If there is nothing below to support it, the beams and rafters will tilt and collapse, leaving nothing above to sustain them; if fire suddenly breaks out, sickness and suffering will arrive.
To be attached to play and sport is to be unaware of impending terror. The owls, crows, eagles, and vultures represent their predatory striking;
the crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons represent their clamorous lust; the vipers, snakes, adders, scorpions, and centipedes [represent their venomous nature].
The centipede is used to represent its poison; the *śatapadī* (hundred-legged lizard) to represent its agitation; the weasels, wildcats, and mice to represent their stealth and concealment;
the dung beetles and various insects to represent their filth; the foxes, wolves, and jackals to represent their greed;
the pack of dogs howling and barking to represent their strife; and the *yakṣas* vying with one another to represent their cruelty and the *pigeons*.
The *pūtana* demons signify their hollow hunger; the *preta* ghosts signify their burning affliction;
and the *piśāca* demons signify that while they originally intended to harm others, they themselves are also harmed by them. All such categories arise from the three poisons;
when ignorance increases, they become the eighty-four thousand afflictions. Yet, within the minuteness of a single body—

That they are thus fully endowed is entirely due to their attachment and longing; out of compassion for them, the Buddha delivers them from the burning house by means of the three vehicles and leads them forth.
He bestows upon them a single Great Precious Vehicle, drawn by white oxen, adorned with ornaments of pure, singular substance, and radiant with the marks of the myriad practices.
Thus they awaken to the principle of the parable and attain it through these words.
This preface explains why these śrāvakas were granted their successive predictions.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Four: "The Parable of the Faith and Understanding.
At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya... [until] "obtained without seeking."
The Treatise states: The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "If a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, they should purify their own mind;
as the mind becomes pure, so does the buddha-field become pure. This means that when the mind is empty, the buddha-field is empty.
The *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*) says, "Because one world is pure, many worlds are pure; because one world is empty, many worlds [are empty]."
Regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*), how is it known that what is called "emptiness" is purity? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Purity is the very meaning of emptiness.
Because sentient beings fear emptiness, [the Buddhas] speak of 'purity' as a means of averting that fear.

When the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas discourse on the dharma of emptiness, it is like a sound passing through a wall without obstruction; it is like clouds emerging from a mountain, never coming to an end.
Ultimately, all sentient beings do not realize that from beginningless time they have been undergoing false experiences;
external objects such as sounds, fragrances, tastes, and so forth are all truly non-existent, yet because their attachments are so deep, they are deluded and do not believe this.
Therefore, through the skillful means of great compassion, he empties all that exists, causing all sentient beings to awaken to it for themselves.

It is as stated in the sūtra: "One accomplishes the playful mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhivikrīḍita*) within the bodhisattva-dharmas, purifies buddha-fields, and brings sentient beings to maturity.

Yet Subhūti himself says that he only now contemplates the dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and that upon hearing of the bodhisattva realm, his mind finds no joy.
Question: Regarding the bodhisattva’s playful mastery of supernatural powers and the purification of buddha-fields...
"It is appropriate that the land be perfected," he said. "But what is meant by 'accomplishing sentient beings'? He replied:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas desire to accomplish sentient beings just as heaven and earth relate to the myriad things: first, they use thunder to startle them into awakening;
then, they use rain and sunshine to bring them forth; finally, they use wind and dew to nurture their growth, and snow and frost to bring them to fruition."
Because he has matured them, his sternness in wrath and his harmony in benevolence— whether acting in opposition or accord,
whether bestowing or taking away— are never arbitrary. By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha caused the canopies of the five hundred sons of elders from Ratnākara to merge into one,
covering the three-thousandfold world system, such that the dimensions of this world were entirely [encompassed].

Within it, there further appeared all the Mount Sumerus and so forth, up to the great oceans, rivers, streams, and springs, as well as the sun, moon, stars, and the palaces of the nāgas of this trichiliocosm; all these were manifested within the canopy.
Furthermore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma also appeared within the canopy. What is the meaning of this?
It is said that one wishes to destroy the delusions of view of the two vehicles and ordinary beings through the skillful means of this samādhi.
When the delusions of view are destroyed and extinguished, the body of wisdom manifests before one. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"To know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind is to accomplish the body of wisdom, which does not depend on the teachings of others. Furthermore, it shows Ānanda the light from his five limbs, which flows far to irrigate the ten [directions].
The Tathāgatas from the various directions within the atoms, as well as the Dharma-princes and all the Bodhisattvas, placed their crowns upon [the Buddha’s head];

those Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs, which came from the atoms of the various directions to drench the Buddha’s crown, as well as the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats in the assembly.
The forest trees, ponds, and marshes all proclaimed the sounds of the Dharma, and the interlacing lights formed a vast lattice.

What is the meaning of this "jewel-lattice" (*ratnajāla*)? It is said that it intends to use the light of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to shatter the darkness of ignorance of the two vehicles and ordinary beings.
Once the darkness of ignorance is shattered, one's own mind is revealed. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"Due to the attachment of one's own mind, the mind manifests as external objects; what is seen therein does not exist. Therefore, it is so called."

Using the essential principles of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* sūtras to corroborate the meanings of the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* sūtras, one unifies the intent of this scripture;
it is like a bellows beaten within the wind—though one possesses great wisdom, none can distinguish its source.
Furthermore, it is asked: when a bodhisattva sports with supernatural powers to purify buddha-lands, is this called emptiness?
"How does this differ from the two vehicles' mere contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)? It is said:

"The followers of the two vehicles contemplate emptiness to attain realization; how could they dare hope to equal a Bodhisattva who sports in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and manifests the emptiness in which form and mind are non-dual?"
“World-Honored One, we [have come]... to clarify this meaning. The treatise says:
“The Buddha’s instruction of his disciples uses what is easily understood to illustrate what is difficult to know.
Subhūti, on the contrary, wishes to use parables to instruct the Buddha; is this not a lack of self-awareness? He replied: “I did not dare.”
I employ these metaphors in the hope that the Buddha will attain understanding. It is like a person who has an illness and is cured by a physician;
they cannot themselves describe the evidence of their recovery, yet they speak to the physician, saying: "When I was ill, my fever was like boiling water and my pain was like a wedge;
now that I have recovered, it is as if the boiling water has cooled and the wedge has been removed. Thus speaks the patient to the physician.
It is not that they do not know; rather, those who employ analogies do so merely because they wish to illustrate for themselves their own inability to speak [the matter directly].
It is likewise with the disciples of the Buddha, who clarify their meaning through metaphors.
It is like a person who, having reached the city where he dwells.
The commentary states: It is like a person who, being young in years, was foolish, deluded, and ignorant;
he abandoned his father and fled, dwelling for a long time in another land, thereby losing his original aspiration, drifting through the six realms of existence, lonely, solitary, and suffering.

And they are to be pitied; when they reach ten, twenty, or even fifty years, there are five defilements—the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣkaṣāya*), the defilement of sentient beings (*sattvakaṣāya*), the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*), and the defilement of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*). Since the eon is designated by its temporal divisions, it is referred to here as "years.
Once their years have grown long and they further encounter poverty and distress, the perfuming of seeds gradually becomes familiar, whereby birth, old age, and sickness arise.
The suffering of death causes one to loathe [this state] and race about in the four directions seeking food and clothing;
following after external paths rather than the Middle Way, and lacking the garment of shame and patience as well as the food of meditative concentration, one is said to "seek.

Wandering gradually, one thus seeks gradualist teachings (anupūrva-yāna) without knowing the sudden vehicle (tathāgatagarbha/ekayāna); yet, upon encountering one's original country, one meets [the truth].
While the Buddha was in the world, they did not know how to lose themselves in the pursuit [of liberation]; their fathers had previously come seeking them but could not find them.
Thus, being born in difficult places where they do not hear the Buddha-dharma, they dwell in a single city, which represents birth within the triple world for the sake of sentient beings.
A granary is for storing grain, representing the source of the food of *dharmaprīti* (joy in the Dharma) and *dhyānāsvāda* (delight in meditation); a treasury is for storing wealth, representing...

The gathering place for the precious jewels of all dharmas; those who are servants, young, lowly, yet intimate are the bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain enlightenment but have not yet emerged from birth-and-death and various views.

Those who are ministers and assistants, already noble, are the bodhisattvas who have attained patience (*kṣānti*) and assist the Buddha in propagating his transformation. The elephants, horses, and carriages are the vehicles of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Its power is exceedingly great; with countless cattle and sheep, its methods—both Great and Small Vehicles—are not uniform.
Its profits and interests extend throughout other lands, and its teachings flourish wherever they reach.
There is no path it does not traverse, for merchants and traders are also exceedingly numerous; these "Dharma-merchants" seek the jewels [of truth], traversing every perilous road.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages, which represents the cycle of the four modes of birth;

he passed through kingdoms and cities, representing the coming and going within the three realms. Eventually, he arrived at the city where his father resided, which signifies the fortunate convergence with the Buddha’s era.
While previously it was said that he "encountered" [his father] upon returning to his native land, the present mention of the "city where he resides" indicates his final return.
[The father] draws ever closer.
"Whenever the father thinks of his son" (up to) "he regrets having come here.
The Commentary says: "Whenever the father thinks of his son" means that his fundamental vow to deliver sentient beings is never for a moment abandoned, as he [seeks] his son.
Having been separated for more than fifty years, sentient beings dwelling in the five turbidities have not seen the Buddha;
that they have never spoken of such a matter to others means that the teaching of the two vehicles attaining Buddhahood was not yet proclaimed.

Rather, as they contemplated within themselves with hearts full of regret, they were taught the Buddha-way, whereby all their wealth and possessions were lost and there was no one left to whom they could entrust them.
Thus, one may grieve that the treasury of the Dharma has no successor; yet upon obtaining a son, one finds joy and is freed from further anxiety.

Thus, one may rejoice that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. To live by hire and labor in succession is a life of hardship for one’s livelihood, not one of enjoying wealth and nobility by sitting idly.
Thus, one may wish to seek realization of the various fruits through the conceptualizing mind, yet these are not originally inherent; nevertheless, one encounters them.
If one leaves one’s father and encounters him by chance, it is not the same as departing to inform him of one’s whereabouts or returning to face him;

likewise, though one happens to meet a Buddha appearing in the world, it is not the same as truly knowing the meaning of taking refuge. To stand by the gate and be unable to enter is to remain ignorant of the Buddha’s wisdom that is correct and all-pervading;
to see one’s father from afar and be unable to draw near is to fail to behold the Dharmakāya.
How subtle and wondrous! Previously it was called the "Father’s City," and now it is called the "Father’s House"; the house is even more proximate than the city.
As for the lion throne, it signifies the subduing of the various māras and the conversion of non-Buddhists, thereby attaining the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
As for the precious footstool supporting the feet, it signifies arising from the realm of *tathatā* (suchness) to cultivate merit and wisdom, for merit and wisdom constitute the two feet. All...
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders all paid him reverent homage and surrounded him;
likewise, the great Bodhisattvas of the various ranks of the Dharma-position encircled him with single-minded devotion.

Adorned upon his body were pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold, from which the radiance of ten thousand virtues and rare jewels shone forth brilliantly. His officials, citizens, and servants held white whisks in their hands.
Standing in attendance at the left and right, the newly initiated bodhisattvas use the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) to sweep away the dust and mist, thereby entering the station of the Dharma.
Covered by jeweled canopies and draped with various flowered banners, the great clouds of compassion pervade all things;
the flowers of the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) are sufficient to bring joy, and the banners of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are sufficient to inspire movement.

Sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground and scattering various renowned flowers signifies that the perfumes of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation cool the ground of the mind, while the seven flowers of purity are spread abroad.

The arraying of precious objects and the taking out, putting away, receiving, and giving signify that among the treasures of all dharmas there is nothing that does not exist; whether they are brought forth or given away, it is for the sake of benefiting others.
He may accept these things and take them for his own benefit; such are the various adornments and majestic virtues by which he is preeminent.
When the impoverished son sees that his father possesses great power and authority, he feels possessed of strength and fearlessness, yet he immediately conceives terror and regrets having come here.
Thus, though he is urged toward the Great Vehicle, he delights in the Lesser and completely forgets his original aspiration.
...I had this thought (up to) I fainted and fell to the ground. The Commentary says:
"This may be a king or one who is like a king; it is not a place where I can obtain goods through hired labor."
The Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya bodies are fundamentally enlightened; they are not something to be attained through the severance of existence or the grasping for realization.
This is like going to a poor district where land for labor is available and food and clothing are easily obtained;

thus, in the empty space of the Two Vehicles, one may realize through wisdom that the garments of shame and patience and the food of meditative concentration are easily sought and sufficient. If [this state] endures for long...
To dwell here or to see oneself being coerced and forced to perform [the work of] the Lesser Vehicle is what those of the Lesser Vehicle fear.
Having formed this thought, they flee in haste; this represents the urgency with which they retreat from the Great Vehicle and the firmness with which they pursue the Lesser Vehicle.
Because the empty dharmas of the Two Vehicles lack the *tathāgatagarbha* that contains all virtues, the analogy of a "poor village" is used; [in contrast,] the *Gandhavyūha* Bodhisattva...
Śāriputra said: "This refers to Śākyamuni Buddha, who conceals his immeasurable power of mastery and instead delivers sentient beings through the Dharma that accords with their humble inclinations.
At that time, the wealthy elder, sitting upon the lion throne, recognized his son as soon as he saw him;
yet although the son saw his father, he did not know him to be his father, and thus he was terrified and regretted having come.
Upon seeing his son, he immediately recognized him; therefore, he was filled with joy and his wish was fulfilled.
Thus, although [the son] had forgotten him, that which the Buddha entrusted and protected remains forever unforgotten. Although I am old in years, I still cherish [my children] with longing;
thus, even though the darkness of afflictions has been eternally extinguished, I do not abandon sentient beings, but rather dispatch my attendants to them.
When people pursued him in haste to bring him back, the messengers ran swiftly to seize him;
thereupon, the Bodhisattvas transformed him by means of the Sudden Dharma and caused him to relinquish his provisional expedients.

The impoverished son was struck with alarm and startled by hearing the Great Teaching of the One Vehicle, crying out in lamentation and calling for help, fearing the entry into the afflictions of birth and death, and clinging to the Lesser Vehicle out of distress.
Regarding "affliction as an enemy": because one hears it taught that afflictions are themselves bodhi, they are called an "enemy. Regarding "taking birth-and-death as suffering":
because one hears it taught that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, there is a great outcry.
"I have not offended you; why do you seize me? is said because one is forcibly subdued despite seeking no such thing; thus the messengers seize him ever more urgently and drag him back by force.
Because they were forcibly dragged along despite their refusal to comply, they reflected that though they were innocent, they had been imprisoned;

thus, they feared entering the triple world as if it were a prison. Thinking they would certainly die there, they became even more terrified, fearing the loss of all spiritual fruits and the extinction of their life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).
Out of great compassion, the Bodhisattva enters the prison of birth and death together with sentient beings.
Because those of the Lesser Vehicle who seek only their own deliverance lack this [understanding], they consider it to be without fault and do not enter [the path].
If one faints and falls to the ground, yet is not urged on further, they will slander the Dharma and fail to believe, thereby destined to fall into the evil realms.
The father saw him from afar... [it was] filthy and impure.
The commentary states: When the father saw him from afar, he told his attendants, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come here.
This was because he knew his son’s resolve was inferior and realized that his own wealth and status would be difficult for his son to accept.
Thus he knows that his son’s former mind delighted in the small, and when it was compared with the great, he did not believe it and was not diligent.
He sprinkles cold water on his face to cause him to awaken, and does not speak further with him;
this is because he knows clearly that this is his son, and by means of skillful means (*upāya*), he does not tell others, "This is my son. Therefore, he is liberated through the water.

Although he was bewildered and distressed, [the Buddha] knew thoroughly that he would ultimately become a son of the Buddha; yet, by means of skillful means (*upāya*), he designated him as a "Hearer" (*śrāvaka*).
As for what is meant by the phrase "for what reason" (*so-yi-so-ye*): in all cases, it is an expression used to elaborate upon the preceding meaning.
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you wish. Thus, acting as a messenger of the Tathāgata, one follows the Buddha’s skillful means without being coerced.
Driven by necessity, he rose from the ground and went to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing;
thus he avoided the sin of slandering the Mahāyāna and was liberated from the sufferings of the three miserable realms, employing the Dharma that accords with what the poor delight in.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised a skillful means and secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and devoid of dignity.
As for the virtuous one, because he transforms others through shared activity, it is said that there are two people. To speak softly to the impoverished son, saying, "There is work here;
I will give you double wages," means that he guides him with the gradual teaching of conditioned dharmas while intending to grant him the realization of unconditioned nirvana.
He may then say to him, "I will hire you to remove the dung," thereby causing him to...
Contemplation is the clearing away of the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
We two shall likewise follow your example and provide you with skillful means and engage in the same work as you. Once we have attained it, we shall fully explain the aforementioned matters;
thus, by following the Buddha, we shall extend our transformation. First, we take up the task of removing the dung; this is to cultivate practice out of a longing for the fruit.
This is because his father saw his son and felt both pity and wonder; he pitied him for having lost the great and marveled at his attachment to the small.
Furthermore, on another day, from within a window, [the father] concealed his wondrous, pure, and sublime body, intending not to show it to him.
Seeing from afar that his son’s body was emaciated and haggard, [the father realized] his merit and wisdom were meager.

If one fears all the impurities, filth, and defilements of the dust and soil of suffering, yet still delights in contemplating impurity while discursive proliferation (*prapañca*) has not been eliminated,
this is called being like a child who has merely removed his ornaments.

The Treatise says: Having cast off his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments of adornment, and having concealed those marks of supreme subtlety and wondrous excellence—the signs of his perfection of the ten thousand virtues and all the secondary characteristics—he instead dons coarse, tattered, and soiled clothing, allowing dust and grime to cover his body.
Thus he manifests himself as being beset by the defilements of the five coarse desires, the heavy impurities of the five turbidities, and manifold afflictions.
Having gathered them together at his dwelling, he held a refuse-removing vessel in his right hand;
appearing as though he were afraid, he employed skillful means by using this same method to sever the fetters and attain Buddhahood, manifesting the fear of birth and death.
He said to the laborers, "You all must work diligently and not be indolent. By means of such skillful means, he was able to draw near to his son, and thus [the son] attained [liberation].
He instructs those who are provisional persons manifesting as teachers, yet are actually individuals near to or regressing from the Great Vehicle, saying:
"Ho! Man, you must always act in this way and not go elsewhere; I shall increase your wages.

Thus, by means of harsh words, he urges them to apply themselves with diligent effort therein, whereby they are further strengthened by the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas.
Whatever they may require—such as basins, vessels, rice, flour, salt, or vinegar—let them not hesitate or feel constrained;

rather, provide them with the food of the factors of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), the sustenance of the four dhyānas, the flavors of the limbs of meditation (*dhyānāṅga*), and the various concentrations and samādhis, so that they may practice contemplation and cultivation without stinginess.
Furthermore, if there are aged or infirm laborers who need such things, they should be given to them.
Thus, that which is now employed as a manifestation for the Two Vehicles—providing what they should receive and granting their necessities—is the sound of "Tut," a cry of awakening and reprimand;

therefore, it is used as a metaphor for suffering. Although the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*) are untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*), they merely assist the path and do not transcend the realm of form and substance;
hence it is said they are like a basin or vessel. In the first dhyāna, there is both directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Because the first dhyāna has vitarka but no vicāra, it is coarse and thus likened to rice;

because the second dhyāna has neither vitarka nor vicāra, and because from the third dhyāna onward there is no inhalation or exhalation, it is refined and thus likened to flour. However, as for the absence of factors such as joy and bliss, these are like bland food that lacks satisfying flavor;
one must use salt and vinegar to harmonize them, which is why they are likened to salt and vinegar. Thus, there are three types of meditative concentration.

All obscurations arise from the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma); therefore, they are merely categorized as such. Indeed, while their names are small, the categories they encompass are vast.
"Old and decrepit" refers to the two men previously mentioned who were secretly dispatched and whose appearance was haggard.
"Taking pleasure in one's own settled mind" is a phrase meaning to find peace in that which is not yet peaceful. Do not worry about this further.
These are words intended to cause the abandonment of afflictions. Why is this so? My years are advanced while you are in the prime of youth;
thus, I have already severed the fetters, whereas you must diligently eliminate the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*).
You should not take offense at the harsh words spoken previously. When you perform your work, you are never deceitful, lazy, resentful, or complaining, unlike other laborers.
If you believe deeply in my Dharma and apply yourselves with diligent effort, do not be like those heterodox practitioners who slander the Dharma and hold false views.
From this day forward, I shall give you a name as if you were my own sons; I shall call you "children.
Thus, although you have not yet become my sons, the Tathāgata has always said that we are the children of the Buddha.
"At that time, the impoverished son... [until] he should realize this intention.
The Commentary says: "Although he rejoices at this encounter, he still considers himself a lowly hired laborer;
