If for ten years one were constantly ordered to remove excrement, even while remaining among the thirty sons, such a person would still be regarded as belonging to the two vehicles;
yet once the residual fetters are exhausted, and after this time has passed, the residual fetters are severed and the realization of *nirvāṇa* is attained.

Then, with minds that accord in essence and mutual trust, I may offer praise without being resentful, and they may reprove me without feeling bitterness; thus, there will be no difficulty in coming and going.
This expresses the principle that one may speak of the Great while not withdrawing from the Small;

yet, as long as one's dwelling remains in its original place, even if one is capable of hearing the Great, one still abides in the stage of fruition (*phala*). World-Honored One, at that time, the elder was ill and knew for himself that he would not live much longer.
His work of transforming conditions was about to end, and wishing to manifest the signs of entering *parinirvāṇa*, [he prepared] gold and silver...

When the treasury of rare jewels overflows, you shall fully know all that is within—that immeasurable wealth of the dharmas, its quantity, and what should be taken or given—and thus cause them to teach and transform the bodhisattvas through those dharmas. My mind is such;
you should embody this intent, which demonstrates that all dharmas are solely one's own mind, so that they may realize it.

Speaking in terms of gold, it refers to the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unimpeded knowledges, eighteen unique qualities, and the knowledge of all modes, which are subtle and wondrous, their characteristics indestructible.
Speaking in terms of silver, it refers to the six *pāramitās* of the bodhisattvas, by virtue of their supple, pure, and white dharmas. These are the treasures.

"Treasure" (*ratna*) refers to speech, which is the radiant flame of all myriad practices; "granary" (*koṣṭhāgāra*) refers to that from which the food of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) emerges;
and "storehouse" (*kośa*) refers to that where the wealth of the Dharma-treasure is gathered.
When speech overflows, it is already given to others, yet one possesses more; having already given it to others, it becomes even more abundant.
To some extent, one should give and take according to what is appropriate and measured: for those to whom much should be given, one should not be stingy;

for those to whom little should be given, even if they love the Dharma, one should not speak excessively. At the Prajñāpāramitā assembly, the Buddha commanded Śāriputra and others to teach the bodhisattvas;
there is no dharma among all dharmas that was not fully explained, yet it all ultimately converges upon the Truth.
Emptiness is precisely that matter.
Why is this so? (Up to: "This is what you, my son, know.
The treatise says: Why is this so? If now I and you were not different, then [the Buddha] would have informed him of the Buddha’s bodhi.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, the noble sages, and all dharmas are of one suchness, without distinction or difference. You should apply your mind with diligence so as not to let this be lost;
thus, he exhorted him: "Simply abandon arising and ceasing, and maintain the true permanence, so that you do not lose the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
At that time, the impoverished son accepted the instructions and took charge of all the goods, the gold, silver, and precious treasures.
Furthermore, regarding the various treasuries, they act in accordance with the Buddha’s intent;

they expound the Buddha’s teachings for the sake of bodhisattvas without harboring the slightest desire to obtain even a single meal. Thus, although they teach for the sake of bodhisattvas, they regard the Mahāyāna as their own domain of wisdom.
Nevertheless, because they remain in their original state, their inferior mindset has not yet been abandoned.
"You delight in the great yet do not know how to advance toward the small; you have not yet been able to relinquish it.
Mahākāśyapa said, "All śrāvakas and bodhisattvas should weep for this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm.
All bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this dharma upon the crowns of their heads; this is indeed a joy."
This expresses the sentiment that the great disgraces the small. After a short time had passed, the father realized his son’s mind had gradually become open and settled;
having achieved his great ambition, he came to despise his former thoughts. Thus, when I see a son of the Buddha who aspires to the path of Buddhahood, I shall likewise rouse myself.
At the time of my death, I shall summon my son, assemble my kinsmen, the king, ministers, and the [kṣatriya] clans.
When all the wealthy householders had assembled, the time for his parinirvāṇa arrived;
it was the occasion of the great gathering of devas and humans when he was about to preach the Lotus Sūtra. He then made this proclamation: "This is my son, born of me.
Having abandoned me in such-and-such a city, he fled and wandered in hardship for more than fifty years. [Thus it was that] the realms of desire and form were empty.
For a long time in the five turbidities of birth and death within the realm of form, he lost his original vow. His original name was so-and-so, and my name is such-and-such;
he was formerly known as a non-Buddhist or as an ordinary person, while I am such-and-such a *srotāpanna*, up to an *arhat*.
Having previously sought him with anxiety in our native city, I have now unexpectedly encountered and found him here.
Being currently in the midst of the five turbidities and unable to attain liberation, they nevertheless hear and believe and understand this sutra. "This is truly my son;
I am truly his father. Having thus heard the Dharma, they receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood and are made to succeed to the great throne.
All the wealth and property I now possess belong entirely to my son; all that was previously brought in and sent out belongs to my son.
As for those who are to be known, they are entrusted with the intent of the Dharma-treasury.

As for kinsmen, these are the various bodhisattvas within the assembly, as well as the kings of the eight classes of beings—namely, the Buddhas of the ten directions who have gathered here—and the ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders, who are the bodhisattvas of the ten directions attending upon the Buddhas; all such things are naturally perceived within this sutra.
...Thus it was.
At that time, the World-Honored One [said]: "...the dung of conceptual proliferation.
The Commentary states: "I originally had no mind that sought anything; this Dharma is beyond thought and discrimination."
Because one does not seek the causes for what can be understood with the mind, this treasury of jewels now arrives spontaneously;
thus, the Way of the Buddhas manifests of its own accord at times, rather than being obtained from others. As the tradition says:

"The various craftsmen dwell in their workshops to accomplish their tasks, and the gentleman studies to realize his Way; when nothing is sought, it arrives of its own accord"—this is why it is so called.
Is it not so? Subhūti and others have clarified this for themselves through parables; there is nothing about the Buddha that is difficult to understand.

Nevertheless, it is as if the Buddha remains difficult to comprehend for his disciples within the context of these parables. This is because, although the parables are detailed, their application to the actual meaning is extremely brief.

Thus, there are four stages: (1) fleeing from one's father, (2) seeking the son and stopping midway, (3) arriving at the father’s house, and (4) entrusting the son to him after considering how to do so.
The analogy can be understood by joining the individual strands together. Regarding the three types of suffering:

the process formed by the five aggregates and the formations—from ignorance-conditioned formations up to the six sense bases—is *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of conditioning); contact is *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of pain); and the remainder is *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of change).

Because they are deluded and ignorant, it is said that they "see from afar and run toward it in haste. Because they take pleasure and attachment in minor dharmas, it is said that they are "hastening."
"Urged" means to cause alarm; "released" means to allow them to act as they please. He secretly dispatched two messengers to find a way to approach him.

If one says "exerting oneself to advance," it refers to this. Although the texts concerning the four similes are numerous, their essential purpose is to lead one to contemplate the meaning of removing filth;
therefore, they are combined here into a single point. All dharmas have been eternally pure and eternally characterized by quiescence from the very beginning. One.
The non-arising of thought is true cessation; thus, there is no "excrement" to be removed.
Yet the followers of the Two Vehicles cling to it as if it were existent—this is called the excrement of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Because they possess the intention to eliminate it through contemplation, yet the mind of contemplation is ultimately not their own possession, it is like a person who hires out his labor for wages: the work he performs does not truly belong to him.
There is. Among these, we have spoken in verse.
Today, we shall speak three [verses] as appropriate.

The Commentary states: From this point onward, because the metaphors and their corresponding meanings are not equal in detail or brevity, if we apply ourselves with diligent effort therein, it corresponds to your constant labor without deception, indolence, resentment, or complaints.
Reaching the price of a single day’s wages for Nirvana corresponds to further granting you a title and naming you [a son].
Once the son had obtained this, his heart was filled with great joy and he considered himself sufficient; he then said to himself:
"Because I have applied myself with diligent effort within the Buddha-dharma, that which I have gained is vast and abundant.

Thus, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, the World-Honored One, knowing beforehand that our minds were attached to base desires and delighted in inferior teachings, simply left us be.

Had it not been for the fact that you were not distinguished as having a share in the treasure-house of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, you would still be considered lowly laborers, as you have been made to clear away dung for twenty years. The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means, spoke of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
that is to say, he taught the Mahāyāna Dharma in contrast to the three vehicles, as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
If one were like Vimalakīrti and others in the various sutras, then it would be easy to enter and exit through the integration of mind, marks, essence, and faith;
yet we have obtained from the Buddha the price of a single day’s worth of nirvana and consider this a great gain.

Thus, we have no aspiration for this Mahāyāna, which is indeed as one might expect; our dwelling place remains as it was before. Furthermore, it is by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom that we have attained this.
When the Wisdom [of the Buddha] reveals and expounds it for all Bodhisattvas, you shall fully know what therein should be taken up and what should be relinquished;
thus you are instructed and commanded to know the treasury. Why is this?
Because the Buddha, knowing that our hearts delight in the Lesser Dharma, has taught us according to our capacity through the power of skillful means; yet we did not realize the Truth.
"O sons of the Buddha, this further clarification of the previous meaning implies that even the inferior minds have not yet been able to relinquish [their attachments].
Now we, for the first time, know that the World-Honored One has no begrudgingness regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, as he now entrusts the entire treasury of Dharma to us;
thus, all wealth and possessions rightfully belong to the sons. Why is this so?"
"How is it that we, who have been true sons of the Buddha since long ago, are now told 'these are my sons' and 'I am truly their father,' yet we took pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma?
Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma], the Buddha would have taught us the Mahāyāna Dharma.
In this sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle, whereas previously, in the presence of the bodhisattvas, he disparaged [us]."
Although those śrāvakas delight in the lesser Dharma, the Buddha has in truth taught them through the Mahāyāna;

this further clarifies why the Buddha has no sense of stinginess or regret. Therefore, we say that originally there was no mind harboring any hope or seeking, yet now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously.
Whatever a son of the Buddha ought to obtain, all of it has already been attained.
This concludes the principle that immeasurable treasures are obtained without seeking.
While it was previously stated that there are "immeasurable treasures," the present term "Great Treasure" refers to the rank of the Dharma King.
Once one attains this rank, immeasurable treasures are obtained without seeking; it is like a king who, when he travels, is followed by his retinue—thus they come together.
"Now this treasury of jewels has arrived spontaneously.
The Inexhaustible Layman (Wujin Jushi) commented: "Subhūti, Mahākāśyapa, and others originally delighted in the minor dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
yet they suddenly heard Śāriputra receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Having conceived faith and understanding toward the Dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to comprehend, and having thus gained faith and understanding, he was immediately able to employ appropriate parables and speak of the Dharma.
Then, with single-minded devotion and palms joined, he spoke before the World-Honored One, using the analogy of a poor man who,
as a youth, abandoned his father and fled, only later obtaining great treasures at his father’s dwelling, to illustrate the rare and marvelous Dharma he had heard.

Regarding "single-mindedly joining the palms," Liu Qiu held that single-mindedness means the body is free of divergent thoughts, while joining the palms means the mind has no other objects of attachment.

A poor man who has lived long in another land—perhaps for ten, twenty, or even fifty years—has not yet escaped the ten fetters (*daśa-saṃyojana*), the two views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in what he perceives and clings to. [The Buddha] secretly dispatched two men.
Those lacking majesty were hired to remove excrement; for twenty years he constantly performed this service.

This is the Dharma of the Two Vehicles, which can cleanse away defilements. Shedding his superior, wondrous robes and wearing tattered, soiled garments is the act of transforming beings according to their faculties.
Your mind is now open and serene; you have disparaged your former resolve and gathered together your kinsmen and the king.
"O ministers, kṣatriyas, householders, and citizens, this is my son; all these riches and possessions belong to him.
Thus, before the Śakras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the fourfold assembly, do I bestow this prediction."

At that time, the World-Honored One... [up to] ...the ground of all-knowledge.
The treatise says: When the Buddha speaks of "the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means, knowledge, and vision," he refers to the wisdom that resolves delusion and dispels confusion.
However, this must necessarily be brought forth by means of words.

When sentient beings are in a state of confusion—like those wishing to cross a river but not knowing the ford—they hear the Buddha’s teachings as if finding a raft and thereby achieve salvation. Once they have achieved salvation, the raft should be abandoned.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft.
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "even the Dharma should be relinquished," this means relinquishing the raft.

However, ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, due to the causes and conditions of craving and views, engage in various conceptual proliferations; they give rise to attachments following what the Buddha has taught, and upon hearing it...
To speak of existence gives rise to the view of existence; to hear that one speaks of non-existence leads to falling into the view of annihilationism.
One speaks of existence so as to eliminate the view of annihilationism, and one speaks of non-existence so as to eliminate the view of existence.

As stated at the beginning of the sutra regarding the parable of the burning house, this is not merely to evaluate the three vehicles, but also to serve as an antidote for ordinary beings who long for the excellence of gods and humans.
Regarding the attachment to the fruits [of the path], the Parable of the Poor Son is taught not only to encourage proximity and compliance,

but also to counteract the attachment of those in the two vehicles who, while still in training, give rise to the notion that their own vehicle is equal to the Buddha-vehicle and thus no longer seek further; furthermore,
it is for those who have already gained faith in the Mahāyāna to realize that there is only the Single Buddha-vehicle and that, fundamentally, there are no two vehicles.

Because of this attachment, the Buddha has now explained that although all are moistened by the same rain, the three types of grasses and two types of trees reveal the distinctions of the three vehicles;
yet the Dharma taught by the Buddha is equal and without distinction. Therefore, the sutra says:
"The Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never false. It is indeed never false.

This means that all [actions] have their purpose and are not launched in vain. It is like people who have lived far away in a foreign land, returning together with their servants to their native country;

as they travel along roads that are long and obstructed, encountering many hardships and perils, those who are exhausted and weak reduce their loads, while those who are strong and agile increase their burdens.
Those who linger in cities and towns are encouraged to advance. Thus, a person in this regard...
What other skillful means do those who serve employ than the desire that [the traveler] may quickly reach his native land?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Regarding all dharmas, he expounds them through wisdom and skillful means;
all that he preaches reaches the stage of omniscience."
The Tathāgata perceives and knows [up to] all-encompassing wisdom.
The commentary states: A verse from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;

they do not arise from both, nor without a cause; therefore, it is said that they are unarisen. If one says they arise from themselves, how could a mind ever give rise to another mind? If one says they arise from another...

If arising were from itself, it would have no intrinsic nature; how then could one say it arises from another? If one says it arises from both self and other, since both self and other are non-existent, by what means could there be "togetherness"?
If one says it arises without cause, we do not even assert arising when there is a cause, let alone when there is no cause.
Thus, through such investigation, all four [possibilities] are found to be without connection; this directly realizes non-arising. Non-arising is precisely that which is the mind-only.
Because the manifested mind is the locus where all dharmas converge, the Sūtra states that the Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all dharmas:
namely, that ordinary beings seek the vehicle of the Two Vehicles through the pleasures of gods and humans;

they seek the state of a Bodhisattva through the pleasure of meditative joy (*dhyāna-prīti*); and they seek Buddhahood through the pleasure of the six perfections and the myriad practices (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā-sarva-caryā*).
Because he perceives the various mental activities of those of the three vehicles and is able to bring about their liberation according to their respective inclinations, the Sūtra says:
"He also knows the deep-seated mental activities of all sentient beings and penetrates them without obstruction.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he thoroughly investigates and clearly understands all dharmas," this reiterates the previous meaning of the ultimate destination (*gati*) and serves to eliminate [any remaining] doubt.
"Mind reveals to all sentient beings all-encompassing wisdom" reiterates the previously mentioned meaning of unimpeded penetration;
one knows this wisdom [by this].
Kāśyapa, it is as if... (up to)... name-and-form are each distinct.

The treatise says: The three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is a single level ground, yet its mountains, rivers, high and low terrain, and deep, precipitous valleys serve as a metaphor for how there are distinctions among the various realms of existence (*gati*) within a single Buddha-field, such as the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Nevertheless, the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal herbs all grow from this same ground, yet they differ in their species and natures.

The differentiation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) serves as a metaphor for how the fundamental nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is originally one, yet manifests the distinctions of devas, humans, the three vehicles, and bodhisattvas.

Just as there are clusters of flowers and forests of trees, and medicinal herbs arise from these flowers and trees, the specific mention of "grass" is used as a metaphor to indicate that the devas, humans, and those of the three vehicles are minor in comparison to the bodhisattva. As for "seed," it refers to the category of seeds.

Regarding "clans" (*jāti*), their names are designations; regarding "forms" (*rūpa*), they are physical appearances. By way of analogy, there are likewise distinctions in the names, descriptions, and essential titles of the celestial beings, the three vehicles, and the bodhisattvas, as well as in their faculties, natures, companions, and assistants.
"Dense clouds spread everywhere" (up to) "each having its own distinction.

The Treatise says: "Dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the trichiliocosm," which is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, whereby with a great voice he universally reaches the realms of the sands [of the Ganges], and the assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras are all simultaneously and equally drenched.
Its moisture is universally pervasive, comparable to the great rain of the Dharma; there is nothing it does not satisfy.

Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata knows this dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor. A question is asked: "Regarding what are called the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation—since these all repeat the three previous meanings, why is the name 'all-aspect wisdom' (sarvākārajñatā) here changed to 'ultimate nirvana' and the 'characteristic of eternal quiescence,' while specifically stating that it ultimately returns to emptiness? The Buddha replied: The Buddha said: "Good son, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the single characteristic and single flavor is as follows: He knows that all dharmas are characterized by suffering; he knows that all dharmas are characterized by impermanence; he knows that all dharmas are characterized by selflessness; and he knows that all dharmas are characterized by tranquility. Furthermore, he knows that all dharmas are characterized by emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purity. Good son, because the Tathāgata knows that all dharmas are characterized by emptiness, he speaks of the characteristic of liberation. Because he knows that all dharmas are characterized by signlessness, he speaks of the characteristic of detachment. Because he knows that all dharmas are characterized by wishlessness, he speaks of the characteristic of cessation. Because he knows that all dharmas are characterized by non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purity, he speaks of ultimate nirvana and the characteristic of eternal quiescence. Good son, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the single characteristic and single flavor is thus. A further question was asked: "World-Honored One, if the Tathāgata knows that all dharmas are characterized by emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and non-purity, and yet speaks of ultimate nirvana and the characteristic of eternal quiescence, why does he specifically say that they ultimately return to emptiness? The commentary states: Subhūti was by nature compassionate, gentle, respectful, and affectionate; he constantly cultivated the practice of emptiness, entered the samādhi of emptiness, and dwelt in the *araṇā-samādhi*.
He delighted in sitting in silent seclusion within quiet forests, mountain caves, and stone grottoes. Whenever anyone came to approach him, [he would speak].

Because he analyzes the meaning of emptiness for the sake of sentient beings and ensures that those who make offerings to him necessarily obtain immediate retribution, he is named Śubhūti (Good Fortune).

Furthermore, he is able to protect the minds of sentient beings so that no obstructive thoughts arise; that is to say, if he does not wish for them to walk, they immediately stand still, and if he does not wish for them to stand, they immediately walk.
He is unconcerned with coming or staying. When the Buddha sat in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven during the summer retreat, Śubhūti descended once the retreat had concluded.

When hundreds of millions of people vied with one another to see the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, prostrating themselves at her feet in worship, Subhūti was sitting upright in his stone cave contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas. He thought:
"Form is not the Buddha, and so on up to consciousness is not the Buddha; the eye is not the Buddha, and so on up to the mind is not the Buddha. Suddenly he attained awakening to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, "It was not you who saw me first; it was Subhūti who saw me first.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā addressed the Buddha, saying, "Why is this so inverted?
The Buddha replied, "You pay homage to my physical body (rūpakāya), whereas Subhūti sees my Dharma-body (dharmakāya). The Buddha once sent her to visit Vimalakīrti...
When Subhūti was asked by Mañjuśrī if he would go to inquire after his illness, he said, "I am not fit to go.
I recall that once, when I entered his house to beg for alms, Vimalakīrti took my bowl and filled it with food, saying to me:
'If you can regard food as equal, then all dharmas are also equal; if all dharmas are equal, then food is also equal. One should practice in this manner.'"
One may take food only by begging; yet, Subhūti, if one does not sever lust, anger, and delusion, nor remains joined with them;
if one does not destroy the body while conforming to the single mark; if one does not extinguish ignorance and craving while giving rise to clarity and liberation;

if one attains liberation through the marks of the five heinous crimes, being neither liberated nor bound; and if one neither perceives the Four Truths nor fails to perceive the Truths—[then this is true renunciation].
One who has attained the fruit is neither an ordinary person nor separate from the dharmas of ordinary persons; neither a noble one nor not a noble one.
Although they have accomplished all dharmas, they do not depart from the characteristics of dharmas; only such a person may take this food.
Subhūti, if you do not see the Buddha and do not hear the Dharma, then those six non-Buddhist teachers—Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, and so forth—[would be the ones].
“Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Keśakambalin, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—these were your teachers.
Because you went forth under them, and since those teachers have fallen [into error], you too have followed them in their fall;
only then may you take this food. If Subhūti enters into all...
Holding wrong views, you do not reach the other shore; dwelling in the eight difficulties, you do not attain freedom from them;
being identical to afflictions, you are separated from the pure Dharma. You have attained the *araṇā-samādhi*, yet all sentient beings also attain this concentration.
Those who give to you are not called fields of merit; those who make offerings to you fall into the three evil paths, for you act in concert with the various Māras.
"You act as a companion to all forms of toil; you are no different from the various Māras and the afflictions (*kleśa*).
You harbor enmity toward all sentient beings, seduce the Buddhas, and destroy the Dharma. You do not enter the ranks of the assembly and shall never attain *nirvāṇa*.
If you are such as this, only then may you take this food. At that time, World-Honored One, having heard these words, I was bewildered.
However, not knowing what these words meant and not knowing how to answer, I set down my bowl and was about to leave his house.
Vimalakīrti said, "Take up your bowl; do not be afraid. What do you think? If a person created by the Tathāgata through transformation were questioned on this matter, would they feel any fear?
I replied, "No. Vimalakīrti said, "All dharmas are likewise."
Like the nature of illusions and transformations, you should not have any fear now. Why is this?
Because all verbal expressions do not depart from these characteristics; yet for the wise, they do not cling to words, and therefore they have no cause for trepidation.
Why is this? Because the nature of words is detached; there are no words, and this is liberation. Liberation is [the state of] all...
Because of this, that Buddha remained silent and ceased [speaking]. First, when Subhūti was born, all the granaries, treasuries, vessels, and implements in his household were empty.
Furthermore, throughout his life he had cultivated the practice of emptiness and preached the Dharma of emptiness;

now he receives the prediction of becoming a Buddha, whose name shall be Nameless (Amogha), and whose realm shall be named Jewel-Born (Ratnasaṃbhava). Observing his causal ground, it was through the Dharma of emptiness that he attained this state.
The state of fruition is designated as "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "jeweled canopies," which are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because emptiness gives rise to these fruits, they also manifest the meaning of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*).
At that time, the World-Honored One... [up to] adorned his land.

[The Master] said: "If those who die are reborn in heaven, why do they not return? [The disciple] replied: "It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine and managed to escape;
would they ever be willing to enter the latrine again? Furthermore, one day in the heavens above is equivalent to a hundred years in the human realm.
Those beings have not even finished a single day [there], yet your bones have already decayed; how could you possibly know of them? He asked again: "I take sinners and boil them in cauldrons."
"Because one does not see their spirit depart, one knows there is no other world. He replied, "When you sleep during the day, have others ever seen your spirit go out on an excursion?
He asked again, "I have sought the spirit by cutting human flesh into pieces and grinding my bones to powder, yet in the end I found nothing;
therefore, I know there is no other world. [The Master] said, "It is like a person breaking firewood into inch-long fragments—could there truly be [a continuity]?"
"Can fire be obtained? He asked again, "I weighed living people on a scale and found them all lighter than the dead. If the spirit (shen) had departed, they should have become lighter;
yet they are instead heavier. Therefore, I know there is no other world. [The Master] said: "Ordinary iron is light when in the fire, but heavy once it has left the fire.
When a person is alive, they possess a spirit and are thus light; once dead, having lost that spirit, they become heavy. Why is this so?"
"Is it not different from this? He asked again, "Since I cannot find my soul (ātman) even when seeking it at the moment of death, I know there is no other world.
The Buddha said, "When you hear the sound of a conch shell, can you possibly find it at that very moment?
Thereupon, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika), looking dejected and distressed, said, "You have refuted my various attachments in many ways; however, I still cling to [the notion of] a self."
"How can I bear to abandon this after having long cherished it? Kātyāyana smiled and said, "Have you seen those who gather wild hemp?
When gathering wild hemp, if they see common hemp, they take the hemp and discard the inferior. This is the natural inclination of human beings to prefer the superior over the inferior;
do you alone not wish for this as well? He asked again, "What all people perceive is thus; it is not merely I who am so."
"How can you presume to judge me alone as wrong? [The other] said: "In the past, there were two men traveling together who encountered a ghost.
The ghost said to them: 'Both of you and your oxen are strong; why do you go forward toward places of lush grass and abundant grain? What benefit is there in carrying fodder and rice?
Upon hearing these words, one man immediately discarded his fodder and rice, while the other said: 'I see the lush grass and abundant grain.'"
Upon reaching that place, he cast it away; having discarded the fodder and grain, he traveled for three days without obtaining anything, until he was devoured by ghosts.
Those who saw him were like those to whom the ghosts had said, "I have given this to you," yet you did not accept my words, just as he discarded the fodder and grain.
The non-Buddhists prostrated themselves on the ground, striking their heads, and said, "We cannot abandon what we hold fast to."
Furthermore, he saw that Nanda was greatly incensed and said: "I am not reproaching you; I am merely recounting an old story.
Once there was a man who kept many pigs at home. While traveling, he saw excrement by the roadside, collected it in a basket, and carried it back on his head.
On the way, he encountered rain, and the foul liquid flowed down his face. A passerby urged him to discard it quickly, but the man replied in anger: 'In your house...'"
"Do you not raise pigs? You are truly of our kind! Thereupon, the non-Buddhists were humbled and said with joy, "When we first heard your discourse on the sun and moon, we already understood it;
however, desiring to hear further of your profound wisdom and eloquence, we ventured to speak thus. How marvelous!
Great Being, you have skillfully dispelled the clouds of delusion. The Buddha once sent him to visit Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness, whereupon he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I was unable to go [to him], for I recalled that in the past, when the Buddha had briefly explained the Dharma to the bhikṣus, I subsequently elaborated upon it—namely, the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of non-self, and the meaning of cessation.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: 'Do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the true mark.'"
Kātyāyana, that all dharmas are ultimately neither born nor extinguished is the meaning of impermanence.
To penetrate the five aggregates of clinging as empty and without arising is the meaning of suffering. That all dharmas are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of emptiness.
That "self" and "non-self" are non-dual is the meaning of non-self. That dharmas are fundamentally unborn and thus now have no extinction—this is [the meaning of non-self].
Because the meaning of quiescent extinction is such, Kātyāyana’s eloquence was unable to prevail;
he could dismantle the arguments of the heterodox, yet he could not escape the rebuke of Vimalakīrti. This is because the tenets of the Mahāyāna and the Two Vehicles differ.
Nevertheless, although the Buddha has now granted him the prediction that he shall become a Buddha—his name to be Jambūnada-prabhāsa-golden light—it is only said that his land will not... [be so].
To say that the name of the country is "Immeasurable" (Amitābha)—is it not because its meaning is immeasurable while its name is insufficient to exhaust it?
At that time, the World-Honored One [said]... "You all, listen well.
The commentary states: Maudgalyāyana is called Mahāmaudgalyāyana because there are many who share the same name, Rāyaṇa.
By nature grand and spirited, he rose above the crowd with a striking brilliance; he was renowned as the foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
When the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta, the dragon of that lake thought to himself, "Does this assembly not see Śāriputra?
The Buddha then commanded Maudgalyāyana to go to the Jetavana Vihāra and summon him. Just as Śāriputra was mending his robes, he looked up and saw Maudgalyāyana.
Maudgalyāyana said, "You go on ahead; I will finish sewing it and follow immediately. Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana reached out his hand and rubbed the place where the needle had pierced;
the robe was instantly finished. Śāriputra took the remaining thread from the needle, placed it on the ground, and said, "Can you lift this?
Maudgalyāyana exerted all his supernatural powers but could not lift it. He began to doubt that he had lost his supernormal faculties, and he grew increasingly distressed.
Having departed, he reached the Buddha’s location in the time it takes to extend and contract one's arm; Śāriputra was already before the seat.
There was one named Jīvaka who had been born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven not long ago.

As Maudgalyāyana ascended to heaven and encountered the devas going out for recreation on the way, he saw Jīvaka riding in a chariot and not alighting; Maudgalyāyana halted him so that he could not proceed. Jīvaka...
He joined his palms in reverence and said, "I was enjoying celestial pleasures so exquisitely that I had no leisure to visit your honor; only now that my carriage has been able to proceed am I here.
He then entered the heavenly palace, whereupon all the palace maidens fled in shame. Maudgalyāyana, mindful of their attachment to pleasure, set fire to the palace until it collapsed.
He then preached the Dharma for Śakra, who rejoiced; in an instant, the golden and emerald towers and pavilions stood majestic once more.
As before, when the Buddha’s Brahma-voice was infinite, Maudgalyāyana sought its source with his supernatural powers;

though he traveled westward across lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Brahma-voice still seemed to be at his ear. Upon reaching a certain land, he encountered a community of bhikṣus who were in the midst of a meal.
Maudgalyāyana withdrew his powers and ascended onto their food bowls to perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). The great assembly was greatly astonished and asked, "From where did you come?"

"Have you obtained this head of the *śiśumāra*? That Buddha said, "This is merely Śākyamuni Buddha’s disciple of supernormal power from the immeasurable buddha-fields of the east, who has arrived here following the sound [of your voice].
The Buddha once sent him to visit Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness, and he replied to the Buddha, saying: 'I am unable to go there. I recall entering Vaiśālī in the past...'"
While [the Buddha] was preaching the Dharma to the lay devotees in the city, Vimalakīrti said to me:
"When preaching the Dharma to householders, you should not preach as the Venerable One has done. One who preaches the Dharma should preach the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma:

because it is free from the defilement of sentient beings, the Dharma has no sentient beings; because it is free from the defilement of self, the Dharma has no self; because it is free from birth, the Dharma has no life-span."
Because it is deathless, the Dharma has no person; because the prior and posterior limits are severed, the Dharma is eternally quiescent;
because all marks are extinguished, the Dharma is free from marks; because there is nothing to be perceived, the Dharma is nameless; because speech is cut off, the Dharma cannot be spoken;

because it is free from vitarka and vicāra, the Dharma has no form or appearance; because it is like empty space, the Dharma is without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is ultimately [peaceful].
Because it is empty, phenomena have no self; because they are free from "mine," phenomena are without discrimination; because they are free from all consciousnesses, phenomena have no comparison;

because they are without mutual dependence, phenomena do not belong to causes and do not abide in conditions; because they are identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), phenomena enter into all dharmas;
because they accord with suchness (*tathatā*), phenomena have nothing to which they accord; because they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), phenomena do not dwell in any extremes.
Because it is unmoving, the Dharma is without agitation; because it does not rely on the six sense objects, the Dharma has no coming or going;
because it never abides, the Dharma accords with emptiness, follows non-existence, corresponds to non-action, and is detached from beauty and ugliness.

The Dharma is without increase or decrease; the Dharma is without birth or extinction; the Dharma has no place of return. The Dharma transcends the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the Dharma is without high or low; the Dharma is eternal.
Abiding in the immovable Dharma and detached from all contemplative practices, such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) for Mahāmaudgalyāyana alone—how could it be described?
Now, one who preaches the Dharma neither speaks nor indicates; one who listens to the Dharma neither hears nor attains.
It is as if a conjured being were to preach the Dharma for a conjured person. You should establish this intention when preaching the Dharma, and you should understand the assembly.
Their roots of goodness are sharp or dull; they are skilled in knowledge and vision, free from all obstructions, and praise the Mahāyāna with a heart of great compassion.
Mindful of repaying the Buddha’s grace, they ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted, and only then do they preach the Dharma.
World-Honored One, because I fear their eloquence, I am unable to bear this task. Devadatta constantly leads five hundred bhikṣus as his followers.
Maudgalyāyana grew weary of him and caused him to fall asleep; thereupon, Devadatta snored loudly. Kokālika kicked him with his foot, yet he did not wake.
Śāriputra was preaching the Dharma for five hundred people, and they all turned their hearts back to the Buddha, while Devadatta was just then yawning.
Maudgalyāyana held him up with his hand, and the Saṃgha was thus able to reach harmony. Now, the Buddha—
He was granted the prediction that he would become a Buddha named Tamālapatracaṃdanagandha Tathāgata;
the kalpa would be named Priyasaṃpūrṇa and the land Manojña, located in the northwest. Of the two Buddhas [there], one is Tamālapatracaṃdanagandha.
"Supernatural fragrance" (*śrotragandha*) is a metaphor for supernatural power (*abhijñā*). However, it is his desire for the light of the causes practiced by Mahākāśyapa.

Regarding the fact that the fruit is also luminous: because it establishes the identity of cause and effect and so forth, Subhūti’s practice is a cause that is empty, while the fruit he attains is not empty;
this demonstrates the meaning of non-abiding.
As for Kātyāyana’s practice, the cause consists of the conceptualization of names, marks, meanings, and phrases, whereas the realm of the resulting retribution does not establish names.
The title "Zi" (Character) is intended to clarify that the principles of meaning cannot be fully exhausted by mere names;

thus, the cause practiced by Mahāmaudgalyāyana was spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), while the fruit he attained was designated as "Sandalwood Fragrance" (*candana-gandha*) to demonstrate the identity of the Dharma and its metaphor.
Generally observing these four great disciples as archetypes, their spiritual powers and radiance were such that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) were empty and quiescent.
He also asked: "The definitive teaching that one receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of becoming a Buddha is explained here by means of the elephant;
were it not for those of superior faculties, how could they dare to escape suspicion and slander? He replied: "Indeed. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

'If there are those who, upon hearing this teaching, enter into accord with joy and quickly attain Buddhahood, yet give rise to thoughts of contempt and are granted a prediction of slowness, it is because [others] say that Buddhahood is difficult to attain.'"
Because they had undergone diligent suffering for a long time before finally becoming such persons, he bestowed upon them the prediction of swift enlightenment (*kṣipravyākaraṇa*).

Furthermore, to those whose roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) were mature, he bestowed the prediction of swift enlightenment; to those whose roots of goodness were not yet mature, he bestowed the prediction of delayed enlightenment (*dīrghakālika-vyākaraṇa*).
As for the four great disciples who received their predictions, they had all made offerings to three hundred million *koṭi* of Buddhas; these four individuals are said to have been virtuous.
"If one's faculties are not yet matured, would it be permissible to delight in entering [the path] alone, without following what the Buddha has taught?
Vimalakīrti once said to Maitreya Bodhisattva: "The World-Honored One has bestowed upon you, O Noble One, the prediction that in one more birth you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By which birth do you receive this prediction—is it by a past one, or a future one?"
Is it present? If it were past, birth would have already ceased; if it were future, birth would not yet have arrived;
as for present birth, there is no abiding in present birth, as the Buddha has said: "O Bhikṣu, at this very moment you are being born, aging, and ceasing.
If one attains realization through non-arising, then non-arising is itself the state of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); within this state of true reality, [there is no birth].
There is neither the bestowing of a prediction nor the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
how then, Maitreya, can you receive the prediction of only one more birth? How excellent are the words of Vimalakīrti! They should indeed be contemplated with profound insight.

The Layman Wujin (Vimalakīrti) argued: Since the Buddha used the parable of the medicinal herbs to teach Mahākāśyapa and others that the path they practice is the bodhisattva path, and that by gradually training in it, they shall all attain Buddhahood;

and since practicing the bodhisattva path must have its fruit, attaining Buddhahood must have its name, and the appearance of a Buddha must have its kalpa, the kalpa must necessarily correspond [to these].

In that land, he was formerly given the prediction that Kāśyapa would, in a future age, behold three hundred trillion buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them, and widely proclaiming the Great Dharma;

that during the Great Adornment Eon, in the land of Radiant Virtue, he would attain buddhahood under the name of Light-Radiance Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles. As for Subhūti, in the coming...
In a future life, he shall behold three hundred trillion Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, and praising them;

constantly practicing the Brahma-faring and perfecting the Bodhisattva path, he shall attain Buddhahood in the eon called *Ratna* (Possessing Jewels) in the land called *Ratnasaṃbhava* (Birth of Jewels), with the name *Nāmanimitta* (Name-Aspect) Mahākātyāyana.
In that future world, he shall serve eight thousand billion Buddhas with exquisite and wonderful offerings.
Furthermore, he made offerings to twenty-two trillion Buddhas and attained Buddhahood under the name Jambūnada-kanaka-prabhāsa;

Mahāmaudgalyāyana made offerings to and revered eight quadrillion Buddhas and attained Buddhahood during the Kalpa of Joyful Fulfillment in the Land of Delight under the name Tamālapatracandanagandha. The number of my disciples is as follows:
All five hundred shall receive predictions that in a future age they will attain Buddhahood.

Birth, old age, sickness, and death are the great terrors feared by all people; only by practicing the Bodhisattva path and attaining Buddhahood can one be free from birth, old age, sickness, death, and suffering.
The past Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa was also like this; it is the same for those currently present.
The Buddha, the World-Honored Śākyamuni, is also thus; the prophecy for future Buddhas and their śrāvakas is likewise.
If this is so, why is it that the Buddha is neither born nor dies, yet there are former Buddhas and later Buddhas, those kalpas and these kalpas, and those lands and these lands?
It is said: because empty space is boundless, worlds are boundless, and lands are boundless, due to the conditions of past lives.
Whether through causes and conditions in this world or in other lands, the Buddha manifests in accordance with conditions throughout immeasurable and boundless vast eons.
While the Śakras, Brahmās, devas, and the fourfold assembly perceive his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha is in truth not subject to extinction.
They see his True Dharma abide in the world and his Semblance Dharma abide for a certain number of kalpas, yet as for the Dharma...
In reality, there are no such things as the True Dharma or Semblance Dharma periods, nor are there truly long or short kalpas.
Therefore, regarding the Buddha Kanakamuni of the Jambūnadī river, he simply said that he "attained Buddhahood" without specifying which kalpa or which country;
reflecting on this by analogy, one sees that the Buddha’s intention is profound.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Seven: The Parable of the Phantom City.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... and spoke in verse:
"I recall past ages... penetrating immeasurable kalpas."
The Treatise says: The Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū is the Buddha who can realize the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
By means of the three characters "Mahābhijñājñāna" (Great Pervasive Wisdom), he encompasses the threefold Dharma-realm;

because he enters the threefold gates of contemplation through the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and further completes their meaning with the single character "Victorious" (*śreṣṭha*), it is said that he contemplates for a long duration.
From a distance, it is as if today one first enters the contemplation of true emptiness and the transcendence of marks. The verse says:

"If a person wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, the True Suchness within the body extends everywhere outside; sentient and insentient beings share a single essence, for in every place they are identical with the True Dharma-realm.
Therefore, the sutra speaks here of "Greatness. Next, one enters the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena. The verse says:
It is said: "Simply by using a single thought-moment to contemplate a single object, all objects are simultaneously integrated within that one object;
because all wisdoms and all dharma-realms are contained within that single wisdom. Thus, the sutra speaks of this as "pervasive penetration.

Next is the contemplation of universal inclusion and containment, expressed in verse: "A single thought-moment illuminates and enters into many eons, And each individual thought-moment and eon encompasses all."

Because the wisdom that penetrates all things at all times and places manifests in infinite layers like Indra’s net, and because this all-encompassing wisdom functions without obstruction, the Sūtra uses the term "wisdom" (*jñāna*) here.
By means of these threefold sublime contemplations, one enters the threefold Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
thus, this samādhi is revealed as being beyond the reach of any other samādhi that is still subject to emotional attachments or dualistic views. Therefore, the Sūtra uses [this term] here.
This refers to "supremacy. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"The World-Honored One, while in the Bodhimanda of the Aranya Dharma in the kingdom of Magadha, having first attained perfect enlightenment, entered the 'Momentary Boundary' Samādhi of all Buddhas within the Hall of Universal Radiance.
By the sovereign supernatural power of omniscience, he manifested the body of a Tathāgata—pure, unobstructed, and without..."
That which serves as the basis of reliance is this Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; he is also called "One Who Dwells in the Utmost Tranquility of Śamatha Without Any Object of Attachment.
His land is named "Excellent City" (*Sundarapura*), because this place of utmost tranquility is not a conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*).
He is also called "Possessor of Great Majestic Virtue" and "One Unstained by Attachment."
He causes all who see him to attain awakening, appearing in accordance with what is appropriate and never missing the proper time;
he eternally abides in the single mark, which is so-called "marklessness.

Because this mark of marklessness is not the realization of the small fruit of emptiness, the sutra necessarily speaks of his "extinction and parinirvāṇa in the past" to clarify that his essence is eternally quiescent.

The statement that because [the Dharma] has been extinguished, one must contemplate it as if from the distant past it were as if today, clarifies that not a single thought has shifted between the ancient and the present.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus... up to... *samyaksaṃbodhi*.
The Commentary says: “About to attain” means that one will soon attain it. “For ten minor kalpas sitting cross-legged with body and mind unmoving” refers to the samādhi of dhyāna-concentration.
Why is it that while in the samādhi of dhyāna-concentration, the dharmas of all Buddhas do not manifest before one?
It is said: The dharmas of all Buddhas do not belong to the samādhi of dhyāna-concentration. Why? Because they are the Wisdom-body (jñānakāya).
Because there is no place of abiding; if there were a place of abiding, then the conduct that Samantabhadra constantly practices would have to come to a cessation.

It is after ten intermediate kalpas that the Dharma of all Buddhas manifests before one and one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, because the body of clear wisdom brings forth all functional activities. Why is this? Because...

Because the wisdom-body is not associated with any defiled phenomena, even the subtle habitual tendencies of delusion and the most excellent meditative concentrations are all considered defiled phenomena within the categories of impurity and purity.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states: "After the fruition of Buddhahood has been attained, one constantly practices the conduct of Samantabhadra and constantly dwells within the worlds of the ten directions and the six realms of existence without rest, just as in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*)."

When Dao-man sought to behold the conduct of Samantabhadra, he used the power of samādhi within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to enter immeasurable samādhis in ever-doubling measure, yet ultimately he could not see the body or the realm of Samantabhadra.
This is because the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is the embodiment of wisdom itself;

thus, although Dao-man perfected the paths of the ten stages, even through the power of samādhi within those ten stages, he entered immeasurable samādhis in ever-doubling measure [and still could not perceive him].
"Passing ten small kalpas" refers to the period exceeding ten small kalpas. "Ultimately not seeing" refers to the fact that the various Buddha-dharmas do not manifest before one.

According to the treatise, it is said that the Tathāgata constantly takes pity on all the great bodhisattvas in the assembly who seek Mañjuśrī but cannot see his body or his seat; the Buddha then commands each of them...

If one gives rise to thoughts of devotion and performs three prostrations with earnestness to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, he will then manifest his body according to the needs of the practitioner through his supernormal powers.
This body of wisdom cannot be sought within the state of samādhi, for as the essence of wisdom, it abides nowhere and relies on nothing.
If one gives rise to thoughts of aspiration and longing, he will immediately manifest his body according to the needs of the practitioner; yet this manifestation has no fixed location or basis.
Because it is quiescent, it is like an echo in a valley, possessing only the sound that responds to objects; if one calls out, it responds, yet no location can be found for it.
Therefore, those who wish to see Samantabhadra need only give rise to the mental image.
Before that Buddha had left the household life (up to the point where he) spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World has no equal" (up to the point where he said) "he shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.
The Commentary says: According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are the five consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as the *manas* which discriminates objects.
Regarding the consciousness [of the] *ālayavijñāna*, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Based on the *ālayavijñāna*, it is said that there is ignorance which, through non-awakening, gives rise to the capacity to see, the capacity to manifest, and the grasping of objects;
because it gives rise to the continuity of thought, it is called 'manas' (*the mind*). This manas further has five names. What are these five? The first is named 'karma' (*action*)."
Consciousness refers to two things: first, it is called the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which, depending on the moving mind, is able to perceive objects;
second, it is called the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), which manifests all objective realms just as a clear mirror reflects forms and images.
The manifesting consciousness is likewise: as the five sense-objects arrive before it, they are immediately manifested without any sequence of before or after.
First, it is called the *ādāna-vijñāna* because it spontaneously arises at all times and is ever-present. Second, it is called the *manana-vijñāna* because it constantly reflects upon itself.

Third, it is called the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* because it manifests in various ways through the six sense-bases. Fourth, it is called the *jñāna-vijñāna* because it discriminates between defiled and pure phenomena. Fifth, it is called the *saṃtati-vijñāna* because it is associated with mindfulness and continues without interruption. Furthermore, there are eight types;
together with the sixteen causes and conditions of the arising and ceasing of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, these constitute the basis for the birth of sentient beings.
The destination of death is the realm of the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). The *Daśavidha-śāstra* states:

"That which is called the twelvefold dependent origination is the ocean in which all sentient beings, pursuing delusion and losing sight of the truth, follow the currents of birth and death with waves that never cease.
This ocean is vast, profound, and boundless; it is also the treasure of all Buddhas and noble sages."
The Great City is adorned because these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);

thus, by following ignorance (*avidyā*), one enters into birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and by following wisdom (*prajñā*), one realizes the path of enlightenment. A sutra states that before that Buddha left the household life, he had sixteen sons;
the first was named Jñānakūṭa (Accumulation of Wisdom), which refers to the names and characteristics of the sixteen kinds of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It arises from the *ālayavijñāna*; this *ālaya* is the accumulation of various rare and exquisite playthings, which are the subtle afflictions of defilement.

As the Sūtra says, "Hearing that his father had attained *bodhi*, he abandoned all his treasures and went to the place of the Buddha," this signifies following after wisdom to realize the path of enlightenment; thus, it is through the principle of the same essence (*tongti*).
Out of sorrow and pity for sentient beings, it is said that "the various mothers weep and follow in the funeral procession.

Furthermore, because he gathers and embraces sentient beings through unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*), it is said that his grandfather was the Cakravartin King Buddha. Here, the father is used as a metaphor for compassion;
this refers to the grandfather, who is the great-grandfather. Thus, unconditioned compassion is indeed the Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). Moreover...

Because they follow along with the various dharmas of the path—the four immeasurable minds and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—it is said in general that one hundred great ministers and the remaining hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of people all surround him and follow him to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states: "The initial mind of the ten stages is called 'seeing the path' (*darśanamārga*); if there are remaining habitual tendencies..."
Thus, by means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, he employs this to treat [the afflictions].
The sūtra states that after the sixteen princes praised the Buddha with verses, they exhorted him to preach the Dharma; this is intended to purify residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā).

Therefore, there are many expressions concerning providing peace, compassion, and benefit. Question: Regarding the eight names, substances, and characteristics of the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as you have shown them—
At dawn, he arose with faith, yet found it difficult to distinguish between the eight types of meanings that had become conflated; he requested, "Please explain this in detail for me.

[The Master] said: "Because the five consciousnesses are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it is said that based on the *ālaya-vijñāna*, ignorance arises non-awakened, capable of seeing, capable of manifesting, and capable of grasping objects. These three types of consciousness refer to the explanation of the *nimitta-bhāga*. If...
Because that which possesses discrimination belongs specifically to the domain of the *manas*, it is said: "Because thoughts arise and continue in succession, it is called the *manas*.

Furthermore, a question is asked: "Even though this *manas* has been clearly explained, there are five types of consciousness; how do we know they do not overlap with the two aspects of the *ālayavijñāna*?
Specifically, regarding the *karmavijñāna*, the *pravṛttivijñāna*, and the *pratibhāsavijñāna*, as well as the 'capable of seeing,' the 'capable of manifesting,' and the 'capable of grasping'?"

"What difference, then, is there in their objective spheres? [The Master] replied: "The reason they are called *xiang-fen* (objective parts) is that they have not yet undergone discrimination (*vikalpa*).
If they flow into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), then discrimination arises. Once discrimination arises, there is a distinction between the refined and the coarse;

therefore, what is called *ye-shi* (karmic consciousness) is the most subtle movement. The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) follow one after another."
Since its characteristics (*ākāra*) are thus, it is known not to be confused with the three types of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) of the *ālayavijñāna* mentioned previously.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, and having done so, spoke these verses:
"Our various palaces [shine] everywhere throughout the ten directions.
At that time, five million billion [beings] spoke in verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma... having practiced the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas."
The Treatise says: The chapter on the "Transformed City" is titled "Exhortation" and is taught to stimulate those of the Two Vehicles who have become weary and fallen;
it reveals the reality to shatter their attachment to words as found in the "Introductory Chapter. How is this known?

The "Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings" is the *kṣaṇika-samādhi* (momentary concentration) of all Buddhas; it is the primary principle of this sutra, and the subtle essence of that principle.
There is nothing more subtle than this to which one may entrust [the teaching], yet it is entrusted solely to the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings.

Fearing that the faculties and thoughts of learners might not be subtle and that they would instead cling to the literal meaning, the preceding section demonstrates that although the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, his Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him; only after ten minor kalpas had passed...

That the Buddha, having attained the ear of presence, emits light from between his eyebrows that illuminates only the eastern direction, is a subtle indication of the signs of the Samādhi of the Immeasurable Meaning.
It is like pointing out a steamer to one who is hungry;
the hungry person sees only the steamer but does not see the rice. Therefore, those in the assembly, such as Maitreya, did not know its significance and questioned him.
It is said that Mañjuśrī’s intention was not merely to emit light to illuminate the eastern direction;
fearing that practitioners might lack subtle discernment and instead cling to the literal meaning, this section demonstrates that natural light universally illuminates the ten directions,
such that when the Brahmā devas seek the origin of this light, they find it coming from all ten directions and are able to perceive it wherever they turn.

The Buddha has no fixed place of abode; the body of realized wisdom (*jñānakāya*) cannot be sought through the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because it has no location upon which to rely—just as when one observes a "chicken-startling" rhinoceros horn pillow, every side is perfectly correct.
All that has been shown above serves to refute attachment to words. When the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had not yet left the household life, there was...
The Eight Princes followed their father in leaving the household life; through the instruction of Bodhisattva Miaoguang, they all attained Buddhahood.
Yet, there were differences in the speed with which they achieved Buddhahood, demonstrating how the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms.

If one observes the sixth and seventh consciousnesses through the power of knowledge and vision, this refers to those who attain Buddhahood swiftly during the causal stage of transformation. As for the fifth and eighth [consciousnesses]...

It is understood that this refers to those who will eventually attain Buddhahood through the transformation of their consciousness within the fruit [of enlightenment], though the full meaning has not yet been exhausted.
Therefore, it is now said that when the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was still a layman, there were sixteen princes;

because their father attained the Way, they followed him to make offerings, and soon thereafter they themselves left the household life. Their mothers wept as they saw them off, and their grandfather and various kinsmen joined them.
Approaching and drawing near to behold his attainment of the Way, he further expanded upon the eight kinds of consciousness previously indicated to sixteen kinds,

in order to accord with and draw near to him; through the nourishment and maturation of all wondrous merits— such as unconditioned great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and coessential great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)—
the sixteen princes’ attainment of Buddhahood is not spoken of in terms of priority or sequence.
Regarding the fact that among the eight princes of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, only those who attained Buddhahood as Prabhāsa, Mañjuśrī, Dīpaṃkara, and Maitreya are mentioned,

this is because one has only seen the principle of the transformation of the *indriya-kāya* (the body of faculties) and has not yet seen the meaning of the transformation of the *bhājana-loka* (the receptacle world).

Therefore, [the sūtra] now presents the sixteen princes who will attain the Way of Buddhahood, receiving names according to their respective directions, in order to demonstrate the transformation of the receptacle world.
The realms (*dhātu*) likewise undergo a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), whereby one attains Buddhahood according to the respective directions.

Now, since both the sense-faculties and bodies (*indriya-śarīra*) and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) have undergone this transformation of the basis, and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have already become a domain of the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkha*), yet the subtle modes of activity of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) have not yet been analyzed;

therefore, the three turnings of the four noble truths and the twelve links of dependent origination are again detailed. Since these passages all appear below [in the text], [the preceding section concludes here].
All that has been discussed here continues the unfinished meaning [of the previous section].
At that time, the Great Penetration... up to ... this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

The Commentary states: "The three turnings" are: first, the turning of the manifestation of characteristics; second, the turning of exhortation to practice; and third, the turning of realization. Regarding the manifestation of characteristics:

The "turning toward" (*parivṛtti*) indicates their characteristics, namely that [the truths] range from suffering up to the path. The "turning toward through exhortation to practice" exhorts one to cultivate them, meaning that suffering should be known, and so on, up to the path which should be known.
The "turning toward through realization" refers to citing one's own realization of them, meaning: "Suffering has been known by me;
it need not be known again," and so on, up to: "The path has been cultivated by me; it need not be cultivated again."
Furthermore, practicing the three turnings of the Four Noble Truths constitutes the twelve [aspects].
It is also called the "twelve modes of conduct" (*dvādaśākāra*), which means causing those who hear the Dharma to give rise to the untainted, true, noble eye of wisdom.

Within each Truth, observing the three periods of time collectively is the general [mode], while within each Truth, observing the past as knowledge (*jñāna*), the future as clarity (*vidyā*), and the present as awakening (*buddhi*) is the specific [mode].
The Four Truths are thus one revolution consisting of four aspects; with three revolutions of these four aspects, there are twelve aspects in total.

The wheel has the function of crushing and refining; how could teaching alone, without practice, be able to crush delusions? It is only by establishing practice that the meaning of a "wheel" is realized;
therefore, it is called the Wheel of the Dharma of Twelve Aspects. As the Sūtra says: "Whether they be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas..."

That which cannot be turned back by the celestial Māras, Brahmās, or any other worldly beings is because the Dharma attained by me is transferred into the minds of others so that it remains uninterrupted.
Although Pratyekabuddhas awaken by themselves, they are unable to speak it;
Śrāvakas, however, come to know it through the Buddha’s teaching. Thus, it cannot be turned back even by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or celestial Māras.
Although Brahmā heard its name, he did not understand its meaning, nor was he able to turn it; thus, the state of other worldly beings can be known by this.
Furthermore, he extensively expounded the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.

The Treatise says: Regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma in three phases and twelve aspects, although it was originally spoken in terms of the Four Noble Truths, the detailed exposition of the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination clarifies that these twelve links are themselves the subtle observation of the Four Noble Truths explained in detail.
In terms of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), there is ignorance conditioned by [past] formations, up to birth conditioned by aging and death.

When the path is extinguished, there is the extinction of ignorance; when ignorance is extinguished, there is the extinction of volitional formations, and so on until the extinction of old age and death.

The reason these twelve factors are collectively termed "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is that the primary cause constitutes the "cause" (hetu) and the secondary conditions constitute the "condition" (pratyaya).

Just as a tree depends upon its roots and the soil, ignorance serves as the primary cause and condition; because of ignorance, volitional formations arise, and because of volitional formations, consciousness arises.
The cause of these fundamental dependent origination practices is, in turn, consciousness; thus they proceed in succession, each acting as a causal condition for the other.

Vimalakīrti said: "If one knows that because ignorance is ultimately extinguished, volitional formations are also ultimately extinguished, and so on until because birth is ultimately extinguished, old age and death are also ultimately extinguished—then these twelve links of dependent origination are the transcendence of the world."
Regarding the essential path of the pratyekabuddhas, there are those who attain awakening through self-awakening;
when the Buddha encounters such individuals, he teaches them according to their capacity, as described by Vimalakīrti—that which is the object of contemplation for bodhisattvas.
"Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations... [and so on] until the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.
The treatise states: In the sixth stage of the "Ten Stages Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
"All that exists within the triple world is but the single mind; it is regarding this that the Tathāgata has analytically expounded the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*)."
How is it established from a single mind? Why is this so? Craving arises in accordance with objects and co-arises with the mind.

The mind is consciousness, and the object is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Delusion regarding these formations is ignorance (*avidyā*). That which co-arises with ignorance and the mind is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The growth of name-and-form is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The union of the three parts of the six bases constitutes contact (*sparśa*). Contact, together with...
Birth is the arising [of the aggregates]. That sensation is never satiated is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Being grasped by craving and not relinquishing it is clinging (*upādāna*).

Those various links of existence that arise are becoming (*bhava*). That which is called "becoming" arises as birth (*jāti*). The ripening of birth is aging (*jarā*). The decay of aging is death (*maraṇa*). O Son of the Buddha, herein ignorance has two functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to be deluded regarding their objects of perception; second, it serves as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

The causal activity of arising (*utpatti-pratyaya-karma*) also has two functions: first, it can produce future retribution; second, it acts as the causal condition for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Consciousness also has two functions: first, it can cause the continuity of the various realms of existence (*bhava*); second, it acts as the causal condition for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Name-and-form also has two functions: first, they mutually assist and complete one another; second, [they act as the causal condition for the arising of the six sense bases].
It acts as the productive cause for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The six sense bases also have two kinds of functions: first, they each apprehend their respective objects;
second, they act as the productive cause for contact (*sparśa*). Contact also has two kinds of functions: first, it can serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*) for contact;
second, it acts as the productive cause for feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling also has two kinds of functions: first, it can experience craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The two factors such as aversion serve as the cause for the arising of craving; craving also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes deep attachment to the objects of affection;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of grasping. Grasping also has two kinds of functions: first, it causes the continuity of all afflictions;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of existence (*bhava*). Existence also has two kinds of functions: first, it is able to...
It causes birth within other realms of existence. Birth has two functions: first, it can give rise to the aggregates;
second, it acts as the generative cause for aging. Aging also has two functions:
first, it is the transformation of the sense faculties; second, it acts as the generative cause for death. Death also has two functions: first, it can...

Because the destruction of all formations (*saṃskāra*) occurs through two factors—the lack of conscious awareness and the non-interruption of the continuum—when observed from this perspective, the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) arise through mutual dependence. They possess no functional activity and no intrinsic nature;

they are merely like a magnet and iron, which attract one another without deliberation. For how could the magnet have any cognition or thought? Yet, it nevertheless causes movement and turning to occur.
Regarding this point, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The magnet has never attracted iron, nor has iron ever attracted the magnet;
yet when the magnet and iron meet, they necessarily join. Ignorance does not attract formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nor do formative forces attract consciousness (*vijñāna*);

This is because meditative seclusion in *samādhi* does not transcend silence, while delighting in preaching does not transcend speech.
Discerning wisdom does not exceed speech; yet that which is self-realized is beyond the reach of thought—how could speech or silence possibly describe it?
Nevertheless, when the sixteen princes first called themselves "princes," they gradually left home and were then called *śrāmaṇeras*;
