The Treatise by Master Wu-jin states: "Since the great disciples of the Śrāvakas have already received predictions of their future attainment of Buddhahood, what serves as proof for the Buddhas of the past and present?
The Buddha then explained that in the immeasurable and boundless [past...]"
Inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I contemplate that remote past as if it were today. A verse says:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the path of Buddhahood. Why was this so?

The sixteen princes invited the Buddha from the Brahma heavens of the ten directions to turn the wheel of Dharma; although the Buddha granted their request, the time for its proclamation had not yet arrived, and thus the Buddha-dharma did not manifest.

When he first turned the wheel of Dharma, he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, delivering six million billion beings to the state of Arhatship alone. Upon turning the wheel of Dharma a second time, he delivered ten million.
An assembly as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, having not grasped at any dharmas, attained merely the state of Arhat;
then the sixteen princes left the household life to become śrāmaṇeras and requested the Buddha to preach for them the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After his acceptance of their request had passed twenty thousand kalpas, he then preached the Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

When the Buddha-dharma manifests before one through sutras as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one turns toward it—just as those sixteen novice monks of old are now called the sixteen Bodhisattvas.

The Sixth Patriarch said: "If former thoughts, subsequent thoughts, and present thoughts are not stained by delusion and ignorance, it is because the disciple and the teacher share a karmic affinity from past lives, such that right mindfulness remains ever-present."

If one were to experience arising and ceasing, how could one have planted the roots of virtue throughout the sands of worlds and sown the seeds of goodness over kalpas past, as if it were this very day?

Furthermore, from the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū until Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world to teach and transform beings, how long was it before the śrāvakas received their predictions of enlightenment? It is because of human greed and attachment.
It is not easy to cast off [suffering]; when one is weary of suffering, one comes to admire it; once one admires it, one becomes attached to the Lesser Dharma.

For this reason, the Buddha spoke the parable of the conjured city and the gathering of treasures: he first used the *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles to rest their exhaustion and weariness, and finally revealed to them the treasure of the Buddha.
Thus, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are the conjured city, serving to provide rest.
Because one attains the Buddha-treasure within the conjured city, the verse says: "These sixteen princes shall all attain the path of Buddhahood;
the Dharma does not arise falsely, and the enumeration is not established in vain. By penetrating this, one penetrates that; by knowing the metaphor, one knows the reality.

The treatise says: Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was born in a small, cold, and humble state that was a dependency of the Five Indias.
However, as a person, he had a prominent nose and fair, finely-textured skin; he was exceptionally sharp and intelligent, peerless in his great wisdom and skill.
The Buddha frequently praised him as the foremost in preaching the Dharma. His mother was also brilliant and possessed exceptional insight;

she could recite the four Vedas, and her voice reached throughout many kingdoms. Pūrṇa once addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to return to my native land to perform buddha-work for the benefit of sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "Your country is corrupt and evil; how can you do so? Pūrṇa...
He said: "I shall cultivate patience. If someone insults or humiliates me, I shall reflect: 'May they not strike me with their fists.
Even if I am struck by their fists, I shall again reflect: 'May they not beat me with clubs. Even if I am beaten with clubs, I shall again reflect:
'May they not attack me with weapons. Even if I am attacked by weapons, I shall again reflect: 'It is because I have received these weapons [that this occurs]."
"Kṣāntivādin has fortunately escaped this poisonous vessel of the five aggregates. The Buddha praised him, saying, "It is not only you who maintain this power of patience;

I too have realized [enlightenment] through it. Śāriputra also joined his palms and extolled him, saying, "All fellow practitioners of the holy life should wrap their robes around your head as a crown; whoever sees you will obtain great benefit."
Initially, his father prayed at a shrine by the riverbank—the image of which was Mahābrahmā—vowing to seek an heir.
He encountered the river in full flood and further dreamed that a precious vessel filled with various jewels entered his mother’s womb.
When the son was born, because his wish had been fulfilled, he was named Pūrṇa. His mother was Maitrāyaṇī; this word means "Compassion."
When asked about his clan and surname, he replied: "My father’s name is Pūrṇa and my mother’s name is Maitrāyaṇī;
thus, fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Now the Buddha has bestowed upon me this prediction:
after immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this land, and my name shall be Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata."
Even unto the extent that as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River are made into a single buddha-field, filled with towers and pavilions of the seven treasures;
in an eon named Jewel Radiance, in a land named Well-Purified, his lifespan lasts for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and the Dharma remains for a very long time;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven treasures arise and fill that land—such is its cause.

Because he skillfully expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma, he is titled "Dharma-Light" (*Dharmaprabha*); because his conduct is noble and worthy of esteem, the eon is named "Jewel-Light" (*Ratnaprabha*);

and because his compassion is harmonious and gentle, the land is named "Excellent Purity" (*Suvimala*). When he appears in response to conditions, whether through prayers at the river or visions in dreams, fulfillment is always regarded as an auspicious sign;
and when he realizes the fruit of enlightenment, the lands he transforms will be adorned with various jewels and filled to capacity.
After his parinirvāṇa, all stūpas and temples likewise became everywhere filled; for the three periods of time, ancient and modern, are fundamentally but a single thought-moment.
At that time, [the assembly from] the twelve hundred [arhats]... their hearts were filled with universal joy.
The Treatise says: As for Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya, he was magnanimous, widely learned, and possessed great wisdom through which he attained thorough penetration.
Because he was the first to realize the Dharma, among the great disciples he was ranked foremost for his early awakening and called "the Sun" (Dīpa).
Kauṇḍinya was like the morning star; when the sun first rises, the morning star appears, and by means of this star, the long night is dispelled.
It is because while others remained in the darkness, Cunda broke through the darkness of ignorance.

When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom to enter the mountains and study the Way; his father, King Śuddhodana, could not forget him and dispatched five close ministers to attend to and protect him, of whom Cunda was one.
Two of them, however, held the view that desire is purity.
Because they regarded asceticism as purity and the Prince was exclusively practicing asceticism, the two men abandoned him and departed.
Later, when the Prince accepted food, ghee, oil, and warm water, the three men said, "Alas!
The Prince has also abandoned asceticism," and so they too abandoned him and departed. Nevertheless, the Prince attained the Way first.
For these five people, the Buddha preached the Dharma. This was because, during a time of famine in a previous life, the Buddha had transformed himself into a great fish.
As he leaped from the waves onto the shore, the tide receded with great speed, leaving him stranded in the salty sands where he appeared to be dead.

Five carpenters happened to see him; one of them first hacked away at his flesh, while the others, driven by hunger and exhaustion, scrambled to seize it. It was then that the Buddha [manifested his true form].
While in the form of a fish, he made a vow, saying: "If I am to attain Buddhahood, I must first deliver these five carpenters.
Now, the Buddha has received the prediction that he shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas before attaining Buddhahood, at which time his name shall be Samantaprabhāsa.
He and five hundred *arhats* shall share the same name, for by this cause he was the first to awaken to the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because he is free from the darkness of ignorance and delusion, his attainment of Buddhahood is also named "Universal Radiance" (Samantaprabha).
Kālodāyin means "Black Light"; Udāyin means "Appearance"; Cunda is fully called Dhanuśaka; Sāgata means "Welcome.
The others have already been explained in the Introduction Chapter. These great beings were all among the assembly.
Because he was one selected for this [assembly], he is specifically highlighted.
The Discourse by the Layman Wujin Zhang Shangying states: "Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was foremost among men in preaching the Dharma.
Having heard that the 'City of Transformation' was not real and knowing that the 'Jewel Site' was not far off, the World-Honored One knew the depth of his fundamental mind."
"I vow that you shall immediately receive this prediction: in the future, you will attain Buddhahood and be named Dharmaprabhāsa.
Furthermore, I grant successive predictions to one thousand two hundred who have attained mastery over the mind; Kauṇḍinya shall be named Samantaprabhāsa.

Once the five hundred arhats had received the Buddha’s prediction, they immediately attained the Tathāgata’s skillful means—the sound of the Dharma—and were able to preach the Dharma according to what was appropriate for each occasion.
The analogy of the intoxicated guest’s robe and pearl is cited to clarify this meaning; it is not the same as the previous claim of having attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Nine: "Bestowing Predictions upon Those Still Learning and Those Who Have Completed Their Learning."
At that time, Ānanda... [to] uphold the teachings of all Buddhas.
The commentary states: "Ānanda" means "Joy. He was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment; he was a younger brother of Śāriputra.
At the age of twenty, he became the Buddha's attendant. His physical appearance was beautiful and auspicious. Initially, the Buddha sent him...
Wearing a garment that covered her shoulders, a woman carrying a child approached a well intending to draw water;
she looked upon Ānanda and could not blink her eyes, mistakenly tying the child’s neck with the water-rope, nearly strangling him.

Furthermore, when he followed the Buddha into the palaces of devas and nagas, although he had not yet completely eliminated all residual thoughts, his mind was already free from defilement. For these reasons...
The Buddha, who is revered by devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, often remarked that Ānanda was superior to his other attendants.
Upon hearing this, the others understood; they realized that even before the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda could comprehend his intent, knowing fully what was required and what was not.
Later, when the Dharma-treasury was entrusted [to him], the four heavenly kings each...
He offered his bowl to the Buddha; the Buddha stacked them one upon another and leveled them with his hand so that they became one, yet the rims of the four bowls remained perfectly distinct.
This bowl was heavy and large; Ānanda always carried it following the Buddha without ever showing signs of weariness.
At the age of twenty-five, while attending upon the Buddha, he heard eighty thousand *khandakas* and recited them all without omission, never asking a question twice.
The power of his mindfulness was thus subtle and wondrous. When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa upon the lion throne, Mahākāśyapa and the great assembly saw this and praised him, saying:
"His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses. The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma flows into the heart of Ānanda.
Ānanda then made a vow to enter nirvāṇa; yet he remained there, fearing that if he proceeded, the Licchavis would harbor resentment.
Fearing that King Ajātaśatru might harbor resentment, he went to the Ganges River and entered the *Vāyu-pravega-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Swift Wind), dividing his body into four parts:
one he gave to the devas, one to the nāgas, one to the Vaiśālī people, and one to King Aśoka.
King Aśoka paid homage to his stūpa, offered ten million taels of gold, and praised him with a verse:
Because he is able to uphold the Dharma-body and the lamp of the Dharma, because he maintains the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom through mindfulness of the endurance of the Dharma,

because he offers supreme offerings and maintains what he has heard with mindfulness, and because his mouth utters subtle and wondrous words praised by the World-Honored One and beloved by devas and humans—
now the Buddha grants him this prediction: in a future age, he shall become a Buddha named Śaila-sāgara-mati-vikrīḍita-vaśavartin.
The land of the Tathāgata Universal King is named Constantly Erected Victorious Banner, and its eon is named Wondrous Sound Pervading All.
Its cause is that by upholding the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, he is able to intimidate and subdue all celestial Māras and followers of external paths;

therefore, the name of his buddha-land is Constantly Erected Victorious Banner. Because he proclaims the sound of the Dharma so that it reaches every place, the name of his eon is Wondrous Sound Pervading All.
From the time of Śūnyarāja Buddha, Pūrṇa, together with the Buddha, resolved his mind upon enlightenment;
he is courageous and sharp, immovable as a mountain, and vast as the ocean, for he has deeply penetrated the wondrous meaning.
Thus, his wisdom and eloquence are sovereign over all phenomena, and because he is unimpeded in both affirming and negating, his thorough mastery is like that of a king.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula... [as if] being sprinkled with nectar.
The commentary states: Rāhula was the son of the Buddha. When the Buddha was first a crown prince and was about to renounce the world, he informed his father, King Śuddhodana.
The King would not permit it, yet the Prince’s earnest entreaties did not cease. The King said: "If..."
"You have a son; listen to what you request. Thereupon, the Prince pointed with his finger at Yaśodharā’s belly and said, "Six years hence, you shall give birth to a son.
It was exactly as he had predicted, and thus he was named Prince Gopaka.
That night, the Prince leaped over the wall and departed. Yaśodharā then became pregnant, and the Śākyas considered this an ill omen.
Desiring to punish him by execution, they relied upon the testimony of the maiden Ratnā and Gopikā to stop him. Once Rāhula was born, he could never prove his innocence;
he took the child in his arms and stood before a great mass of fire, saying, "If I have done wrong, let mother and son be consumed together;
if not, let Heaven bear witness. He then stepped forward and entered [the flames], whereupon the mass of fire transformed into a lotus.

The doubts and slanders of the people of the city of Kapilavastu were thus quelled. Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment and returned to his native land, Yaśodharā sent Rāhula to offer him fruit.
Rāhula, relying on his youth, went directly through the midst of the great assembly to present it to the Buddha;
the Buddha joyfully accepted it. King Śuddhodana said, "My son has entered the Way, yet my grandson is like..."
This [son] could have succeeded to the rank of a Golden Wheel-turning Monarch; what cause for regret was there? When he grew up, the Buddha ordered him to leave the household life.
Yaśodharā, out of her deep affection for him, hid him in a high tower. Mahāmaudgalyāyana flew through the air, carried him away, and made him attend upon Śāriputra as his disciple.
Among the śrāmaṇeras, his courage surpassed all others, and he delighted in bold and unconventional speech.
He told the king, the ministers, the brahmins, and the householders: "If anyone comes to attend upon the Buddha, Rāhula will certainly tell them, 'The Buddha is not here;
it is so that immeasurable people may not see the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him.
Once, when the Buddha had him wash his feet, Rāhula turned the basin upside down three times. The Buddha asked, 'Why do you not pour water? He replied, 'The basin is overturned.'"
[He] was able to pour [the water]. The Buddha said, "You are fond of exaggeration; it is like an overturned basin within the Buddha-dharma, wherein the water of the Dharma does not remain.
From now on, you must speak the truth. After a long time, he sought the Way but attained nothing, so he questioned the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "You have spoken to others about the emptiness of the five aggregates, yet you have not [realized it yourself]. He replied, "Not yet. The Buddha said, "You should speak it for others. Having finished speaking, once again—
He asked the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You have explained the twelve bases (*āyatana*) to others, but you have not yet explained the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Dharma is the gateway to attaining the Way. If you wish to attain the Way, you should explain it to others; once you have finished explaining it, you shall naturally attain the Way yourself. Later, he indeed attained the Way;
all craving and attachment were eliminated, and his births within the three realms came to an end. Now, the Buddha grants you this prediction for the future.
In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Dabaohuaruo (Treading upon the Seven-Jeweled Flowers);

his lifespan and his land shall be equal to those of Ānanda when he attains the fruit [of Buddhahood], for their spiritual lineages are identical, though he alone is designated as the "Elder Son of the Buddha."
The Layman Wujin (Vimalakīrti) said: "Ānanda will attain Buddhahood with the name King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain and Ocean Wisdom;
Rāhula will attain Buddhahood with the name Treading upon Seven-Jeweled Flowers; two thousand learners and non-learners will attain Buddhahood with the same name, Precious Appearance;
five hundred arhats will have the same name, Universal Radiance; and two thousand learners and non-learners will have the same name."
Baoshang and Guifeng said: "The sands of Ganges-river Buddhas enter my body, and my body pervasively enters the sands of Ganges-river Buddhas;
it is also like the twenty thousand Buddhas who shared the same name, Candrasūryapradīpa. Question:
Why is it that so many future Buddhas receive predictions? Answer: Because the essence of awakening is all-pervasive and the Buddha-body is omnipresent, they enter into the enumeration of names.
This is already in accordance with what is appropriate; if it were not so, who else would cultivate and realize [this]?

By inferring from the various implements of adornment used for offerings and service, we see that while their characteristics appear, they are not clung to, and while their nature is empty, it is not annihilated.
That which is rare and most precious is called a "jewel" (*ratna*); that which is firm and indestructible is "gold" (*suvarṇa*); that which is pure and free from defilement is...
That which is perfumed and universally renowned is incense; that which crushes the heterodox without wavering is a banner (*dhvaja*);
that which stands upright, manifesting victory, is a pennant (*patākā*); that which spreads out and provides shelter is a parasol (*chattra*);
that which unfolds and is beautiful is a flower; that which coalesces and bears fruit is a fruit; a stupa-temple is the locus of the *nirmāṇakāya*; and a necklace (*hāra*) is the *vipākaphala*.
That which adorns the body consists of three, five, six, seven, eight, or up to hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions;

internally, it does not exceed the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and externally, it does not exceed the retributions based upon those thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Once one receives the Buddha’s prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood, [these adornments are perfected].
This is why it is said that the appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter, occurring only once in a great while like the udumbara flower.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Ten: "The Dharma-Master.
At that time, the World-Honored One... [up to] "...the Lotus Sutra is the most supreme."

The Treatise says: The Sūtras contain two gates—contemplation and illumination—which are sublime skillful means. As it is said: "In a single thought-moment, universally contemplate immeasurable kalpas;
they neither come nor go, nor do they abide. By thus understanding the three periods of time, one transcends all other skillful means and accomplishes the Ten Powers.
Furthermore, it is said: "If one illuminates that the mind has no substance, then objects have nowhere to arise; this is the non-duality of mind and object."
When the substance of karma has entirely vanished, there remains only the Universal Radiant Wisdom, which is neither darkness nor light;

thus, ignorance is extinguished, and because the twelvefold false conditions are extinguished, what is called "receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, and expounding this sutra" refers precisely to the skillful means of contemplative observation. As the sutra says: "In the Lotus Sutra, even a single phrase..."
Those who uphold, recite, explain, transcribe, and offer various kinds of worship to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,

even out of compassion for sentient beings wishing to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze its wondrous Dharma— how much more so those who can uphold it and offer various kinds of worship!
Those who desire to awaken to the Single Buddha Vehicle should constantly contemplate with the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
[The Master] said: "It is merely that when emotional views (*qingjian*) are absent, great wisdom becomes even more luminous;

that the essence of the myriad dharmas is true and devoid of the characteristic of transformation is the knowledge and vision of the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), yet it is also a matter of contemplative skillful means (*guanzhao fangbian*). May this [skillful means] also be applied within the One Buddha Vehicle? [The Master] replied:
"If the residual habits of emotional views have not yet been eliminated, how could one possibly abandon contemplative skillful means? — *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Huayan).
The Treatise says: At the initial stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one clearly perceives the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
If residual habits (*vāsanā*) remain, they are purified by means of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*); there is no separate dharma that serves as an antidote to them.

It is simply through this knowledge and vision that one knows without thought (*amanasikāra*). Knowing without thought, attachment and aversion naturally become thin and faint, while compassion and wisdom naturally increase.

One should know that for those who thus uphold [this teaching] and are protected by the Buddha's mindfulness, karmic obstructions will naturally be destroyed and their meritorious practices will naturally reach perfection.

As the Sūtra says: "If, after my parinirvāṇa, a good man or good woman should secretly preach even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of a single person, you should know that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata."
They are those dispatched by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha again [approached] and stroked their heads with his hand.
The Commentary says: In the preceding section of the sūtra, it was taught that the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is constantly manifest in activity; now...
This teaching holds that because one is able to endure and accept [suffering] in an age of enmity and jealousy, the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata then covers them with a robe. This "robe" refers to gentleness and patience.
To fully realize that not a single phenomenon exists apart from one's own mind is called the power of great faith; to universally bestow this Dharma upon all sentient beings is called...
The power of aspiration, through the skillful means of observing with morality, concentration, and wisdom, brings about conformity; this is called the power of all roots of goodness.

Beginning from the stage of ordinary sentient beings until one attains the robe of the Tathāgata and dwells in the same chamber as the Buddha—this is indeed the ultimate degree of intimacy and conformity. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should know that such a person..."
"To dwell together with the Tathāgata is to have the Tathāgata’s own hand stroke one’s head.

Once, after Kāṇadeva had exhausted various non-Buddhist teachers with his unimpeded eloquence, he was walking in a grove when a disciple of those non-Buddhists slit open his belly with a knife, saying:
"You exhausted my teacher with your mouth and tongue; I shall now [revenge it] with..."
"Dao Kun, you have troubled me; can you still perform miracles? Thereupon, Deva’s five viscera were laid bare upon the ground, yet his life had not yet ended.
[Dao Kun] said to him: "I have my three robes and bowl, which remain in the meditation chamber. You must take them quickly and flee!

My disciples who have not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti) will harm you. You have not yet obtained the benefits of the Dharma; do not spare your body, do not spare your life, do not spare your weight."
The man who ranks himself is burdened by both body and name; now you are deceived by a mad mind and scorched by the poison of resentment.

The retribution for your sins is not yet finished, and you must receive it with bitter weeping. That which receives [the suffering] truly has no master; that which acts [to cause it] truly has no person.
When there is neither person nor master, who is it that inflicts such grief and cruelty? Seek the truth through the truth.

That which cannot be grasped yet is perceived as obscure is deluded by madness and inversion; the mind that perceives attainment becomes attached and hardened, giving rise to the notions of self, others, suffering, and pleasure.
Suddenly, the assembly of disciples arrived, collapsing in shock and crying out in such grief that their voices shook the mountains and valleys.
Deva said: "Regarding the reality of all phenomena, who is the enemy? Who is the victim? Who cuts? Who is being cut?"
"All dharmas have been severed at their very core; truly, there is no recipient [of harm]. Who, then, is the enemy?

You are deceived by the poison of delusion and, giving rise to false attachments and views, you cry out in lamentation. Do you not know that what was harmed by that person were your various wholesome rewards, and not me?
Having finished speaking, he passed away. As for Kāṇadeva, he was able to receive the protection bestowed by the Tathāgata.
...the one who wears these garments.
Wherever the Medicine King [is], there is the entire body of the Tathāgata.
The treatise states: The preceding text taught that in an age of resentment and envy, one should don the armor of gentleness and patience.
Robes serve as the remedy for conditions of hatred, envy, and hostility; these conditions do not arise spontaneously, but are produced because of the perception of a self and persons.
As a skillful means, one remedies them with the Dharma, just as medicine is used to treat a disease:
once the illness is cured, the medicine is discarded. One has never seen anyone who remains healthy without having first taken medicine. As the Sūtra says: "Wherever the King of Medicine resides..."
Whether it be where [this teaching] is expounded, read, recited, written, or where the scrolls of the sutra reside, one ought to erect a stupa made of the seven precious substances;
this is not said in vain. A stupa bears the symbol of nirvana, demonstrating that all things are in a state of quiescent extinction.
When all things are in a state of quiescent extinction, how could there be a world of resentment and jealousy? It is a world of gentleness and forbearance.
Yihu asked: "How do you know that the term 'stūpa' (塔) is a symbol for quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa)?
He replied: "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: 'The householder Viśvantara constantly made offerings at a sandalwood stūpa of the Buddha.
The commentator says: 'Sandalwood stops the heat and poison of snakes and vipers; the fragrance of wisdom and liberation eliminates the fever of all sentient beings.'"
Regarding the "Vexing the Stūpa": wherever an image of the Buddha is located, one now specifically sets up a seat; it is the gateway to liberation wherein empty wisdom is not extinguished.

It is also said that Mañjuśrī transformed and entered the human realm at the site of the Great Stūpa Temple to the east of the City of Awakening (*Bodhimaṇḍa*), where he turned and preached this sūtra titled the *Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*. The commentator says: "Stūpa."
Because it is the place of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), it is necessarily called a "great stūpa"; this demonstrates that the essence of the mind is ultimately quiescent.

While the previous mention of a "stūpa" referred to the location where the Buddha's physical image resides, the present mention of the stūpa as the place of quiescent extinction indicates that the physical image itself is quiescent—this is not annihilation.
As the Sūtra says: "Construct stūpas of the seven treasures, making them exceedingly high, vast, and magnificently adorned."

There is no need to further enshrine śarīra, for the adornment of the seven treasures is a mark of merit (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa*), and there is no need to further enshrine śarīra, for it is a mark of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
Since the adornment of wisdom by means of merit is not a doctrine of annihilation, the sutra states:
"Within this is the complete body of the Tathāgata."
"One should [venerate] this stūpa" (up to) "one shall attain the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Treatise says: The Sūtra states that because this sūtra is profound, solid, remote, and unfathomable, no one can reach it;

thus, it is the secret treasury of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) wherein all Buddhas themselves abide in the stage of *samādhi*. It is precisely because no one can reach it that [this teaching] is heard.
[They] will be startled, terrified, doubtful, and slanderous; yet, can it not ultimately be used to awaken sentient beings?
[The Buddha] said: "For the sake of sentient beings whose faculties are mature, one should employ images to demonstrate [the Dharma]. It is as if one were to say:
'In every place—whether it be spoken, read, recited, written, or wherever a scripture volume resides—one should erect a stupa made of the seven treasures, making it exceedingly high and wide.'"
There is no need to further install śarīra relics within this [stūpa]. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s entire body already resides herein, causing sentient beings to awaken and see for themselves without depending on words or written characters. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"This sūtra opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the true reality. This refers precisely to this point. As for those whose faculties have not yet matured...
Sentient beings might then feel intimidated by extensive explanations, parables, and verbal formulations; when these are being expounded, they may give rise to doubt and slander, saying:

"If, while this sutra is being preached, someone reviles one with foul language or strikes with knives, staves, tiles, or stones, one should endure it because of mindfulness of the Buddha. Therefore, the Buddha spoke with circumlocution and entrusted [the teaching], saying:
"You should extensively preach this sutra for the fourfold assembly. When it was said, "If, while preaching this sutra... and so forth, [the Buddha] provided this instruction.
To enter the Tathāgata’s chamber: the chamber of the Tathāgata is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

One should don the Tathāgata’s robe: the robe of the Tathāgata is the mind of gentleness and patience. One should sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat: the seat of the Tathāgata is the emptiness of all phenomena.
As for what is called the "chamber," it is the place of refuge; as for "sitting," it is the place of rest.

That which is worn is the rite of solemn adornment; it is precisely within this that one daily practices walking meditation, sits in quietude, looks up and down, and engages in conversation and laughter.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Abiding securely therein, one then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively preaches the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly"—this refers to this very point.

The Layman Wujin (Vimalakīrti) said: "If it is not doubted that the śrāvaka disciples have received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, why is it that the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all such classes as these are also granted predictions? He replied: 'These are all [surrounded by...']"

If the assembly circling the Buddha’s gathering to listen to the Dharma lacked a heart of reverence, a heart of joy, a heart of faith and acceptance, and a heart of compliance, how could they possibly be here?

Did not the Buddha say: "After my parinirvāṇa, if one can secretly preach even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of a single person, you should know that this person is an emissary of the Tathāgata, [sent by] the Tathāgata"?

Regarding those dispatched to perform the work of the Tathāgata, it is said: "If there are people in secluded places, I shall dispatch devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, and spirits to serve as their assembly for hearing the Dharma.
If one carefully examines these words of the Buddha, then those such as myself belong to the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*).
What we know is only the human realm; yet when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, the entire assembly [partakes in it].
If those born into their respective classes each attain understanding, then why should there be any doubt regarding the bestowal of predictions upon devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits?

Pei Xiu said: "Asuras are currently in a state of rage; the devas are in the midst of pleasure; ghosts and spirits are submerged in the suffering of profound sorrow; and birds and beasts harbor the grief of frantic flight.
To rectify the mind and its deliberations and advance toward Bodhi—only humans are capable of this. These words of Pei Xiu are a praise [of the human capacity].
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* is indeed excellent; yet, regarding the immeasurable and boundless compassion, wisdom, and vows of all Buddhas, it does not exhaustively describe them.

The Sūtra says: "If there be anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of this sūtra and rejoices with even a single thought, I shall likewise bestow upon them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. A 'single thought' is nothing other than this.
This is not a thought of "not-as-it-is. If one can thus accord with reality and rejoice accordingly, one will ultimately attain Buddhahood.
Just as when excavating high ground, if one gradually encounters moisture, one knows for certain that water is near; there is no room for doubt.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if one draws near to a Dharma Master and follows their teachings, how could one be far from the Buddha?
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
At that time, before the Buddha... [up to] "Excellent, excellent!
The treatise says: As the sutra states, at that time a great voice issued from within the jeweled stupa, praising and saying, "Excellent, excellent."
"How indeed! All that has been spoken by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni is truly real.
Is this great voice that which was spoken by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna?
If it were the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, he is a Buddha who entered parinirvāṇa in the past and should not be able to produce such sounds. Or is it the precious stūpa that is speaking?"
A stupa lacks the faculty of the tongue; since it lacks the faculty of the tongue, it should not be able to speak.
Yet the sutra further states that "this stupa of mine has emerged before you for the sake of hearing this sutra," as if the Buddha Prabhūtaratna were able to hear the sutra.
If this were so, then the Buddha Prabhūtaratna would be a Buddha who has entered parinirvāṇa in the past; and a Buddha who has entered parinirvāṇa should not...
If one can listen to the sutras by regarding them as a stupa or temple, then since a stupa lacks the faculty of hearing, it should not be able to listen to the sutras.
Observing this, one knows that while there is speaking, there is no speaking; while there is hearing, there is no hearing.
Thus, within the active discrimination and afflictions of sentient beings, he is the Tathāgata.
Nirvana is the mark of eternal quiescence. A question was asked: "The emergence of this jeweled stupa—its height, breadth, and magnificent adornment—are certainly not accidental;
may its underlying significance be heard? He replied:

"The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu said that the statement 'the stupa is five hundred yojanas high' demonstrates that it is produced by the pure, supreme, supramundane roots of goodness of all Buddha-lands."
For what reason? Because it is vast and pure; whereas the worldly roots of goodness that arise are neither pure nor vast. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:

"That which arises from supramundane roots of goodness is [the state] where the five—the five faculties (*pañcendriya*)—and the hundred—the hundred practices (*śata-karman*)—are perfected through the hundred practices supporting the five faculties. Thus, it is elevated above the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
Measuring two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth, it extends twenty-five *yojanas* outward;
it is said to "emerge from the earth" to refute the attachment to the eternalism of ordinary beings, and it is said to "abide in mid-air" to refute the nihilism of non-Buddhist outsiders.
It is adorned with various jewels and decorated with exquisite railings, niches, and chambers, resounding with [their] beauty.
By means of the sounds of precious bells and necklaces, all manner of virtues are accomplished and the myriad merits are adorned.
It is at such a time that Mahāpratibhāna appears.
The Treatise says: As the sutra states, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna made a profound and solemn vow:

"If my jeweled stupa appears before the Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra, and there is anyone who wishes to show my body to the fourfold assembly, then those emanations of that Buddha residing in the worlds of the ten directions shall be the emanations of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna."
Regarding the body, and observing the subsequent text, it says: "At that time, the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha gathered one after another in succession.
When Śākyamuni saw that all his emanated bodies had assembled, the entire assembly immediately beheld the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within that stupa, sitting upon a lion throne with his entire body."
Without distraction, as if entering meditative concentration, one realizes that even the Dharma-body lacks the principle of mutual seeing between self and other;
how then could there be the gathering of Śākyamuni’s emanations to cause the entire body of Prabhūtaratna to appear?
This Buddha has embedded his intention within these phenomenal events so that students may observe the signs and seek the truth for themselves; yet, in the end, none have succeeded.
The *Jñānakaraṇḍavyūha-sūtra* (or *Jñāna-utpatti-śāstra*) states: "If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately gather it back and abide in right mindfulness.
One should know that this 'right mindfulness' consists solely of mind, with no external objects.

What is meant by "if the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately gather it back and abide in right mindfulness" is the principle of the emanations from the ten directions gathering together; what is meant by "this" is...

For one who possesses right mindfulness, there is only mind and no external objects; thus the entire body remains undispersed, which is the principle of entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
If the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni were to assemble here and the whole body of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna were to appear, this would not be a matter of mere metaphorical description;
otherwise, it would be the clamorous and deluded false teachings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and could never be the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).

Regarding the teaching, an old commentary states: "This is intended to manifest that the two bodies of Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni in the same stupa are without distinction, that the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions who have gathered as emanations are no different, and that their bodies are my own body.
This is by no means the case; it is merely one of the ninety-six types of heterodox doctrines.
"Mahāpratibhāna, [from] me [to] the Tathāgata’s jeweled stūpa.
The treatise says: "The Buddha uses a single ray of light from his ūrṇā-kośa as a broad and long tongue that pervades the ten directions in order to summon all the Buddhas who are his emanations;
what is the intent of this? The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "All dharmas are originally..."
Coming [into being] is solely mind; in reality, there is no such thing as thought, yet through non-awakening, a deluded mind arises and perceives various objective realms;
therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When the nature of the mind does not give rise to [such] perceptions, this is precisely the meaning of the light of great wisdom.

If the mind gives rise to perceptions, then the characteristic of "non-perception" exists; when the nature of the mind is free from perception, this is the meaning of the universal illumination of the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, this ray of light is likely a manifestation of the state beyond thought and beyond vision.

If one does not discuss it in terms of physical manifestations, then since the Buddha already emitted the light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, which had already illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, why has he not yet withdrawn that light when he now emits another ray from the same white tuft?
Students should contemplate this deeply. The Sūtra says: "At that time..."
The Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "Sons of good family, we shall now proceed to the Sahā world to the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha.
What is the intention behind this? As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Within every single atom of all the worlds of the Flower Treasury, the Dharma-realm is seen; the radiant jewels manifest Buddhas gathering like clouds."

This is the Tathāgata’s own realm; this canopy is such in every thought-moment, such in every instant, such in every particle of dust, and such in every buddha-field—all are harmoniously integrated and subsumed within the image of one's own mind.

If one does not discuss it in terms of images, then the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni and the entire body of Prabhūtaratna would not be identical. How magnificent! Thus is accomplished the dharma that transcends emotion and is beyond compare.
The Buddha must pass through this gate, yet for the student to seek it through mere doctrine and principle is an error.
At that time, the Sahā world (up to) its ground was completely covered.
The treatise says: "From that time, the Sahā world immediately transformed into purity," up until "a single direction was divided."
His body was still not yet exhausted, marking the first transformation of the pure land.

Furthermore, at that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to accommodate the various Buddhas who were his emanations as well as the celestial jeweled flowers spread across the ground, manifested the middle transformation of the pure land.
Moreover, Śākyamuni Buddha [prepared] for the sake of the Buddhas who were to come and sit... [and so forth].

Heavenly jewel flowers are spread everywhere upon the ground; this constitutes the final transformation into a pure land. Question: What is the intention behind the Buddha’s three transformations of the pure land?
Answer: It is also a metaphor. It represents the destruction of the coarse and subtle marks of ignorance and affliction within ordinary sentient beings.
The first transformation changes the defiled land of Sahā into a realm adorned with various jewels and purified.
The defilement associated with the attachments of ordinary beings is what is called the "coarse within the coarse.

The transformation of two hundred trillion nayutas of realms into a vast and pure land is the sovereign mastery of sublime transformation, which is the "coarse within the subtle. Ultimately, it transforms two hundred trillion nayutas...
The objective realm is a subtle and wondrous land of non-obstruction; it is the sovereign liberation of all places, that which is the most subtle among the subtle.

Question: Having already become bewildered by the principle of the three transformations of the pure land, I am now further confused by the discourse on the coarse and the subtle, and I have lost my bearings.
I pray that you will provide a detailed explanation. Answer: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Conditioned..."
Delusively there is arising; because of arising, there is cessation. Arising and cessation are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called the True.
As long as one has not exhausted the discernment of the marks of arising and cessation, one is said not yet to have seen one's nature.

Therefore, the Buddha transformed his pure land three times to demonstrate the subtle marks of the arising and cessation of ignorance and afflictions, so that students might know their essential nature. — *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda Śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith)
The treatise says: There are two kinds of characteristics regarding the analysis of arising and ceasing. What are the two? First, those that are coarse and associated with the mind;
second, those that are subtle and dissociated from the mind. Furthermore, the coarsest among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
the subtle among the coarse and the coarse among the subtle are the realms of Bodhisattvas; [the subtlest among the subtle is... (Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
Regarding the statement "the subtle is the realm of the Buddha," the commentary explains: the faults of ignorance consist of six types of defiled minds.
The first three are coarse, while the latter three are subtle. As for the first three:

(1) the defilement associated with grasping, (2) the defilement associated with non-interruption, and (3) the defilement associated with discriminative cognition. It is said that the realm of ordinary beings constitutes the coarsest among the coarse.
This is because, among the three types of coarse defilements (*audārika-kleśa*), the defilement associated with mental correspondence (*samprayukta-kleśa*) is the most coarse.

If one does not sever these two—the defilement associated with mental correspondence and the defilement associated with discriminative cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna-samprayukta-kleśa*)—they are considered slightly less coarse within the category of the coarse.
To say that the realm of the Bodhisattva is "coarse within the subtle" is because of the present defilement of non-correspondence regarding form (*rūpa-viprayukta-kleśa*) and...
The ability to perceive the non-associated defilement of the mind and the fundamental karmic consciousness that is non-associated with defilement—these three types are all subtle.
Because they are equally non-associated, they are similar to the non-associated defilement of manifest form and the non-associated defilement of the perceiving mind;
thus they are called "subtle. Only the subsequent fundamental karmic consciousness is coarse, and is therefore termed "the coarse within the subtle."
That which is coarse, such as the Buddha’s realm, is the subtlest among the subtle;

for when the fundamental karma, its non-corresponding factors, and the defilements are not yet distinguished between subject and object, the mode of activity is extremely subtle, perceivable only by a Buddha. The old commentary states:

"The first transformation of the great trichiliocosm signifies reaching the stage of the Śrāvakas; the subsequent transformation of two hundred myriads of koṭis of nayutas of lands signifies reaching [the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas]."

The claim that the Pratyekabuddhas subsequently transform into two hundred others indicates the attainment of the stage of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) from the Two Vehicles (Dvayayāna) to its ultimate fulfillment;
therefore, it severely deviates from the intent of the sūtra and is utterly unreliable.
At that time, [from] the East [to all directions], one should make offerings to them all.

The Commentary states: Although the aforementioned passage in the Sūtra concerning the seven-jeweled stūpas containing the complete body of the Buddha demonstrates the essence of his parinirvāṇa, it does not yet reveal the meaning of parinirvāṇa as non-annihilation; therefore, it further describes the ability to manifest great [power].
The sound of praise extols how Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his impartial great wisdom, teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas.

Having already clarified that *nirvāṇa* is not annihilation, yet because it has not yet been seen that the bodies born of the dependent origination of the five aggregates have all realized this meaning, the Sūtra states:
"All sentient beings see the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within the [stupa of] jewels."
Within the stupa, he sat upon a lion throne, his entire body intact and undispersed as if having entered meditative concentration. Furthermore, one heard him say:
"Excellent, excellent! Śākyamuni Buddha, you have skillfully preached this Lotus Sūtra. It is for the sake of hearing this sūtra that I have come here.
At that time, the fourfold assembly beheld [the Buddha] from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas past.
The Buddha of Parinirvāṇa spoke these words, praising what had never before occurred:
"I shall scatter clusters of celestial jewel-flowers over the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha. Having said this, he added, "Śākyamuni Buddha, please take this seat.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stupa and sat upon half of that seat. Why was this?

To know this is to say that although it has already been stated that Buddhas who entered parinirvāṇa throughout immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas have passed away, yet to claim that they can now hear the sutra, praise Śākyamuni Buddha, enter his stūpa, and sit together with him upon the same seat—all of this is suspicious.
One asks: "What is suspicious about it? The answer is: "The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa."
The one who is in the state of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is Śākyamuni Buddha; the one who appears in the world is the Buddha born of conditions (*pratyaya-ja*).
Now, that which is in the state of quiescent extinction listens to the sutras and offers praise—this is the activity of the one born of conditions.

That the one born of conditions enters the stupa and sits side by side with the other—this is the characteristic of the one in the state of quiescent extinction. By this, one knows that [the Buddha] has manifested [these forms].
The bodies born of the dependent origination of the five aggregates are all realized.

The Inexhaustible Layman’s discourse says: "If it is said that from the Buddhas of the past to the Buddhas of the future, they all teach the Dharma for Bodhisattvas by preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and then bestow successive predictions of enlightenment, and that this has been so since the remote past of ancient Buddhas—is this not something that can be believed?"
Before this Buddha, a stupa made of the seven treasures emerged from the earth and hovered in mid-air, reaching as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
From within the stupa, a great voice issued forth, praising: "Excellent, excellent!

Śākyamuni Buddha, you are able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the great assembly; by opening and revealing it through your words, you cause that which has long been extinguished within the stupa to reappear."
This is because it enshrines the entire body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata.

Speaking in terms of realization and entry, the stupa emerges from the earth and dwells in the void, reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven; thus, it is equal and sovereign, without any distinction of high or low.
It emits great sounds, which are a cessation yet not a cessation. This body, though long extinguished, must await the aspiration of the fourfold assembly to appear.
When the Buddhas who are emanations from the ten directions gather and return to a single Buddha before appearing, then the one and the many are mutually identical.
The eight directions are transformed into a pure realm, and the various devas are moved to other lands. Many Treasures (Prabhūtaratna) offers half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha.
When the great assembly beholds these two Tathāgatas, their Buddha-seats appear high and remote; we pray that the Tathāgata will employ his spiritual power [to manifest them].
By means of their supernormal powers, they caused us all to dwell together in the void;
the Buddha, employing his own spiritual power, received us all into the air and, with a great voice, proclaimed to the fourfold assembly: "The Tathāgata will before long enter parinirvāṇa.
Desiring to entrust the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to those who exist, he asks: 'After my parinirvāṇa, who is able to protect and uphold it? He then spoke this vow himself."
Observing from this perspective, if the mind harbors notions of defilement and purity, then distinctions between this land and other directions, or between ordinary beings and sages, arise;

thus, the Buddha’s seat appears high and remote. Upon awakening to and entering into this, the nature and its manifestations become clearly distinct. When one is about to enter nirvana, what further cause for concern remains?
Someone may ask: "The Buddha spoke of the Buddhas of the past, such as Candrasūryapradīpa and Prabhūtaratna—how many Buddhas there were!"
As for names, Zhuangzi mentions Ronghuo, Datingshi, Bohuangshi, Zhongyangshi, Lilushi, Lixushi, and Hexushi.
Guanzi mentions those who ascended Mount Tai and performed the ritual of *shanchan* at Mount Liangfu seventy-two times.
Can one examine these by cross-referencing them with what is heard in the transmitted records? You consider this to be mere idle talk.
[End of Volume One].
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Devadatta.
At that time, the Buddha spoke... [until] born by transformation from a lotus flower.
The treatise says: Devadatta is translated as "Heaven-Heat. Because when he was born, the minds of both gods and men were heated with fervor, he was given this name.

He was the son of King Droṇodana and the younger cousin of the Buddha. Initially, his mother conceived after praying to the heavens; thus he was also named Devaśarman ("God-Given"). However, his conduct was perverse.
At the time when the Buddha’s transformation had already spread throughout the great trichiliocosm, all sentient beings were necessarily filled with reverence and faith.
Devadatta alone sought to harm him by concealing poison under his ten fingernails;
when he saw the Buddha and prostrated at his feet, the Buddha’s feet were not wounded, yet his own fingers fell off of their own accord.

Unable to contain his rage, he instructed King Ajātaśatru to release five hundred intoxicated elephants named Dhanapāla to charge the Buddha’s carriage. When the Buddha pointed his hand toward them, the intoxicated elephants beheld him.
The lion, seeing the ten fingers of the Buddha all manifesting [light], cowered in terror on the ground, voided its excrement, and fled.

Because he had been fond of ghee and ate it in excess, he suffered from a headache and groaned in pain. The Buddha heard him from afar and took pity on him; reaching out his hand, he rubbed the man's head, and the pain immediately ceased.
Greatly overjoyed, the man asked, "From where did you obtain such long hands? He looked closely at them and realized they were the hands of the Buddha, and then once again—
The Bhikṣu Utpalavarṇā became greatly enraged; seeing this, he again lost his temper without cause and struck her with his fist until she died.
The Buddha rebuked and admonished him, yet he did not repent. He once caused a schism in the Saṃgha and led five hundred bhikṣus away to be his own followers.
Śāriputra grew weary of him and fell into a deep sleep, while Mahāmaudgalyāyana used his hand—
He lifted it up and went away; upon waking, he was greatly enraged and vowed to take revenge.

He then hurled a great stone at the Buddha—the stone being thirty cubits long and fifteen cubits wide—but a terrestrial deity shielded him with his hand, causing the stone to shatter. The smaller fragments struck the Buddha’s foot, drawing blood.
Such are the nature of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*); yet the Buddha always felt compassion for them, and now [he] has attained [liberation].

Regarding the prophecy that he shall become a Buddha named T’ien-wang (Heavenly King) Tathāgata, why is it that the name of the world he shall govern—called T’ien-tao (Celestial Path)—and the names of the kalpa and the country, as well as his extraordinary retributions, are all left unmentioned? One might ask:
"Is there ever a case where the form is crooked while the shadow is straight? The Sui monk Zhiyi said: "This sutra has been translated four times in total upon its arrival in Zhendan (China). Now...

Regarding the two versions currently in circulation: the one translated by the Western Jin dynasty Indian monk Dharmarakṣa is titled *Zhengfahua* (The Lotus of the True Dharma), and it was he who further expounded the teachings received by Seng Dao’an.
The one translated by the Later Qin monk Kumārajīva of Kucha is titled *Miaofalianhua* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma); this was in the eighth year of the Hongshi era. Kumārajīva, too—
He was able to expound upon it extensively, and his disciple Sengrui succeeded him in the teaching seat, expanding it into nine similes and twenty-eight chapters;
however, this one chapter was withheld by the palace ladies, so that what was transmitted to Jiangdong consisted of only twenty-seven chapters.
The Liang dynasty monk Tanman lectured on it one hundred times, placing this chapter before the "Chapter on Upholding" (Chih-pin).

Thereupon, at Changsha, he performed self-immolation to repay the kindness of the Dharma; the monk Huisi had researched this [text] over three lifetimes and arranged its sequence after the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*),
which later coincided with the translation by Dharmarakṣa as if two halves of a tally were fitting together.
At that time, [the assembly from] the lower direction [down to] silently accepted it with faith.
The Commentary states: When the Sūtra uses an "elephant" as an illustration, it shows that words are unable to reach its subtlety.
Now, there are several kinds of elephants: some illustrate a single meaning, while others are capable of encompassing many meanings.
Question: What is meant by saying that various kinds of signs all exhaust a single meaning? Answer:
For example, the fact that the Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa remain within the jeweled stūpa with their entire bodies undispersed symbolizes the quiescence of one’s own mind.
Furthermore, the fact that they emit great sounds of praise, saying, "This stūpa has come because it heard the Lotus Sūtra," symbolizes...
The "elephant" refers to quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), not annihilation.
It is like Śākyamuni Buddha entering the Many-Jeweled Stūpa to sit side by side with the Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa;

this is because the body produced through the conditions of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) fully realizes the essence of quiescent extinction and spiritual awareness. Furthermore, it was asked: "What is meant by the 'one kind of elephant'?"
"Is this not the meaning of the multitude [of teachings]? He replied: "This sutra does not depend on stages of cultivation and realization;
it does not depend on the delusion or enlightenment of ordinary beings or sages; it makes no distinction between the forms of those in good or evil realms, nor between men and women;

it makes no distinction between new or old conditioning, nor between slow or swift attainment. Rather, it achieves [enlightenment] in the mere instant that the daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara offers her pearl."
The Perfectly Awakened One is the elephant. The *Huayan lun* states: "It is not as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* describes;
rather, it simply means that when one is free from biased views, great wisdom becomes ever more luminous, and the essence of all phenomena is truly without any aspect of change.
As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: Śāriputra said to the goddess, "For what reason do you not transform this female body? The goddess replied:
“Śāriputra, for twelve years I have sought the characteristics of a female body and could not find them at all;

how then could they be transformed? The girl Antichā said to Śāriputra, “I was born as a male, and you were born as a female. You should know that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is such as it is;
what is there to be transformed? It is like the entry into the Dharma-realm [as described] in the chapter on Sudhana.”
Beholding the fifty-three virtuous friends— Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs,
laymen, elders, youths, upāsikās, maidens, sages, and non-Buddhists— each fully possessing the practices of a bodhisattva and each fully possessing the Buddha-dharma,
they manifest different bodies according to the perceptions of sentient beings; yet it is said that there is no transformation in them.
When viewed with the Dharma-eye, there is nothing mundane that is not true; when viewed with the worldly eye, there is nothing true that is not mundane.
By means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, those of the three capacities whose provisional teachings have not yet exhausted their vision are caused to plant the seeds of faith.

Furthermore, by swiftly transforming the female form into Buddhahood, they are made to perceive this as extraordinary, only then giving rise to the resolve to advance toward true knowledge and vision, which they were previously unable to do.
This dharma-method gives rise to roots of goodness; this clarifies that the three provisional means are now drawn back to the one reality.

Furthermore, it shatters the fixed attachment to the kalpas of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, causing one to realize within a single *kṣaṇa* that the nature of the three periods of time is originally a single limit, without beginning or end, and equal to the Dharma.
It tears asunder the net of views regarding the Three Vehicles and sweeps away the weeds of the Bodhisattvas.
The hermitage causes one to return to the gate of the Dharma-realm and enter the true abode of the Buddha;

thus, it is made clear that the dragon girl attained Buddhahood not because of long cultivation in the past, but because she was only eight years old. Furthermore, this signifies that she did not rely on ancient study, and that the transformation from female to [Buddha] occurred within a single kṣaṇa.
Possessing the full practice of the Buddha-fruit without deficiency even by a hair’s breadth, the fundamental nature of all phenomena is such in its very essence.

At no time have you provisionally studied the three faculties, which have always kept you separated from the vision [of truth]. You are deluded regarding your own true reality, yet you mistakenly regard it as a transformation;
you do not realize that your own fundamental nature has always been thus. Now, while dwelling within this very house, you still harbor lingering views.

How can you point toward the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas beyond the realms? This view does not depart, and you will certainly deviate for eternal eons. Only when you turn your mind back and these views are exhausted will you finally return to the original state.
Dwelling as one does now, one must diminish the karma of various views; only after enduring the hardships and tribulations of many kalpas will one finally return [to the source].

As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies in the "Gate of Dharmadhātu Dependent Origination," the single reality of ordinary beings and sages remains constant, yet it is separated by views. When views persist, one is an ordinary being;

when views are forgotten, one is a Buddha. The dependent origination that accords with the nature (dharmatā) is such that every movement—looking up or down, advancing or retreating, bending, stretching, bowing, or showing respect—is itself Bodhi.
In the practice of the Bodhisattva, there is not a single dharma that possesses a nature subject to transformation, for all dharmas are devoid of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;

thus, this is not the same as the Dragon Girl who transformed her body to become a Buddha. However, regarding what is shown in the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), it is because the Dharma is fundamentally such that one does not realize that the Dragon Girl’s transformation into a Buddha in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is merely an "elephant" [a metaphorical illustration]. Consequently, they take this "elephant" to be a substantial reality and thereby hold it in high esteem.
Is it appropriate to disparage this? Consider the case of the youth Sudhana, who ascended the summit of Mount Māyāgiri and could not see the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī;
he had to go to another peak before he could see him. Furthermore, when he reached the presence of Maitreya’s pavilion, the gate would not open until he tapped it with his finger to awaken him.
Both of these instances are likewise illustrative. Moreover, it was on a different peak that...
Is it not like realizing and deliberating upon it only after seeing the snap of a finger?
The Layman Wujin’s discourse says: "In many kalpas, the Buddha once served as a king;
for the sake of seeking the Dharma, he relinquished his royal throne and attended upon a rishi for a thousand years. The rishi then expounded for him the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
The seer was Devadatta. It was because of Devadatta as a spiritual friend that I became fully endowed with the six pāramitās, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; the purple-golden hue;
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four means of integration, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; and the path of supernatural powers.
Vīrasena’s attainment of perfect enlightenment and his renunciation of the royal throne demonstrate the impermanence of sensual pleasures.
His service to the rishi demonstrates the difficulty of encountering a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

That a rishi was able to instruct the Buddha demonstrates that the Dharma is transmitted through the oral lineage and realized within the mind by the Buddha. Therefore, Sudhana traveled south to seek spiritual friends one by one.
Having served fifty-five spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) throughout various Dharma-gates, Śākyamuni perfected the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;

yet the ultimate goal [of their practice] was one and the same. Fearing that his disciples might hear of such arduous toil and difficulty in attaining the Buddha-way and thus become discouraged or retreat, he further used the inquiry of Jñatikauṇḍinya to ask Mañjuśrī whether there are any sentient beings who can achieve success quickly.
The Buddha did not explain to Mañjuśrī that the eight-year-old dragon girl of Sāgara, being fully endowed with merit,
could attain Bodhi. Jñānakūṭa said, "The Tathāgata has never, throughout the three thousand great thousandfold world system,
failed to sacrifice his body and life for the sake of sentient beings— even down to a space as small as a mustard seed— yet he has thereby attained Bodhi."
Believing that this woman would attain Buddhahood in a mere moment, Śāriputra also declared that she was hindered by the five obstacles and was not a vessel for the Dharma.
At that time, the dragon girl offered a priceless jewel to the Buddha;
as soon as the Buddha accepted it, she was transformed into a man and attained equal and perfect enlightenment in the southern world-realm called Vimalā. Viewed from this perspective...
For one who skillfully receives and upholds the Lotus Sūtra, that which occurs in an instant is not swift, and that which spans immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas is not distant.
The Three Vehicles are not provisional, and the One Vehicle is not ultimate.
When all dharmas are interfused, the Dhāraṇī of the Revolving Dharma-Sound through Expedient Means manifests clearly before one.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Thirteen: Encouragement to Uphold.
At that time, Bhaiṣajyarāja... [up to] "...the Buddha himself knew my mind.
The commentary states: Eight thousand persons, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because the people of the Sahā world were corrupt and evil, desired—
While this sutra was being extensively taught in other lands,
the bhikṣuṇīs Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā also desired to extensively teach this sutra in other lands; the Buddha then looked upon eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas,
regarding the eight thousand learners and non-learners and the six thousand bhikṣus as inferior.
Because the aspirations of the bhikṣuṇīs were not yet vast, the bodhisattvas initially hoped that the Buddha would clearly issue an instruction;
however, as the Buddha remained silent and spoke nothing, they knew where his intention lay—just as a fine horse perceives the shadow of a whip.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence for and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, and desiring to fulfill their own original vows..."
Then, before the Buddha, they let out a lion’s roar and made this vow:

“World-Honored One, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions, causing all sentient beings to copy, uphold, read, recite, explain the meaning of, and practice according to the Dharma this sutra with right mindfulness; all of this is through the majestic power of the Buddha.”
I earnestly pray that the World-Honored One, while remaining in other lands, will behold us from afar and provide protection;
thus we shall know that the Buddha’s resolve is such that this sutra is not abandoned to an age of turbidity, evil, hatred, and jealousy.

As for those who recite these verses with one voice, they speak exclusively of firmly maintaining the power of patience (*kṣānti-bala*), just as a master mariner does not fear the perils of surging waves, but only...
Fearing that the bulwarks and rudders might not be secure, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If there were good sons or good daughters who, with as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, practiced giving;

yet if there were another person who, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, or even recite a single four-line verse for others, the merit of the latter would be far greater. At that time, Subhūti...
Upon hearing this sutra being preached, Pūrṇa deeply understood its meaning and purpose; he wept with tears of sorrow and said to the Buddha, "It is rare, World-Honored One!
Since the Buddha has preached such a profound sutra as this, I have never before heard a scripture like it since I first attained the eye of wisdom.
The commentator says: [This was said] to cause one to abandon indolence and the pleasure of gain and offerings.
Regarding "tasting": it means that the merit of such bodily life gained through giving is by no means equal to the merit of upholding a four-line verse.
Thus, one might become attached to a single body and fall into indolence; is this not the body itself acting as an obstacle?
As for the "four-line verse," it is the constant cultivation of the contemplation that there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.
That one can propagate this sutra in an age of turbidity, evil, hatred, and jealousy is why Subhūti wept upon hearing it.

The *Awakening of Faith* says: "One should endure the afflictions of others and harbor no intent for retaliation; one should also endure all wholesome deeds with a mind free from indolence or retreat.
One's resolve must be firm and strong, remaining far removed from cowardice and weakness; one should constantly reflect upon past transgressions."
"Since the distant past, one has experienced all manner of great physical and mental suffering without any benefit. To explain this:

throughout countless kalpas, in the pursuit of worldly objects of desire, one has encountered the severing of body and life, yet ultimately there has not been even a fraction of flavor [to be gained].
To counter these conditions, one should apply oneself with diligent vigor and establish a firm resolve.
Because such a person can render the objective field compliant, can contemplate the essential characteristics of all things, can prevent the conditions from diverging,
and can accomplish difficult worldly and world-transcending tasks— if they constantly do not forget this resolve,
they will be able to propagate this sutra in an age of turbid evil, hatred, and jealousy. This applies both to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra*.
The account provided here merely describes how one cannot endure suffering and thereby loses great benefit, urging one to exert further diligence.
However, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says that patience (*kṣānti*) is the most excellent and wondrous practice;
when encountering such conditions, one should form this thought: "If I were to retaliate against him with anger, I would be harming myself. Furthermore, in my past lives..."
Since these transgressions exist, one cannot have things as one wishes; they must inevitably be repaid.

If one does not accept them from this person, others will likewise harm me, and neither can escape [the consequences]. Why, then, give rise to anger? Furthermore, patience is like mother-of-pearl, capable of polishing all merits.
If someone inflicts evil upon one, it is like a pig rubbing against a mass of gold; it only serves to further manifest its brilliance. This is because one seeks the Buddha-way.
Because it is a sharp instrument for saving sentient beings, it is said that patience is the most excellent and wondrous practice.
Thus, in the Western Regions, there is a priceless jewel called *kāca* (lapis lazuli): if it falls into mud, it immediately surges upward, rising a fathom high;
if placed in turbid water, it causes the turbid water to become as clear as dust; yet it remains settled only within pure water. If...
Just as when one places [a jewel] in a *pudgalaka* grove, a sublime fragrance is emitted that wards off all foul odors and causes them to depart far away;
so too does the Bodhisattva’s power of patience in this degenerate age act like a jewel in a *pudgalaka* grove,
emitting the fragrance of all-knowing vision and warding off the filth of all hatred and envy.

The Dharma Master Wujin (Inexhaustible) said: Since the Buddha has already proclaimed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the dharma protected by all Buddhas, to the fourfold assembly, he observed with his boundless wisdom and sovereign supernormal powers that sentient beings of the future would have meager roots of goodness and weak power of faith;
that those who slander it would be many while those who uphold it would be few; and thus he spoke [this teaching].
“Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata has long since entered parinirvāṇa, yet he has come for the sake of the Dharma.
In the past, for the sake of seeking this Dharma, I renounced my kingdom and served as an attendant to sages. Now that I have finished preaching the Dharma, who among you is able to protect it?
You should all make great vows. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and twenty thousand others from this assembly...
The reporters made a vow with one voice, saying: "We do not worry; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and widely expound this sutra.
The Buddha beheld eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas, and each of these bodhisattvas thought to themselves:
"The World-Honored One remains silent and does not issue a command to us; we shall respectfully comply."
The Buddha’s intention was also to fulfill his own original vow; he then uttered a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made this solemn declaration:

"After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions, enabling sentient beings to copy, uphold, read, recite, explain the meaning of, and practice according to the Dharma this Sūtra on Emptiness."
Yet, as for this signless quiescence that is without essence, it cannot endure without faith and acceptance, nor can it be maintained without the power of aspiration.
Thus, twenty thousand bodhisattvas were granted predictions and earnestly entrusted with the teaching; each made great vows, and so it was.
This extended even to eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas, who, without waiting for further instruction, respectfully complied.
When the Buddhas each give rise to great vows, then the path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas exists within the space of a glance;
together they proclaim its meaning and speak these verses, which are far-reaching.
