The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Fourteen: The Practices Leading to Peaceful Bliss.
At that time, Mañjuśrī... [up to] preached the Lotus Sūtra.

The commentary states: As previously mentioned in the text, it says that one must enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat before preaching this sūtra;
this is because such actions represent the ultimate degree of intimacy and conformity [to the Buddha], starting from the level of ordinary beings.

To be born in this land and yet be able to possess great compassion, gentleness, and patience, and to realize the emptiness of all phenomena—how could this be attained were it not for the ultimate intimacy and conformity [to the Dharma], and the profound acceptance, protection, and mindfulness of the Buddha?
Now, it is merely said that in the future evil age, those who wish to preach this sutra should abide in four dharmas; the first is:
These refer to those who, while about to approach, follow, and attend upon [the Buddha], abide on the ground of patience and contemplate all phenomena as empty according to their true nature;
second, who provide seats and couches and put on fresh, clean robes; third, who conceive the thought of him as a great compassionate father;
and fourth, who give rise to a mind of great compassion. How is this made clear? It is said that the preceding words describe this very point.

This sutra now states that because it intends to preach this very sutra, it previously mentioned "donning the Tathāgata’s robe and sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat," whereas here it mentions "providing a bed and seat and donning new, clean robes.

Because it previously mentioned "entering the Tathāgata’s chamber," it refers here simply to conceiving the thought of the Great Compassionate Father and giving rise to the mind of Great Compassion. Thus, by this one knows that these cases are not the same.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "It is like a traveler who suddenly receives a magnificent mansion from the Heavenly King;
though he has obtained a great dwelling, he must enter through the gate. Thus, for the initial cessation of delusions, nothing is as essential as *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

From *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one realizes concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). From concentration and wisdom, one is able to harmonize with the mundane world (*sāṃsārika-dhātu*). From harmonizing with the mundane world...
This is indeed what constitutes the convergence of compassion. What is meant by "stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*)? The Sūtra says:

"Abiding on the ground of patience, it is through the power of patience alone that one can dissolve adverse conditions. That which is called "the mind being neither impetuous nor startled" is "stopping" (*śamatha*), like a mountain that does not move.
As for "not engaging in any activity regarding phenomena while contemplating all phenomena as they truly are," this is "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Emptiness, being empty, is free from the marks of conceptual discrimination; thus it is said that "neither practicing nor discriminating" refers to the provisional (the conventional).
To contemplate emptiness without obstructing the provisional is the contemplation of phenomena within the provisional.
In the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, when the youth Sudhana ascended Mount Māyā on its peak, he [surveyed] the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above.
Looking downward in observation and seeking him with longing to see the bhikṣu Dechen (Guṇamegha), he passed seven days before seeing that bhikṣu walking slowly in *caṅkrama* on a separate mountain.
The commentator says: "The 'Exquisite Peak Mountain' (*Miaofengshan*) represents the image of *śamatha* (calm abiding);
'observing in all ten directions' represents the image of *vipaśyanā* (insight); and 'dwelling predominantly in *śamatha*' represents the prevention of the extreme of sinking."

Regarding the seven days of guarding against distracted speech during contemplation: one uses the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) to investigate and advance, thereby eliminating both lethargy and agitation;
thus it is said that "walking slowly" implies not being bound by distraction, while "wandering" implies not dwelling [in stillness].
Only when purity and concentration are unified can one truly attain realization. One should follow the example of the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī; this is the proper sphere of practice.
What is meant by "concentration and wisdom"? The Sūtra says: "Kings, princes, ministers, officials, and elders are assemblies characterized by haughty pride and self-important airs;

they are spheres of seeking and sycophancy. Regarding the mention of "non-Buddhists, brahmins, and Nirgranthas," the brahmins are those who have left the household life yet hold false views, while the Nirgranthas are those who remain in the household life yet hold false views. Thus it is said.
Worldly literary compositions that praise non-Buddhist texts consist of flowery yet groundless speech and heterodox, syncretic learning.
Regarding *Lokāyata*, it refers to the discourse in which the teacher refutes the disciple;
regarding *Pratilokāyata*, it refers to the discourse in which the disciple refutes the teacher. As for "vicious games," these refer to boxing, wrestling, and *nagna* (wrestling with the naked).
The various transformations and performances such as those of the *nara* and others are the distractions and inverted habits of worldly toil (*kleśa*), objects for the eyes and ears to behold.
*Nara* here means "power" (*bala*); *caṇḍāla* means "rigid insignia" (*cihna*).

This refers to those who adorn themselves with their karma and carry out their practice according to specific marks and signs. It refers to the bodies of women, as well as young girls, virgins, and widows.
Even those of the five kinds of impotent persons, young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, and children are a swift path to the evil realms and a fierce flame that burns the roots of grass;
these are all conditions that obstruct the Path and signs of defilement in this degenerate age.
A Bodhisattva who propagates the sutras should not associate with any of them. Those whom one should associate with are as follows: [text continues].
It is simply a matter of concentration and wisdom; thus the Sūtra says: "He always delights in sitting in meditation, dwelling in a secluded place to cultivate and restrain his mind.

When the youth Sudhana arrived at the village of Malli, he searched everywhere for the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja and saw him by the side of a walking path, seated in the full lotus posture, having entered into samādhi, free from inhalation and exhalation.
Regarding the interpretation by Biesijue (Bie-si-que): it is said that this clarifies the mastery of both quiescence (*śamatha*) and activity (*vipaśyanā*).
To speak of "walking" (*caṅkrama*) refers to activity; to speak of "samādhi" refers to quiescence. Quiescence exists in dependence upon activity.

As for the term "side" (*ze*), it means not dwelling within either quiescence or activity, but being spontaneously and freely sovereign. Thus, apart from inhalation and exhalation, it is called "quiescent" in accordance with principle.
Principles function through the nature which is inherently all-pervasive; this is not the same as the realization of quiescence attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles.

One should follow the example of the Bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, for this is the primary stage of close approach. When the Sūtra speaks of "contemplating all dharmas as they truly are," it clarifies that one must see with self-confidence and be free from error;
for where there is conceptual discrimination, there is perversion. Where there is... [text fragment ends]
Where there is doubt, there is agitation; where there is fear, there is retreat; where there is delusion, there is turning back.
Yet within the nature of emptiness, which is devoid of all existence, there is not even cessation—how could there be birth?
There is not even disappearance—how could there be emergence? There is not even stillness—how could there be arising? By this one knows that it is due to the inversion of causes and conditions.
One cannot know this as it truly is; however, to enter this essential method of contemplation, one must necessarily possess courageous diligence and firm resolve.
Therefore, the sutra expresses its profound intent within the verses, stating:
"In the future evil age, there shall be no mind of fear," and "The bodhisattva acts with a mind free from fear," and "When this sutra is being preached, there is no..."
There was one who was timid, yet it is said that his mind was peaceful and free from timidity.
When the youth Sudhana arrived at the village of Sāgaratīra, he observed the ten directions in search of the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita.

He saw this bhikṣu coming and going, walking back and forth in the midst of the sky. The commentary explains: "By means of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), he observes the three realms with subtlety."
Because the cultivation of pure karma manifests before them, they realize the ten dharma-gates of non-obstruction;
and because they are solely unobstructed, they come and go and walk back and forth within empty space. One should be like the Bhikṣu Sunetra;
this is the second place of intimacy.
Furthermore, from Mañjuśrī... [it is] impossible to exhaustively describe it. The *Śāstra* asks:
"What is meant by 'conforming with the dust' (*rajas-tulya*)? It says:

The Sūtra states that whether one is proclaiming [the Dharma] orally or reading the scriptures, one does not delight in speaking of the faults of persons or the scriptures, and thus forgets such talk. Furthermore, it says that one also does not treat others with contempt.

The Dharma Master forgets his self; furthermore, he says that he does not speak of the good or evil, the long or the short of others, nor even mentions their names to praise their virtues—this is forgetting the conditions.

Furthermore, he says that he does not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion—this is forgetting the mind. Indeed, by forgetting words one reaches the forgetting of the self; by forgetting the self one reaches...
When one forgets conditions, and through the forgetting of conditions reaches the forgetting of the mind, then one surveys the world with a sense of weary detachment;
thus it is said that one skillfully cultivates such a mind of peace and bliss. That one does not oppose their intentions means arising in accordance with conditions.

To answer invariably with the Mahāyāna is to respond according to the inquiry. It is solely through the power of patience and the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) that [this is achieved].
Because one must possess profound discernment to be able to act in this way, the verse says: "The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma for peace and security;
on pure ground he provides seats and couches, anoints his body with oil, bathes away dust and filth, and wears fresh, clean garments, so that both internally and externally he is pure.
When the youth Sudhana arrived at the country of Trayastriṃśa, he went through its cities, towns, villages, hamlets, and marketplaces.

He searched everywhere throughout rivers, plains, mountains, and valleys for the bhikṣu Sudarśana, until he saw him walking back and forth in meditation within a forest grove—of vigorous age, handsome, upright, and pleasing. The commentator says:
"searching everywhere throughout" refers to being in accord with worldly dust (*rajas*); "vigorous age and handsome appearance" refers to the marks of one who accords with worldly dust.
Only when the mind is detached from the world is one fit to dwell among the laity, harmonizing with others to benefit sentient beings.

As for the statement that he was currently practicing walking meditation in the forest, although he manifested conduct that appeared to mingle with the dust of the world, he did not remain stagnant within this pure practice;
he should be understood as being like the Bhikṣu Sudarśana, who thus accomplished the third dharma-practice.
Furthermore, from "Mañjuśrī" up to "there is no fault.
The treatise asks: What is meant by "conforming to compassion"? The Sūtra states:

"One should give rise to the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings"—does this not mean that one must not further expose what they have not yet attained? It says: "One should give rise to the thought of a compassionate father toward all Tathāgatas."
How could one dare to forget that which one must not fail to keep in mind?
When speaking of generating the perception of a Great Teacher toward all Bodhisattvas, up to and including reverently bowing in worship—how could one ever repay the kindness of their Dharma-path?

When speaking of preaching the Dharma with equality toward all sentient beings, up to and including having a deep love for the Dharma—not preaching excessively—is this not so? How could it be otherwise?

There are those who turn their backs on the practice of compliance; one should feel compassion for those who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta, take refuge in those who have already ascended the Unsurpassed Path, and love and respect those who practice the Bodhisattva path alongside them.
Furthermore, when bestowing the Dharma upon sentient beings, one must not contravene the principle of compliance. A Bodhisattva who propagates this sutra in the evil age is like this.
This application of the mind is called the third practice of peaceful conduct (*anurakṣaṇā-pratipatti*).

In an evil age, one who does not forget gentleness, patience, and fierce diligence does so by means of wisdom; thus the verse says: "The son of the Buddha, when preaching the Dharma, is always gentle and able to endure;
with compassion for all, he gives rise to no mind of indolence. Question: As previously shown, all of these...
That a Bodhisattva practices the "Peaceful Conduct" (Anurakṣita-caryā) through wisdom in an evil age reveals the underlying principle of compassion for those who have not yet heard this sutra.
As the Sutra says regarding those among householders and renunciants:

it means that one who has already resolved for Bodhicitta but does not yet know this sutra should give rise to great compassion and preach it for them, bestowing happiness upon those who are not yet Bodhisattvas.
Regarding those among human beings who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta and do not yet know this sutra, one gives rise to great compassion and explains it to them to uproot their suffering.

As for those individuals who do not know, do not believe, and do not understand, one draws them in by means of the power of supernormal faculties and the power of wisdom, causing them to abide within this Dharma; this is the application of wisdom.
It is clear that this accords with compassion. When the youth Sudhana arrived at the place of the Ocean Tide, he entered the Land of Universal Adornment and surveyed it everywhere.
There he saw the laywoman Śreṣṭhadattā seated upon a sublime throne, who addressed Sudhana, saying:
"The Buddhas of the eastern direction constantly come to this place, where they preach the Dharma for me while seated upon this jewel throne; so too do those of the south, west, and north."
"All the Buddhas of the four quarters, the four intermediate directions, above, and below have come here to this place and, seated upon the jewel throne, preach the Dharma for me.
Good son, I am never separated from seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and dwelling together with all the Bodhisattvas.
To explain this: the Buddhas of the ten directions have all come to the place where I sit upon the jewel throne.
To preach the Dharma for me is the manifestation of the union of compassion and wisdom: the laywoman Śūradattā represents compassion, while the Buddhas of the ten directions represent wisdom.
One should act in accordance with the laywoman Śūradattā; this is the accomplishment of this fourth dharma-practice.
"Constantly [acting as] a bhikṣu... (up to) "...the various merits mentioned above.
The treatise says: When the Buddha first went from the Deer Park to Vulture Peak Mountain, he expounded the teachings in succession according to the capacities [of his listeners].
If the faculties of sentient beings were not yet mature, it was inappropriate to preach the Mahāyāna; once they had matured, [he did so].
It is not appropriate to speak of minor dharmas; one should first speak of the Hīnayāna. The Hīnayāna consists purely of existence (*bhava*).

Because ordinary beings are fettered by and attached to worldly phenomena, they regard them as truly existent. Following after the objects of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), they commit various unwholesome deeds;

because of these unwholesome acts, they fall into the realms of suffering. Consequently, they use the dharmas of existence as reins to restrain their minds, and thus employ the precepts for protection.
Because these are all unwholesome dharmas, the Prajñāpāramitā is explained next. "Prajñā" means to destroy existence (*bhava*) and clarify emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
That is to say, the Small Vehicle [teaches] that things truly exist to establish a model for training, thereby regulating the actions of body, speech, and mind so they abide in wholesome dharmas.

Once the contemplations such as the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) have been taught, one then explains the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) to break through attachment to those [phenomena], gradually leading toward the Dharma.
Following the discussion of the body [of the Buddha], the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is next explained.

"Unraveling the profound mystery" (*saṃdhinirmocana*) means to reconcile emptiness and existence so that those with extremist views do not become stuck in either of the two gates; thus, it is neither non-empty nor non-existent.

Since the followers of the Two Vehicles have extinguished their consciousness and realized quiescence—abiding in silence and lacking the desire for knowledge—the text establishes the nine consciousnesses as the purely pure consciousness (the *āmalavijñāna*) in order to redirect this spiritual capacity. [The text further discusses] the five and six [consciousnesses].
The seventh, eighth, and other consciousnesses always take the ninth consciousness as their support;

yet ordinary, ignorant people do not understand this and falsely grasp it as a self, just as a torrential waterfall does not exist apart from the substance of water. Once this mechanism is reversed, it causes these consciousnesses to become wisdom.

Because those of the Two Vehicles harbor fear toward the seeds of karma within birth and death in the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses, [the Buddha] feared they would find it difficult to believe.

By means of skillful expedients (*upāya*), one establishes the name "pure consciousness" (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) as distinct from *saṃsāra*, gradually inducing it to retain its delusions without extinguishing them;
thus, one hopes that compassion and wisdom will gradually arise. As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

"In this way, although a bodhisattva relies on the abiding of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti*) and takes wisdom as their support, they gradually cause views of emptiness to reach the stage where consciousness becomes gnosis (*jñāna*). Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* is subsequently taught.

Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it takes the direct approach as the root of the Mahāyāna. For those who are capable of receiving it, it teaches suddenly that the eighth consciousness, the seed-consciousness of karma, is named the Tathāgata-garbha consciousness.
It is said that when one grasps at characteristics, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*);

when one does not grasp at characteristics, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Furthermore, it is said: "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) abides eternally, yet it is moved by the winds of objective realms. This is because this sutra is direct.
Regarding the seeds of karma within ignorance, through the gateway of clear wisdom, one realizes that the nature of clarity and ignorance is non-dual;
yet, it is said that while the seeds of karma within ignorance are transformed into wisdom, this is still rare and transcends the mundane, as it does not yet manifest in common with worldly dust.
Therefore, next, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* is taught. As for the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, it does not [regard] the śrāvakas of the two vehicles or the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles as...
He is one who knows the Dharma; therefore, even the ten great disciples and the Bodhisattvas Maitreya and Prabhāvyūha did not dare to challenge his eloquence.
He takes Mañjuśrī as the Dharmakāya and Vimalakīrti as the conduct of entering the marketplace.
Thus, the Dharmakāya is the essence and the conduct is the function; these essence and function engage in mutual inquiry and response, forming the three [aspects].

For those who, relying on the joy of study, seek the principle of suchness-emptiness, detest the provisional to cultivate the real, and only attain Buddhahood after accumulating practices over many lifetimes—so that they may realize the simultaneous unity of the dharma-realm’s nature and characteristics, phenomena and principle, and cause and effect—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is subsequently taught. Thus it is said:
"It is like a powerful king who has long guarded a bright jewel, and now finally bestows it upon him."
The Discourse on the Discussion between the Layman Wujin and Qiang Shangying states:

When Mañjuśrī saw that the bodhisattvas were reverently complying with the Buddha’s intention and had made great vows, he harbored doubts regarding the difficulty of preaching this sutra in the evil world of the future. The Buddha said, "If you wish to preach this sutra, you should abide securely in four dharmas.
These four dharmas are the "Peaceful and Joyful Practices" (*sukha-vihāra*). As for the first practice: do not engage in [unwholesome conduct].
One should not approach what is improper to approach; one who practices the second [vow] should not speak of the faults of others;
one should not harbor resentment or malice; one who practices the third [vow] should not harbor flattery or jealousy, nor should they be arrogant or negligent;
and one who practices the fourth [vow] should give rise to great compassion toward those in the household life and those who have left it, as well as toward those who are not bodhisattvas.

One should give rise to the mind of great compassion and abide in these four practices of peace and joy: to bring peace to others and to find joy oneself; having found joy oneself, one brings peace to others. Only after this can the sutras be widely proclaimed and the Dharma be long maintained. If one does not possess these four practices of peace and joy, then even if śrāvakas were as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds, and pratyekabuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— [The text continues: ...it would be of no avail. Why does the Buddha alone oppose their intentions? It is said that in this chapter, the Buddha demonstrates that [the propagation] occurs naturally through the power of the Dharma.
Cultivation is what is valued, while those who cultivate while despising the power of illusion and remaining unawakened are held in contempt.
How is this known? The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* sets forth three types of contemplation: first, quiescence; second, the illusory-like; and third, cessation.
When the Buddha spoke these to the Bodhisattva Praśāntarutasvara, he said: "If bodhisattvas grasp only at extreme stillness, and by means of that stillness..."
By the power [of the Buddha], up to: if bodhisattvas contemplate only that which is like an illusion by the power of the Buddha;
or if bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions and do not grasp at their functioning—these three types are said to be practicing based on the power of illusion while it is not yet realized.
When explained for the sake of bodhisattvas who possess sovereign majestic power, it is said:
If bodhisattvas, having awakened to pure, perfect enlightenment, take stillness as their practice with a mind of pure awakening;
or if bodhisattvas, having awakened to pure, perfect enlightenment, know the nature of the mind through a mind of pure awakening;
or if bodhisattvas, having awakened to pure, perfect enlightenment, do not grasp at illusory transformations or any signs of stillness with a mind of pure awakening—then...
Regarding these three types [of practitioners], one must first speak of awakening to the pure, perfect *bodhi* before subsequently initiating practice and cultivation;

this is called "approaching and conforming. Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles in the Pure Lands cultivate by relying on the power of faith, and thus it is not said that they awaken to the pure, perfect *bodhi*.
Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body on the *bhūmis*, however, cultivate by relying on the power of the Dharma.

Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All are in close proximity to and accord with Perfect Enlightenment. This is not limited to the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*; the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* also says:
"The distinctions between the perfuming of essence and function are further divided into two kinds. What are these two?

First is 'non-correspondence,' which refers to ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, all of whom [perceive] by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)."
Through the power of faith, one is able to practice; because one has not yet attained non-conceptual mind, one accords with its essence.
Because one has not yet attained mastery over karma, one accords with its function.

When these two have already accorded—meaning that a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body has attained non-conceptual mind and accords with the wisdom and function of all Buddhas—one relies solely upon [this].

Because the power of the Dharma naturally perfumes and cultivates practice within True Suchness (*tathatā*), thereby extinguishing ignorance, the Sūtra states that the Buddha addressed the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas:
"Stop, sons of good family! You need not protect and uphold this Sūtra.
This is because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is not for those who practice based on an unawakened illusory power; therefore, it refers to other lands.

as explained at length in this sutra. Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* relies solely on the power of the Dharma for natural cultivation—
where "natural cultivation" means practicing in accordance with it— the old commentary states that there are three reasons why the Tathāgata restrained them.
"O Kāśyapa, each of you has your own respective duty. If you were permitted to remain in this land, it would result in the neglect of the benefit for that other land.

Furthermore, since the conditions for establishing karmic connections between that other region and this land are shallow, even if you wished to proclaim and transmit [the Dharma], there would necessarily be no great benefit.
Moreover, if you were permitted [to stay], you could not be called 'Bodhisattvas from the Lower Regions. As for the Bodhisattvas from the Lower Regions..."
If one does not come to the traces [of the Buddha], one cannot shatter [them]; this is called the threefold meaning. Alas, how base is such a discourse!
When the Buddha spoke these words, [the assembly] came forth from below.

The Treatise says: As stated previously, regarding the various Buddhas who have divided their bodies and reside throughout the ten directions, it is the wisdom of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*).
This is the symbol of purity, being non-dual, indivisible, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.

It refers to the fact that the earth of the trichiliocosm quaked and split open, from within which immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth;
this is the light of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and immeasurable supernormal powers.
This clarity is the manifestation within the ground of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
therefore, it is said that the bodies of all these Bodhisattvas are golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks, and possessed of immeasurable radiance.

Since it is stated that they are beneath this Sahā world, yet also stated that they dwell in the void of this realm, they ultimately have no place of dwelling. This is what is meant by "hearing the explanation."
The sounds spoken by the Buddha Kāśyapa emerge from below, yet ultimately they come from nowhere.
One dwells upon them without seeing their location and knows not whence they originate; one merely sees them surge forth from the earth.
Thus, the immeasurable wisdom, supernormal powers, and radiance cannot be known as to where they come from; that which can be known is simply that they emerge from [the earth].

It is simply the method of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states: "One should, through the power and effort of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, bring [the practice] to maturity before realization is attained.
It is not achieved by haste, nor is it obtained through slackness; one must only know that by never ceasing, one will certainly not waste [the opportunity].
Just as milk contains curd, all things require conditions (*pratyaya*). Within these conditions there is no agent; therefore, once the curd has formed, it likewise has no place from which it came."
Nor is it that Tathāgata-wisdom exists inherently;

rather, it is illuminated by the various skillful means of virtue—namely, morality, concentration, and wisdom—and because within the conditions of objects there is no agent and no accomplishment, one attains a state of brilliant clarity regarding all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes, for among all phenomena there is neither an actor nor an act to be done. Furthermore...
It is neither originally existent nor originally non-existent;
for within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no beginning and no end, no start and no finish, no formation and no destruction, and no past, present, or future.

One should understand that this sutra cannot be treated as having an original existence or being produced through cultivation, and it should thus eliminate all worldly views of nihilism and eternalism, as well as all contentious debates.
I have established this framework and elucidated it through the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), making its explanations as clear as the sun and stars;
yet the old commentaries state that "being neither below, nor belonging to that, nor being this—that is the Middle Way. This is a profound error.

The commentary states: according to the textual descriptions in the sūtra, their retinues consist of many as six, five, four, three, two, or one myriad of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers; yet they are described in descending order as five, four, three, two, or one.
When the text says "the disciple down to the solitary individual," this refers to a small number;

yet when examining the phrasing of the scripture, it says "how much more" (*jìng jiāng*) and "how much less" (*jìng fù*), which implies five, four, three, two, and one—thus the disciples from the solitary individual down to the many.
This density of numerical categories suggests that the intended meaning of these numbers is not clearly anchored, which is suspicious. Upon examining the conclusion of the passage, however...
It is said that such things as these are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy;

only then does one know that what is shown is not a number, but is intended solely to clarify that the light of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and merit is beyond the reach of thought or discrimination.
Indeed, by means of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and supernormal powers...
Having already understood the purport from the passage concerning the light emerging from within the stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one may ask:

what is the intention behind the statement that these bodhisattvas, having emerged from their respective stages, each proceeded to the seven-jeweled, wondrous stupa in space where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha were?
It is said: the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna is a Buddha who entered parinirvāṇa in the past; his body is that of ultimate quiescence.
This is the image [of that]. Śākyamuni is the Buddha of present dependent origination; he is the image of the five-aggregate body.
Because one realizes the wisdom, supernatural powers, and radiance of all Tathāgatas within the active manifestation of the five aggregates, all Bodhisattvas arrive at his abode.
Therefore, it is said that the various Bodhisattvas offer various praises of the Dharma, and...
Having praised them, they stood to one side, joyfully gazing up at the two World-Honored Ones. They asked:
"Is it possible for a body currently manifesting the five aggregates to realize the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and merit? [The Buddha] replied:

"If all devas and nāgas, despite possessing the three poisons, can still manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), how much more so for one whose own mind does not oppose reality and is not joined with delusion?"
Is this not the union of wisdom with the divine? The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra-śāstra* states that when one achieves the prohibitive precepts, they become a person of purity who cultivates *samādhi*.
Without needing the celestial eye, their physical body naturally perceives the ten directions;
they behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and personally receive the sacred commands. Attaining great supernatural powers (*mahābhijñā*), they roam throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "One does not realize enlightenment by extinguishing sensation, for the eyes born of one's parents do not require the divine eye"—this refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
"Nor does one extinguish sensation"—this refers to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
From form and sensation, when one contemplates perception, mental formations, and consciousness, it is the same for all; how can one doubt that they cannot be realized?

The Commentary says: According to the *Huayan lun*, as in the provisional teachings, after the Buddha’s birth, he immediately left the city to renounce the world and attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree;
this is taken as the [initial] time, just as in the case of Vairocana.

The Buddha is not actually like this; rather, the Tathāgata establishes these manifested forms in order to deliver sentient beings of the three vehicles who should see him thus—leaving home and attaining Buddhahood.

This is because Vairocana Buddha, having attained great Bodhi by relying on the fundamental Dharma-realm, still relies upon that same fundamental Dharma-realm, which is without beginning or end, neither appearing nor disappearing, and neither being formed nor destroyed.
When observed through this perspective, there is no temporal duration;
thus, from the descent from Tuṣita Heaven, the entry into the mother’s womb, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, to the entry into nirvāṇa—all occur within a single kṣaṇa-limit.

While he has not yet descended from that heaven, while he has not yet emerged from the mother’s womb, he has already entered nirvāṇa, and all matters of the dharmas are completely finished. As the Sūtra says: [like...]
During this time, fifty intermediate kalpas passed; yet Śākyamuni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for those fifty intermediate kalpas.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he caused the great multitude to perceive the duration as being like half a day.
It was not only when the Buddha descended into the womb and entered parinirvāṇa that he did not pass even a single kṣaṇa.
That limit, when observed over immeasurable kalpas, does not transcend a single kṣaṇa-limit;

by this one knows that the "fifty minor kalpas" are merely conventional manifestations established by the Buddha for the sake of sentient beings. Question: By what means is this proven? Answer: The Sūtra states:
"Among this assembly of Bodhisattvas, there are four leaders: the first is named Urdhvajaṅgha (Upward-Striding). This refers to...
The first is that which was previously called "practicing in accordance with the power of the Dharma";

because this practice is the foremost among all practices, it is symbolized by the second [elephant], the Boundless Practitioner (*Anantacārin*), who is the aforementioned Great Wisdom, Supernormal Power, and Radiance of the Tathāgata.
Because this practice is immeasurable and boundless, it is symbolized by the third [elephant], the Pure One (*Vimala*).
The practitioner is one who, by means of the immeasurable and boundless wisdom, supernormal powers, and radiance of the Tathāgatas,
has purified the Dharma-body; as the aforementioned Bodhisattvas emerged from the earth and approached the two World-Honored Ones,
the practitioner likewise employs skillful means to establish fifty [stages] according to their respective capacities.
A minor kalpa (kṣudrakalpa) is said to be like half a day; this is merely a metaphorical illustration, for there is no duration of long or short time within a single kṣaṇa.
