since their details and brevity do not correspond, it seems as though there was no intention to specify the location.
Here, one should further elucidate the principle that there is no fixed place, and students should investigate and contemplate this deeply.
From the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja until [the period when he was] Sadāparibhūta.
The treatise asks: Why did the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta encounter beatings and expulsion after telling people that they would become Buddhas?
It says: The intention with which the Bodhisattva told them was good, but the words with which he told them were not yet skillful. It is like a bright pearl.
If one throws a white jade disc into the path at night, people will still clutch their swords and suspect it; how much more so when one attains the rank of Buddha without a cause?
One might then ask: "Does this mean that the Bodhisattva did not examine his words and was unrefined in what he told him?
I reply: He knew [the truth] and told him in order to admonish future teachers, so that those who transmit the Dharma should do so with such [caution].

In a future age, the World-Honored One, as the Buddha Dharmakarṇin, once at the assembly of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, caused Ānanda to personally investigate his own mind through seven locations, yet found no place for it to be.
Thereupon, the Buddha raised his fist and asked him, "By what do you see this?
Ānanda replied, "I and the great assembly all see it with our eyes. The Buddha said, "You say that my fist illuminates your eyes and mind."
"What you see with your eyes—what therein constitutes the mind? Ānanda replied, "I am now investigating the location of the mind;
that which performs this investigation and pursuit, I take to be the mind. The Buddha said, "Stop, Ānanda!
This is not your mind. Thereupon, Ānanda was startled and alarmed, and he declared, "To say this is not my mind—"
I was truly terrified... until the Buddha said: "I am not commanding you to grasp at this as something other than mind;
rather, you must minutely examine the nature of the mind. If this discriminating nature exists apart from external objects, then it is your true mind.
If this discriminating nature has no substance when separated from objects, then it is merely a reflection of the discrimination of external objects. Since those objects are not permanent..."
If this mind were to perish upon transformation and extinction, it would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; thus, your Dharmakāya would be identical to annihilation.
Who, then, could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?

The Buddha’s desire for Ānanda to awaken and become a Buddha was even more earnest than that of the monk Never-Disparaging in addressing others, yet his words were so circuitous and indirect. Nevertheless, Ānanda—
A verse was spoken: "The Great Hero, of great power and great compassion, may you further examine and eliminate even subtle delusions.

Thus, the words with which [Śāriputra] addressed the Buddha as "Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta) were not entirely appropriate. This is like the story of Jin Le Guang, who was drinking with a guest;
the guest saw a snake in his cup, and upon returning home, he fell ill. Le Guang realized that the "snake" was actually a painting on the wall of the room where they were seated.
Without informing him, he again invited his guest beneath a painted shadow of a snake. When the guest saw the snake in the cup, he realized it was but a painted reflection;
his illness was then cured. The Tang monk Zhiyong was renowned for his mastery of calligraphy. A student came to study under him and remained in his service for twenty years before departing.
Yong knew that the student’s craft was not yet refined, yet he did not inform him, but merely gave him a single—
The case-bearer said, "I shall open this upon arriving home. On the way, the man grew suspicious and opened it;
inside were several inkstones worn smooth from use. The man then realized that his own learning had not yet reached such a level.

Even in matters as minor as wine and cups or artistic skills, the instructions given by Le Guang and Yi Zhong were so profound and subtle; how much more so must be the teachings of the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging!
If one is to become a Buddha, how can it be so abrupt?
This bhikṣu [attains] *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Commentary states: The sūtra says that "when this bhikṣu is about to pass away" refers to the moment when the six sense faculties cease their activity.
If the six sense-faculties do not function, it constitutes non-activity; yet it is also said that one fully hears the sutras previously preached by the Buddha King of Awesome Sound.
To hear the sutras while in a state of non-activity is the "activity of non-activity.

The essence of this activity of non-activity is inherently subtle and eternally quiescent, such that neither sense-objects nor faculties can intervene, and neither numerical measure nor quantitative limits can obstruct it. Therefore...
It is said that one who is able to receive and uphold two million billion verses immediately attains the aforementioned purity of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Having attained this purity of the six sense faculties, one further increases one’s lifespan by two million billion nayutas of years.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of awakening within the sutras: first, nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*); second, fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Moreover—
There are two kinds of *prajñā*: first, *primal awakening* (*benjue*) *prajñā*, and second, *initial awakening* (*shijue*) *prajñā*.
These four names are established according to their meanings, yet their essence remains eternally identical. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The nature-awakening is wondrously luminous;
primal awakening is luminously wondrous. This is a case where the phrasing is interwoven to establish the meaning, signifying that the nature-awakening is wondrously luminous.
It is the realm of direct realization for all sentient beings; it does not arise from subject and object, nor does it originate through cultivation or realization.

It is primordially wondrous and eternally luminous. Because one can awaken to this wondrous nature of luminosity through the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-prajñā*), it is called "the wondrous luminosity of original awakening" (*mūla-avabodha*).
If it has not yet been illuminated by the wisdom of initial awakening, it is termed [unawakened].

The nature of awakening—because the nature of awakening does not belong to beginning or end. Since it has already been elucidated by means of *ādi-bodhi* (initial awakening) prajñā, it is termed *mūla-bodhi* (original awakening);
for *mūla-bodhi* distinguishes between the fundamental and the derivative. Viewed from this perspective, there are three meanings that possess four names.
When the sutra speaks of the Buddha Vairocana-ghoṣa-rāja, it is the image of the nature of awakening, because [it is] not...
Regarding the location, it merely states that he had heard the sutras previously expounded.

The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa represents the aspect of Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), signifying that after his passing, within his Dharma, the Buddha Meghasvaradīparāja represents the aspect of Initial Enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).
Within the teachings of these Buddhas, a question is asked concerning King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara.

The Buddha then said: "Regarding the sūtra previously spoken, it was spoken within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa; regarding this sūtra, it was spoken within the Dharma of the Buddha Meghasvararāja. [The interlocutor] asked: "Regarding these Dharmas of all the Buddhas, you have stated that they were 'received, upheld, read, recited, and explained to the fourfold assembly.

What is the meaning of these three Buddhas all speaking of the sūtra? He replied: [The Buddha said: "It is because the Dharma of all Buddhas is the same. Why? Because all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, have attained the same Dharma-nature, the same Dharma-body, the same Dharma-mark, the same Dharma-vehicle, and the same Dharma-treasury. Furthermore, the Dharma taught by all Buddhas is also the same. Why? Because all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma of the single vehicle, not the two vehicles nor the three vehicles.

All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings with the same intention, namely, to cause them to enter the Buddha-way. Therefore, I say that the sūtras spoken by all Buddhas are identical."

To manifest this essence that is inherently wondrous and eternally luminous, so as to illuminate the entire Dharma-realm and universally save all sentient beings, enabling its transmission to continue without end—this is the essential meaning.
The Buddha is the one who transmits it; therefore, when it is said, "Who was this Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging?
Was he anyone else? It was I myself."
"Attaining Great Power... [up to] quickly attaining the Buddha-way.
The Treatise says: Regarding the power of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those sentient beings who hear and cultivate its influence will ultimately and necessarily attain Buddhahood;
even if they pass through as many kalpas as there are motes of dust, like Śākyamuni Buddha, they shall not fall into the evil destinies.

Just as Bhadrapāla, Siṃha, Candraprabha, and others all ascended the path of enlightenment, so too did the lifespan of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and the duration of his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma already pass through incalculable dust-motes of kalpas; how much more so for twenty-two billion Buddhas of the same name?
Furthermore, it was only at the very beginning that the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta heard the sutra and resolved his mind upon enlightenment. Thus it is.
The Sūtra says: "If I had not, in previous lives, upheld, recited, and explained this sūtra to others, I could not have so swiftly attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because I upheld, recited, and explained this sūtra for others under former Buddhas, I have swiftly attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Thus, those who have been perfumed by hearing and believe in the sutras will certainly attain Buddhahood after the passing of as many *paramāṇu-kalpas* as there are atoms;

because such persons consume a small amount of *vajra*, and since the nature of this *vajra* does not combine with flesh or blood, it cannot remain even as they progress through each stage (*bhūmi*), continuing until it reaches the *vajra-koṭi* and comes to rest. As the Sutra says: "At that time, the fourfold assembly, and even..."
If one with a mind of anger treats me with contempt, for two hundred billion kalpas they shall never encounter a Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Sangha;
for a thousand kalpas they shall undergo great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell.

Once these karmic retributions are exhausted, if they again encounter the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging who teaches them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall then receive the permeation of hearing the Dharma.
That one who lacks faith will nonetheless ultimately attain Buddhahood even after falling into the evil realms is because it is like the sword of Fengcheng:
though buried beneath the floor of a prison cell, its radiance was seen between the constellations of the Dipper and the Ox; once unearthed, it became a treasure rare in the world.

It is asked: "If it is possible that one who has faith will ultimately attain Buddhahood after as many kalpas as there are atoms, is it not also possible for one who lacks faith to fall [into the evil realms]?"
"To fall into the evil realms and yet also be said to attain Buddhahood—how could such a thing be possible? [The Master] replied: "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

'O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he emitted a great radiance called King of Light-Pennants, which illuminated worlds as numerous as the atoms within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
The sentient beings in the hells within those worlds encountered this light.'"
When their manifold sufferings have ceased and they attain the ten kinds of pure faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, it is likewise so;
they all give rise to joy, leaping for gladness, and celebrating. At the end of that life, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
In that heaven there is a drum named "Exceedingly Delightful"; once those beings are born there, this drum emits a sound and addresses them, saying:
"O sons of the gods, it is because you have cultivated various roots of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgata with a mind free from negligence,
and because of your past proximity to many spiritual friends and the great majestic power of Vairocana,
that you passed away there and were reborn in this heaven; this is the proof thereof."

The Layman Wujin (Inexhaustible) says in his treatise: Whenever the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging saw bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, he would prostrate to them and praise them, saying, "I deeply revere you;
you all practice the bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood. Every person was thus complete, and each individual was fully perfected as they practiced the bodhisattva path.
That one shall attain Buddhahood is the essential purport of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
For instance, when Sudhana asked a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), "How does one practice the bodhisattva path? How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path?

the spiritual friend immediately descended from his seat, prostrated, and scattered flowers over him. Thus, by practicing the bodhisattva path and performing prostrations, how could such a person be looked down upon? You—!
If you consider me mad and thus treat me with contempt, insult, and abuse, it is because you lack self-confidence and slander this sutra yourself.
If that is so, since the merit of a Dharma teacher who rejoices in others' merit is as described above, how can one escape the sin of slandering the sutra?
Therefore, it was at the time of the Buddha King of Majestic Sound that Constantly Non-Disparaging encountered him and together practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for twenty thousand years.
By means of the "Verses on Ten Million Virtues," he attained the purification of the six sense faculties. He further encountered two hundred billion Buddhas named Candrasūryapradīpa;
he further encountered two hundred billion Buddhas named Meghasvararāja; and he further encountered ten million billion Buddhas until he became our present Śākyamuni Buddha.
As for those who treated him with contempt, they shall not encounter a Buddha for two hundred billion kalpas.
For not hearing the Dharma and not seeing the Sangha, one undergoes great suffering in the Avīci Hell for a thousand kalpas;

yet upon completing this, one finally encounters the teachings of the Constantly-Not-Light (Sadāparibhūta). This is the retribution for the offenses and blessings of those who slander the sutra and those who uphold it;
meanwhile, the Buddha’s compassion remains equal and non-dual toward both.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-one: The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata.
At that time, [the assembly from] the thousand worlds... attained what they had never experienced before. The Commentary says:
Although the tongue-organ and the face are small, they do not emerge from the mouth; [this is like] the Brahma-devas of the Form Realm.
Regarding the ultimate limit, the Sūtra speaks of the mark of the broad and long tongue reaching up to the Brahma-heaven;
regarding the subtle minuteness of the body, such as its individual pores, and the vastness of the realms of the ten directions, the Sūtra speaks of light pervading all places.
Now, observing from the mark of the tongue upward to the Brahma-heaven...

Is "heaven" not that which extends vertically through the three periods of time? Furthermore, as observed from a single pore extending everywhere to all places, is it not that which spreads horizontally across the ten directions?
Yet, it is not that the Buddha himself manifests in this way; rather, these Buddhas of the ten directions who manifest as emanations likewise act for one another.
The Sūtra further states: "At this one moment, [a period] filling a hundred thousand years."

Thus, throughout the vastness of the three periods of time and the ten directions, and for a duration as long as a hundred thousand years, all is perceived within the brief moment of the Buddha preaching the Dharma;

even the smallest sounds, such as clearing one’s throat or snapping one’s fingers, and the most expansive realms of the ten directions—all these two types of sounds are able to reach everywhere. Yet, this is not due to the Buddha or his emanations themselves.
The various Buddhas, Prabhūtaratna, and all the Bodhisattvas merely behold it; likewise, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even humans and non-humans also behold it.
How could this be an object within the realm of the discriminating false sentiments of the conscious mind?
[The questioner] asks: If it is not an object within the realm of the discriminating false sentiments of the conscious mind, then it must be the domain of wisdom (jñāna).
Is this the realm of wisdom? Is it the realm of the Buddhas? Do the Buddhas realize it, and do sentient beings also have the capacity to realize it?

It is said in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*: "All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment; when they encounter a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they rely upon the practices for the causal stage as performed by that friend.
At that time, in their cultivation, there are both sudden and gradual approaches. If they encounter a Tathāgata... [text continues].
On the path of the correct practice for supreme enlightenment, there is no distinction between those of great or small faculties; all shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
However, for those whose true faith has not yet reached its ultimate limit, one should examine this through historical accounts. Once, Dignāga engaged in a debate with a non-Buddhist;
the non-Buddhist was defeated and transformed into stone. Dignāga then fashioned a straw effigy in his likeness and whipped it, causing blood to flow from the stone.
Furthermore, when [the Buddha] roared and ascended into the sky, there was no distinction between sentient and insentient beings;

when Cai Shun, a filial son of the Han dynasty, was carrying firewood into the city and suddenly guests arrived at his house, his mother bit her own finger and Shun’s heart was moved so that he rushed back home—there was no distance of separation;
and when Yuan Dexiu of the Tang dynasty had a young nephew who lost his mother while still a child, his family...
When the poor woman had no wet nurse, yet her son of virtuous character nursed her himself, and his milk became breast-milk for her, this was not due to the distinction between male and female.

When Meng Zong, the filial son of the Han, wept among the bamboo because his mother craved bamboo shoots during the winter months, and the shoots grew forth, this was not due to the difference of seasons. Can it be said that these are not proofs?
Immediately, the various devas... [up to] ...practiced according to the teaching.

The treatise says: At the time when the Buddha manifested his supernatural powers on Vulture Peak Mountain, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others who had long resided in this Sahā world.

Regarding the assembly of all beings—householders, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—the sutra speaks only of the devas in the void encouraging others with deep hearts to rejoice.
Why is this? It is because the nature of the devas is the most beneficial.
Seeing that the realm shown by the Buddha was vast, subtle, and penetrating without obstruction, he first attained awakening and gained self-confidence that his realization was free from error;
thus, deeply moved by the Buddha’s grace, he uttered a lion’s roar, exclaiming aloud:
"Beyond this, there are immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds."

There is a land named Sahā; in it there is a Buddha—[you should know that] you all must, with a profound mind, rejoice [in his merit], and you should also pay homage to and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha. He asked:
"If Śākyamuni Buddha is here on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, how is it that a voice from the sky says 'beyond this,' and not merely 'beyond this'?"

Furthermore, it was asked: "If there are immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, why is the name of this one world 'Sahā,' and why is there a Buddha within it?
It was replied: "This is because the body of this Buddha has no fixed location. Why?
Because the realm manifested as previously described is the realm of wisdom; since wisdom and wisdom are pure, how could they have limits?"

How sublime! Yet the Buddha, considering that the voice from mid-air alone could not dispel the marks of the delusion and darkness of all sentient beings, scattered various articles of adornment, rare jewels, exquisite objects, flowers, incense, banners, and canopies upon the Buddha.
These various wonderful offerings arrived from the ten directions and transformed into a precious canopy; those who did this were desirous of—
This reveals that matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are non-dual. Why?
Because these various exquisite offerings scattered [in space] lack consciousness (*vijñāna*), yet they are able to come from the ten directions and further transform into canopies;
this is the principle of the non-duality of matter and mind. Since matter and mind are non-dual, wisdom (*jñāna*) is pure. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "There is no duality."
Because it is without duality, without distinction, and without interruption; because the subtle essence of the sutra exhausts the gateways of the mental factors (*citta-dharma*) of practice;

and because, to state the essential point, all dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata are the realm of non-obstruction and inconceivability—therefore it is said that the Tathāgata possesses all sovereign spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-bala*). This is not false.
Because he reveals this pearl that is difficult to believe, it is called "the treasury of all the Tathāgata’s secret essentials.
Because it cannot be known by humans, devas, or those of the two vehicles, it is called "all the Tathāgata’s most profound matters.
Since what was previously taught in secret is now clearly proclaimed, it is said that "all are declared and expounded within this sutra."
"In whatever land [until] there shall be no doubt whatsoever.

The Commentary says: The Sūtra states, "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you should single-mindedly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and practice according to the teaching," which indicates the principle of drawing near to and following [the Dharma]; therefore, it says:

One should single-mindedly uphold this. If there are those who now uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and practice according to these teachings, they are either those who have seen [the Buddha] or those who associate with and follow him.

Those who associate with and follow him are able to remain uninterrupted in every thought-moment; because they are uninterrupted in every thought-moment, they do not conjoin with delusion. Because they do not [conjoin with delusion]...

Because they are falsely conjoined, they encounter conditions; thus, the essence [of these dharmas] arises in the very place where the various conditioned objects are present and perishes in that very place.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Wherever this scripture is located—whether in a garden, under a tree, in a monastery, in a layperson’s house, in a hall, or in mountains, valleys, or wildernesses—in that place..."
"A stūpa should be erected where there is the place of ultimate extinction.
The Inexhaustible Layman’s Discourse says: "The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future all preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This sūtra contains hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet those who have previously expounded it were [only] the Jewels..."
Through various parables—such as the chariot, the medicinal herbs, the transformed city, the digging of a well, and the intoxicated youth—the Dharma-gate was not yet fully revealed;
it was only upon reaching the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers" that the immeasurable verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* shone forth in their complete splendor.
This refers to the Tathāgata and all the emanated Buddhas from the worlds of the ten directions.
From every pore, they emitted immeasurable rays of light that shone everywhere;

extending their broad and long tongues, they emitted immeasurable light reaching up to the Brahma Heaven for a hundred thousand years. Then, withdrawing their tongues, they coughed simultaneously and snapped their fingers together.
These two sounds reached all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, and the earth in each shook in six ways.
The various devas in the midst of the void raised their voices in loud proclamation, saying:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is now preaching for the sake of all bodhisattvas a Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Having heard this voice from the sky, sentient beings joined their palms toward the Sahā world and scattered exquisite offerings from afar like gathering clouds; these transformed into a jeweled canopy."
When one has thoroughly realized this as a single Buddha-field, at that time the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattvas such as Śikhin:

"All the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata, all his sovereign spiritual powers, all the treasuries of secret essentials, and all matters of profound depth are proclaimed, revealed, and expounded within this sutra. Therefore, after my parinirvāṇa, you and others [should uphold it]."
Thereafter, you should with single-minded devotion receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and practice according to the teaching.
Wherever this sutra scroll may reside, one should erect a stupa to make offerings there;
that place is itself a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it is here that all Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, here they turn the wheel of Dharma, and here they enter parinirvāṇa.
The broad and long tongue of Nirvana is adorned by the non-false speech maintained throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

As for the mark of the tongue reaching up to the Brahma Heaven: the tongue is the faculty that proclaims perfect penetration; it transcends the realm of desire to preach the sutras, and thus cannot be sought through physical characteristics.
From the pores, interlacing lights shine such that every Buddha illuminates one another, with principal and attendant figures manifesting in infinite layers.
That he withdraws the tongue-attribute after a full hundred thousand years shows that mastery over the duration of its withdrawal rests with him.

That the sound of the Buddhas’ clearing of their throats and the snapping of their fingers is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions is the subtle and inconceivable manner in which the Buddhas preach the Dharma.
That the earth shakes in six ways signifies that the preaching of the Dharma has been completed; it is the shaking of the earth as a sign.
This is indeed the Dharma. To discourse according to the nature [of reality] is to perceive the actual realization of practice;

to speak while clinging to signs is to remain mired in the subtle convergence of deluded words. Is it not the case that the intent behind upholding this sutra and entrusting this sutra lies precisely here?
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-two: Entrustment. At that time, Śākyamuni...
[omitted] ...do not give rise to stinginess or parsimony.
The Commentary says: The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding the Tathāgata..."
"Did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara by which he attained *anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi*? "No, World-Honored One.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Buddha obtained under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara by which he attained *anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no..."
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then the Buddha Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. For in reality...
There is no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for this reason, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Viewed in this light, it is clear that the Buddha has no dharma to give to others.
Yet, in this very sutra, it is said that the Tathāgata possesses great compassion, is free from all stinginess, and is without fear, and is able to bestow [the teaching] upon the multitude.
The wisdom produced by Buddhas—the Tathāgata-wisdom and spontaneous wisdom—is that which the Tathāgata bestows as a great benefactor upon all sentient beings.
Considering this, it is clear that the Buddha possesses dharmas to bestow upon others.
When the meanings and characteristics of what is taught according to the nature of reality (dharmatā) are so contradictory, how can one find a middle ground? It is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
When the Tathāgata’s morning star appeared, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. Surveying immeasurable sentient beings, he sighed and said:
"There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize them.
If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-knowledge, self-arising knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge are immediately present."

When one attains presence before oneself, one realizes that deluded thoughts and attachments lack any real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). It is like a person who is confused about directions, mistaking east for west;
when a person of realization suddenly points it out to them, their state of confusion regarding the west naturally dissolves, yet the eastern direction does not come from outside.
Thus, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is spoken of in terms of both delusion and awakening; it is innate wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*).

The Wisdom-Cover (Prajñā-āvaraṇa) is realized at the moment of awakening from delusion. It is the Buddha’s wisdom that, through skillful means (*upāya*), can direct all sentient beings so that they awaken from their delusion.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is that which is realized (*prameya*), while the Buddha’s wisdom is that which realizes (*pramāṇa*).
As for natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), however, it does not belong to the category of the "realizer"; therefore, it does not depend on others.
Because it was attained [by others], alas, natural wisdom is not obtained from another person;

thus, Śākyamuni Buddha at the place of Dīpaṃkara merely received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). That which can, through skillful means (*upāya*), point out to all sentient beings so that their delusion is resolved is called the Buddha’s wisdom;
this is what this sutra refers to when it says it can bestow the Buddha’s wisdom upon sentient beings.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is spontaneous wisdom; otherwise, it would have been sufficient for the sutra simply to speak of "the Buddha's wisdom.
Yet, because the profound and wondrous intent of all Buddhas cannot be fully exhausted by a single word, it further speaks of "the Tathāgata’s wisdom" and "spontaneous wisdom."
Regarding the grace of all Buddhas in future ages, the treatise states:
Those who have faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom are called "good sons" or "good daughters," by which it is known that they are beings whose faculties are matured.
As for those who do not believe or accept it, they are merely referred to as "the multitude."
By this, it is known that he is a sentient being whose faculties (*indriya*) are not yet matured. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Subhūti, with reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying: 'It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata well protects and attends to all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Vasubandhu Bodhisattva explains this, saying: "'Well protects and attends' means..."

For sentient beings whose faculties are mature, he speaks of "skillful entrustment"; for sentient beings whose faculties are not yet mature, he speaks of the Buddha’s Dharma-giving without ever neglecting any being.
This is like the lion king seizing an elephant or seizing a rabbit; his power is never unequal.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Ānanda, I have now delivered you and you have been born [into the lineage]."
“Śāriputra, you have fulfilled the Buddha’s words; this is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. To understand and uphold his final instructions is what constitutes knowing gratitude.
At that time, the bodhisattvas (up to) all were greatly filled with joy.
The Layman Wujin (Akṣayamati) said in his discourse: "The Buddha rose from his Dharma-seat and manifested great supernormal powers;
with his right hand, he touched the crowns of the heads of immeasurable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and entrusted them, saying: 'You should single-mindedly propagate this Dharma.

All the Bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison three times, as commanded by the World-Honored One, saying: 'We pray that you will have no further concern. The Buddha then commanded all [the Bodhisattvas].
That the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas each returned to their respective seats of Dharma is the essence of immovability.

That they arose and performed the *samāya* with their right hands is the manifestation of function in accordance with that essence. That it was the crown [of the head] signifies being honored and unsurpassed.

That the single mind was disseminated signifies that the Buddha has no dual teachings. That the voices were raised three times in unison signifies that the beginning and the end mutually complete one another. Each...

That which returns to its place of rest is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*), which pervades the entire realm of sand-grains; initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaṇika-bodhi*) is such that every Buddha shares the same path.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-three: "The Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
At that time, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña... [until] he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The Treatise says: Regarding the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, it states that the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja was formerly named Jyotīrasa.
He once heard the Venerable Sūryagarbha expound upon the Buddha’s wisdom. Thereupon, he offered medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains to the assembly of monks and made a great vow, saying:
"May I, in future ages, be able to cure all the physical illnesses and mental afflictions of all sentient beings. Thus he made his aspiration.
Because this vow brought joy to the entire world, it is called the *Bhaiṣajyarāja Sūtra*. It says:
"At that time, the Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, as well as for the assembly of bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
Thus we know that the reason the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja was named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana during his stage of practice was because of this.
Because the original vows of this place are pure and vast, bringing joy to all sentient beings, this sutra serves as an excellent medicine for those with diseased minds.
Those who believe and uphold it will surely obtain the retribution of the purification of the six sense faculties;
those who hear it but harbor doubts are like people entering a pharmacy—though they have not yet taken the medicine, they are nonetheless permeated by its fragrance.

To have illness is also to suffer loss. When the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja in the past was able to relinquish his beloved body and his adorned arm, he did not merely heal the various physical and mental illnesses of all sentient beings; he was also able to cure the illness of the Buddhas and the illness of the Dharma.
"This is the Samādhi of the Form Body (rūpakāya) for all sentient beings.

The *Huayan Shiming Lun* (Avataṃsaka-śāstra-daśavidha-prakāśa) states: "The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra constantly manifests his form body before all sentient beings to teach and transform them without ceasing;
this refers to the multitude of beings benefited by a Bodhisattva of the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*)."
Birth and other states are identical to the Dharma-realm; according to faculties and seasons, he manifests a form-body that acts without effort and responds without contrivance.

By means of the wisdom of universal radiance, which does not belong to any specific location, he appears in forms according to the minds of sentient beings, yet because there is no coming or going, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva performs the "Elephant King’s Turn" to observe Sudhana.
The term "youth" (*kumāra*) indicates the intent of gathering [beings] under his care. For the Great Sage’s non-localized wisdom is perfect and its form is omnipresent;
he manifests in accordance with their faculties and appears before them without turning his back on any sentient being.

All sentient beings, according to how they ought to see him, perceive him as if facing them directly; yet each being is unaware of the others, thinking only, "The Sage is speaking to me alone. Thus it is asked:
He asked: "By what cultivation can one realize this samādhi? He replied: "It is realized solely through the power of diligence;
there is no other dharma for its maturation. There are four kinds of diligent practice for this samādhi: first, constant walking; second, constant sitting;
third, alternating between walking and sitting; and fourth, neither walking nor sitting. One should exclusively embrace these four types."

The *Sūtra on the Uninterrupted Succession of Moments of Mind* states that the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana delighted in practicing asceticism within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī;
his diligent walking meditation and single-minded pursuit of Buddhahood represent his delight in practicing the *Samādhi of Constant Practice*.
Beginning with diligent walking meditation and single-minded pursuit of Buddhahood, it culminates in...
To manifest physical bodies before all sentient beings and teach them without ceasing is called the effect of maturation through the power of diligence.
Having attained this samādhi... [up to] ...to make offerings to the Buddha.

The Commentary states: The Sūtras encompass all differentiated meanings through three natures. First, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is called the attachment to conceptual discrimination;

this attachment is only dispelled when one attains the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*). Second, the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is called the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*);
this attachment is only dispelled when one attains the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*). These two attachments are [to be abandoned] in successive order.

When [the former] is exhausted, one enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "A person with cataracts is like the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
the appearance of blue and yellow is like the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and a person with clear vision is like the perfected nature.

The Bodhisattva Dignāga, illuminating these three natures through wisdom, spoke a verse as a metaphor: "The cognition that arises regarding a vine as a snake— when the vine is seen, the snake is no more."
If one knows that the object is merely a portion of a vine, then the knowledge of the vine is like the knowledge of the snake;
since both the knowledge of the vine and the knowledge of the snake are all confused cognitions, they are not originally wondrous and eternally knowing. Why is this so?

It is because when a person sees a vine and mistakes it for a snake, they are deceived by the object; yet once the vine is seen, the snake of divergent characteristics immediately vanishes—this is the parikalpita-vikalpa (imagined construction).
The mind that clings to the heart is severed. Now, as for the vine, it is constituted by color, fragrance, taste, and touch;

yet when this vine is analyzed, there remain only color, fragrance, taste, and touch, and the vine of distinct characteristics also ceases to exist. This is the severing of the mind that clings to other-dependent phenomena.
When these two types of clinging are exhausted, the perfected nature manifests, and all sentient beings behold it with joy.

Because Bodhisattvas attain the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies through ascetic practices that accord with the three dharmas, they intend to demonstrate its essential characteristics so that all sentient beings may realize them;

therefore, they do not regard offerings made through supernatural powers as true diligence. As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, it rains the sandalwood incense of this side of the ocean; this incense [has six...]"
The value of a single *zhū* [of incense] is equal to that of the Sahā world when used as an offering to the Buddha;

this incense manifests through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and is said to be "six *zhū*" because it represents the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Yet, even so, its value is still equated with the Sahā world;
it is not something where all present activities are entirely devoid of subject and object.
Having made this offering... (up to) they offered it as such.

The treatise says: The sutra itself states that they thought to themselves, "Although we have made offerings to the Buddha through supernatural powers, it is not as good as making offerings with our own bodies," and so on, until each remained silent and their bodies burned for twelve hundred years.

After this, when his body has finally come to an end, because he has attained the wisdom of the emptiness of persons by being free from the conceptualization of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-vikalpa*),
and having further performed such a Dharma-offering himself, after his life has ended,
he shall continue for seventy-two thousand years to offer worship before eighty-four thousand stupas by burning his arms, adorned with a hundred merits.
This is because one attains the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena by departing from the attachment to phenomena based on the dependent nature;
for when the characteristics of the body are exhausted, attachment to phenomena likewise perishes. Question: Why is it said that "one immediately partakes of various fragrances"? Answer:
The feverish afflictions of the five desires are cooled by the precepts; since sandalwood can eliminate these feverish afflictions, it is said that sandalwood [removes] the pain of enmity and hatred.
Because *kunduruka* (incense) can pacify pain through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called the "congealed branch of dhyāna";

because *jātipuṣpa* (resin) can remove sores and eruptions through the illumination of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called "glue-fragrance. Merely being free from false delusions is what is termed "liberation" (*vimukti*).
As for *turuṣka* and *bhallātaka*, they are the coarse varieties of *udakagarbha* (water-sunken incense). Thus one contemplates.
Since what has been for a long time is just as it is today, that which sinks in water will inevitably reach the bottom of the abyss.

Therefore, *dūrvā* grass and *pilikā* are taken as metaphors for liberation (*vimukti*), while sinking in water is taken as a metaphor for the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
Thus, it is said that *dūrvā* grass and *pilikā* sink in water; by means of these five kinds of incense, one symbolizes the precepts (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding the liberation through wisdom and the knowledge and vision of liberation: furthermore, one uses the fragrance of *campaka* flowers as oil and anoints oneself, just like an elephant with a wish-fulfilling gem.

Again, he asked: "Why is it said that one wraps one's body in celestial jewel-clothing and pours various oils over it, so that by the power of supernatural faculties and vows, the radiance of one's own body naturally shines forth, pervading eighty [yojanas]?"
[The Buddha] said: "Regarding those worlds as numerous as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers, what is meant by 'spontaneously [igniting] one's own body'?

It is not with ordinary fire, but with the fire of wisdom. When it is ignited, because the sense faculties and their objects are stilled and illuminated, its radiance penetrates everywhere without obstruction.
He asked again: "Why is it said that this is true diligence and that this is called the true Dharma-offering?"
He said, "To make offerings through supernatural powers is neither true diligence nor the true Dharma-offering.

Only by using great wisdom to illuminate this physical form and realizing it is utterly unattainable—by means of this wondrous non-attainment to universally offer to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—is it the true Dharma-offering.
He asked again, "Why is this called 'attaining liberation'?"
Regarding the *Sarvasattvabhāṣā-dhāraṇī*, it is said: "This is called the Samādhi of Unimpeded Entry into Language.
As the sutra states: if one wishes to demonstrate that the body cannot be apprehended, one says, "For twelve hundred years, he burned his own body";
if one wishes to demonstrate that attachment to dharmas cannot be apprehended, one says, "For seventy-two thousand years, he again burned his body of a hundred blessings."
If one considers these words of the Ornamented Arm to be true, then sentient beings would have no basis for developing faith;
if one considers these words to be untrue, then that which is expounded by the Buddha’s untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) ought not to be false or deceptive.
This is because all speech of sentient beings is a mixture of falsehood and deception; furthermore, it is said that [the Buddha’s] *dhāraṇī*...
"Dhāraṇī" means "the true. When the false is mixed with the true, the true can ultimately never be understood;
yet there are those who do understand it. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "That which cannot be understood is itself Prajñā;

Prajñā is neither that which can be understood nor that which cannot be understood. Furthermore, it is asked: when the characteristics of the body are exhausted, one speaks of the dharma-attachment of twelve hundred years.

When [the lifespan] is exhausted, it is stated to be seventy-two thousand years. Having already described the birth and death of the Buddha Sun Moon Pure Bright Virtue (Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī), why then is the birth and death of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana also described?
It is said: regarding the physical form, that which is expressed as twelve hundred years refers to the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the "universe" (*kṣetra*), as for the statement that the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) lasts seventy-two thousand years, this refers to what is grasped and maintained by the defilements of the seven consciousnesses.
As for the physical form (*rūpakāya*), it is said to be "birth," while the attachment to phenomena is said to be "death.
Because these two attachments do not transcend the realm of birth and death, there is no [fixed duration] for the Buddhas whom they serve, whether they remain in the world or enter *parinirvāṇa*.
This refers to their distinct characteristics.
It causes countless seekers (up to) to naturally return to the original state.
The *Śāstra* states: Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna said that because there is not a single dharma with a fixed nature that can be grasped, it is called "ungraspable."
It is "refuted" because sentient beings are attached to empty phenomena that arise from causes and conditions; thus, it is said to be refutable.
For example, it is like a small child who sees the moon in the water and, out of attachment, desires to grasp it but cannot do so, and consequently harbors distress in their heart.

A wise person instructs them, saying: "Although it can be seen by the eye, it cannot be grasped by the hand. This merely refutes what can be grasped, not what can be seen. As the Sūtra says: [at this point, the text continues with the scriptural citation].
At that time, the Bodhisattva stood amidst the great assembly and made this vow:

"If I shall surely attain the golden-hued body of a Buddha after casting away these two arms, and if this is truly not false, may my two arms be restored as they were before. Having made this vow, his arms were naturally restored.
Thus one knows that although the wisdom of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) relinquishes the two types of grasping, it is neither severed nor extinguished.
This is merely the principle of refuting that which is graspable (*grāhya*) without refuting that which is visible (*dṛśya*). The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"Good son, those newly initiated bodhisattvas, dwelling among their followers and sitting in meditation in a quiet room, should constantly form this thought:
'This body of mine is a combination of the four great elements—namely, hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities.'"
All return to earth: saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, spittle, phlegm, tears, vital essence, and the large and small excretions all return to water;
warmth returns to fire; and movement returns to wind. When these four great elements have each separated, where then can this delusory body be?
Even ultimately, there is no conditioned mind to be seen—this is what it means to enter the human realm.

This is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, it is said: "O son of good family, because the illusory body of those sentient beings is extinguished, and so on, up to the extinction of the extinction of illusion, that which is not illusory is not extinguished.
This is like polishing a mirror: when the defilements are exhausted, the clarity appears.

This refers to entering the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Thus, by treating them with the medicine of contemplation, they are empty; therefore, it is said that the characteristics of defilement are eternally extinguished and the ten directions are pure.
Because one has not yet seen the purity [of the mind] and cannot perceive the characteristics of the original body and mind, it is further said:
"For example, when a pure maṇi jewel reflects the five colors, each direction appears with its respective hue; yet those who are foolish see that maṇi as actually possessing the five colors.
Son of good family, the pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment manifests within the body and mind in the same way."
According to the respective capacities of those who are deluded, it is taught that Pure Perfect Enlightenment truly possesses such physical and mental characteristics;
this is likewise according to their respective types.
Thus, the body burned for twelve hundred years is manifested as the five colors, and the arm burned for seventy-two thousand years is manifested as the pure maṇi jewel.
As for its essence, it is the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana.
From this bodhisattva [it extends] to all sentient beings.
The Commentary states: As discussed in the preceding section of the sūtra, in order to demonstrate that bodily form (*rūpakāya*) is ungraspable, it says "one."
For twelve hundred years he burned his own body to demonstrate that attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) is unattainable;

then, after seventy-two thousand years, he again burned his arm adorned with a hundred merits to clarify that once the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are exhausted, attachment to dharmas likewise perishes.
Thus, the imagery established in this sutra to convey its meaning is perfectly clear and beyond doubt. At this point—

If it is said that one who resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and is able to offer their fingers, even down to a single toe, as an offering to a Buddha-stūpa, this is truly like a command; why is that? It is because they are like an elephant.
This means that they have not yet been able to suddenly obtain the two kinds of wisdom—the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). However—

Just as an Anāgāmin abandons coarse attachment to the characteristics of arising and ceasing through discrimination, so too may one abandon the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) among the five afflictive views.
The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of characteristics of arising and ceasing through discrimination.
What are the two? First, the coarse, which is associated with the mind; second, the subtle, which is [associated with] the mind..."
Because they are dissociated [from the mind], those associated with the mind are called the coarse aspects of the defilement of grasping (*upādāna-kleśa*). As the Sūtra says:
"If one were to burn one's own fingers, then once the grasping has occurred, there would be no power [to stop it]; thus the coarse characteristics are exhausted. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Although the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is free from the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), when experiencing equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), the craving for 'I' (*ātma-sneha*) manifests and arises; therefore, the view of a self-body is not yet entirely exhausted."
The *Yujia jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) also states that even having only one toe remaining is a sign that the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has not yet been completely exhausted.
The Jin monk Fayu recited the *Lotus Sūtra* throughout his life and admired the sacrificial offering of self-immolation by the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
He informed Yao Xu, the Jin Prince of Pufan, saying, "There are many gateways to the Way; why must one burn one's own body? To this, [the Prince] replied: [Fayu said: "..."
"I wish it were so," he said, and immediately wrapped his body in cloth soaked in fragrant oil, recited the "Medicine King" chapter (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*), and ascended the fire-rack.
Furthermore, the Song dynasty monk Huìyì possessed supreme conduct;

having abstained from grain for many years, he prepared a cauldron and oil at Zhōngshān, mounted a bullock cart to visit Yúnmén to take leave of Emperor Wǔ, and then entered the cauldron, sitting upon a small chair.
He poured oil over his *karpāsa* (cotton) cap and was about to set it ablaze. The Emperor ordered the Grand Chancellor to exhort him, saying, "The Way has many paths;
why must you burn your body? He replied, "My original vow is such; I dare not trouble Your Majesty's holy concerns. He requested that twenty monks be ordained, which was granted.
He then recited the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter; even as the flames reached his eyebrows, his voice remained clear and distinct. On the following day—
The Emperor established a vegetarian feast and founded a temple named Yaowang (Medicine King). Alas! Fayu and Huiyi regarded their precious bodies as mere firewood;
this was an error born of insufficient mastery of this chapter—how tragic it is! Question:
The Sūtra states that when this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Medicine King" was being preached, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained liberation.
Regarding the *Sarvasattva-bhāṣā-dhāraṇī*, why is it called a *dhāraṇī*?

It is said that all sacred teachings take four factors as their essence: namely, the body of names (*nāmakāya*), the body of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), the body of phrases (*padakāya*), and the body of speech (*vāk-kāya*).
Because one first understands through habitual familiarity, these four serve to enable hearing, retention, and dissemination.

Because the Dharma abides for a long time, the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time relies upon these names, phrases, and expressions to guard against the worldly, confused, and meaningless discourses.
All the teachings of the Noble Ones are like cow’s milk: by adding a fermenting agent, it becomes curd over time.
Worldly, confused, and meaningless discourses are like donkey’s milk; their color is [the same as that of cow’s milk].
If milk were to reach [the same state] as that and one were to split it, it would become impure.
Now, regarding what is called the "dhāraṇī of the speech of all sentient beings," it is not a realm accessible to discriminative wisdom or consciousness. Why?
Because it is subsumed within all the holy teachings; thus it is named the "speech of all sentient beings. It is also subsumed within worldly writings.

If one asks whether this refers to *dhāraṇīs*, the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" states that one should not associate with worldly literary compositions, praises, or non-Buddhist texts (*bāhyaka-śāstra*).
By "non-Buddhist texts," it means those that are not the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

Yet, the "Dharma Master Chapter" further states that if one speaks of worldly scriptures, secular discourse, or the arts for sustaining one's livelihood, these are all in accordance [with the Dharma].
If one examines the True Dharma from this perspective, how could sounds and speech possess any real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)?
In this land, only the Great Being Zao Bo attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings;
when he commented on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, he stated that Mañjuśrī resides on Mount Qingliang in the northeast, which corresponds to the hexagram Gen.
Gen (Mount) represents the younger son, as it is located in the northeast; thus Gen is the younger son, the childlike ignorant one, and Mañjuśrī.
He constantly transforms ordinary beings by awakening their ignorance and revealing their inherent nature, representing the very beginning of primordial wisdom.

Furthermore, he dwells together with Samantabhadra in the eastern position of Māo; Māo corresponds to the hexagram Zhen (Thunder), which represents the eldest son and is also likened to the rising sun.

In the east, the spring sun brings forth sprouts; there is nothing that does not grow, nothing that it does not illuminate. When wisdom and principle penetrate both simultaneously, the essence is one and non-dual.

Just as the sun rising in the east illuminates all things and the spring sun brings forth sprouts so that nothing fails to grow, because fundamental wisdom and discriminative wisdom are non-distinct in essence and function, giving rise to the myriad practices, you are a Buddha.

The position of Chou (丑) represents the stage of faith; Yin (寅), the ten abodes; Mao (卯), the ten practices; Chen (辰), the ten dedications; Si (巳), the ten stages; Wu (午), the stage of Equal Enlightenment;
and Wei (未), the final day of the month, representing the entry into the mundane world to transform those who are deluded by conforming to the mundane.
Shen (申), You (酉), Xu (戌), and Hai (亥) represent those who are to be transformed. This is the true entry into the Samādhi of Unimpeded Eloquence, sporting among sentient beings through their speech.
When masters of scholastic learning hear of what is called a *dhāraṇī*, their hair stands on end and they lose heart;
for the trampling of a dragon or elephant is not something a donkey can endure.
Master Wujin’s treatise states: "Since the Tathāgata has entrusted these sūtra scrolls, wherever they abide..."
One should erect stupas and make offerings. Then, the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭarāja asked the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, "How does one travel through the Sahā world?
The Buddha told Śrīkūṭarāja: "In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī.
That Buddha expounded [the Dharma] for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and others."

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it is said that the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, having delighted in the practice of diligence for twelve thousand years, attained the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*.
Having made offerings with various incenses and flowers, he further anointed his body with fragrant oil and burned it as an offering;
at the end of his life, he passed away from this Buddha-land and was reborn by transformation in a pure land.
Born into the family of a virtuous king, he said to his father:

"In the past, I made offerings to the Buddha Sun-Moon-Pure-Virtue and heard him preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in eight hundred thousand million billion nayutas of verses. I immediately went to pay my respects and praised that Buddha with verses.
After that Buddha passed into extinction, I collected his relics and erected eighty-four thousand stupas, and furthermore, I burned both my arms as lamps."
Having made offerings, he made this vow, saying: "I shall surely attain the golden body of a Buddha by sacrificing my two arms.
Once he had made this vow, his arms were restored as they were before. At that time, the one named Priyadarśana was none other than the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Furthermore, the merit obtained by those in the assembly who hear this Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja is immeasurable and boundless.
