second, indeterminate ripening karma, which refers to that which has been intentionally performed after prior reflection...
"Not increasing" means that although one has intentionally committed an action, one subsequently regrets having done so.
Generally, when actions are not increased—meaning if there is no regret and no cultivation of counteractive measures—they are capable of yielding their fruit and are termed "increasing karma.
If, however, there is regret and so forth, they are termed "non-increasing. Thus, regarding the karma already committed that has not been lost, when one encounters perilous circumstances...
To invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva amidst hardships is what is meant by repentance.
The Bodhisattva’s compassionate regard for sentient beings in distress is like a kind mother who never forgets her lost son;
if the son is dissolute and does not return, failing to cherish the longing of the mother, they shall not meet again for a hundred years. This lost son was fierce.
If one reflects with urgency and hastens back, one will surely see one’s compassionate mother.
When sentient beings wail in grief, how could the Bodhisattva, by the power of his great compassionate vow, not bear it and extend a helping hand? The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* says:

The Buddha told Resolute Mind, “There is a medicinal tree named ‘Eliminator of Great Armies. When there is a battle between armies, [it provides protection]... (The text continues with the description of its miraculous efficacy.)

Suppose there is a person struck by a poisoned arrow; at that time, a skilled physician takes a medicinal king-tree and anoints the surface of a drum with it, striking it amidst a great crowd so that its sound causes immeasurable poisoned arrows to be extracted all at once.
By the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, there are immeasurable instances where those who call upon their names or keep them in mind [are likewise liberated].
The defilements of sin are naturally eliminated and extinguished, just as a single portion of *sarpis* (clarified butter) can cure all ailments. When the sutra says,
"The majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is thus sublime," does this not refer to the power of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*?
"If there are sentient beings... [up to] "...the benefit of merit.
The treatise states: Maitreya Bodhisattva said, "Those who are greedy, hateful, envious, negligent, and arrogant, who consider themselves enlightened while being ignorant of their own darkness;
who, through the indulgence in negligence, increase their greed for sensual desires and become even more lustful—these are the envious."
Those who are envious and obstructive, yet harbor arrogance, are more foolish; those who are wrathful and resentful are more prone to hatred.
All three possess the characteristic of being mute regarding the truth, yet they are deluded and mistakenly regard this as clarity. Avalokiteśvara is also named Prabhūtaratna (Light-World-Sound);
he is able to shatter the darkness of all fetters and karmic deeds through wisdom. Thus, a verse from the Sūtra says:
It is said: "The Sun of Wisdom, with its stainless, pure radiance, shatters all darkness. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said, "For example, when a lamp is lit, all darkness naturally vanishes; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. It does not come from the east, nor does it go there;
it likewise does not go to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below. It does not come from those places."
When it goes out, it does not go anywhere; yet this lamp-light has no such thought as "I can extinguish darkness.
Rather, by the nature of the lamp-light, darkness is naturally absent. Both light and darkness are empty, without action and without grasping.
In this same way, Kāśyapa, when true wisdom arises, ignorance is extinguished. Wisdom and ignorance—both aspects are empty, without action and without grasping. Kāśyapa...
"Suppose, for example, there were a dark room that had been in darkness for a thousand years, where light had never before entered. If a lamp were lit at that time, what do you think?
Would that darkness think, 'I have dwelt here for a long time; I do not wish to leave'? "No, World-Honored One.
When the lamp is lit, that darkness has no power and does not wish to leave; it must simply be extinguished. "In this same way, Kāśyapa, [even though] hundreds of thousands..."
Karmic bonds and afflictions accumulated over ten thousand kalpas are all extinguished by means of the contemplation of the single reality (*ekasatya*).
That which is the lamp’s light is the noble wisdom; that which is its darkness is the various karmic bonds and afflictions. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"If there are sentient beings who have much lustful desire, they will immediately become free from desire if they constantly mindfully revere and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. If they have much anger..."
If one who is prone to anger constantly and reverently calls upon Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately be freed from hatred;
if one who is prone to delusion constantly and reverently calls upon Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately be freed from delusion—it is for this reason. Question:
If that is so, then why is it that those who seek sons or daughters also obtain them according to their wishes? Answer: This is due to the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The one who has attained mastery possesses the wondrous power of non-action, which is devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
yet, in accordance with the purity of the sentient beings' own minds, it can fulfill their aspirations as they wish. The *Jñānālaṃkāra-sūtra* states:
"For example, when the great earth is composed of lapis lazuli, the reflections of Śakra’s Vaijayanta Palace and its furnishings appear therein."

Among them, the people of Jambudvīpa, seeing the reflections of the various palaces upon the lapis lazuli ground, joined their palms in worship, burned incense, and scattered flowers, making this vow:
"May I be born in such palaces; may I sport therein like Śakra and the other gods.
Those beings did not realize that these were merely reflections of the palaces; nevertheless, they practiced giving, observed the precepts, and cultivated various virtues.
Through merit, one obtains such a palace as a karmic fruit. Mañjuśrī, this palace is truly without arising or ceasing;
because the ground is pure, it appears as a reflection therein. That reflection of the palace both exists and does not exist;
it neither arises nor ceases. Through the bodhisattva’s effortless and wondrous power, which is truly without arising or ceasing, the sons and daughters sought after—
The reflection both exists and does not exist; it appears simply because the woman’s mind is pure.
Being without birth and without cessation, it neither gives nor takes away. It exists when the mind is pure and is absent when the mind is impure.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that for those who constantly maintain mindfulness and reverence, whatever they seek will surely be obtained.
From the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati to the one who bestows fearlessness:
The treatise states that while the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara attained the Samādhi of Manifesting Physical Form through the dhāraṇī for understanding the languages of all sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara entered samādhi by means of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The manifested physical body is not a realm accessible to the mental consciousness; it is accomplished solely through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When I desired to enter nirvāṇa and first set foot upon the road toward the city of Kuśinagara, there were five hundred laborers who were leveling and sweeping the path. Among them was a stone that the multitude sought to [remove]..."
When they exerted all their strength and were unable to move it, I felt compassion and immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Those strongmen then saw me lift this great rock with my big toe and cast it into the air;
I caught it again with my hand, placed it upon my right palm, blew upon it to reduce it to fine powder, and then reassembled it once more, thereby shattering the arrogant minds of those strongmen.
The Buddha then briefly explained various essential points of the Dharma to cause them all to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son, at that time the Tathāgata did not actually lift this great rock into the air with his finger and place it back in his right palm;
nor did he blow upon it to crush it into powder and then reassemble it as it was before. Good son," [he said].
One should know that this is precisely the power of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness and compassion, which causes the Mallas to see such a phenomenon;
this is the reason why the thirty-two marks of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) are fully perfected. Question: Why is it called a "transformation" (nirmāṇa)?
Is it because he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for those who are to be saved by means of this body? Answer: Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty was fond of... [text fragment ends]
The coastal officials of Dahezhong had previously presented this clam in succession, and people were weary of it. One day, among the imperial provisions, there was one that could not be split open.
The Emperor, considering it extraordinary, immediately burned incense and prayed to it.
Suddenly, it transformed into the form of a Bodhisattva, complete with all the features of a Buddha. He then placed it in a casket made of gold-dusted sandalwood and covered it with fine silk.
The Emperor bestowed brocade upon Xingshan Temple and commanded the assembly of monks to gaze upon and pay homage to it. He then asked his ministers, "What auspicious omen is this?
Some replied that there was a monk named Weizheng from Taishan who was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory regarding the Buddha-dharma.

Thereupon, the Emperor summoned him and questioned him about the matter. He responded, saying: "Your servant has heard that no phenomenon occurs without a corresponding cause; this is intended to inspire faith in Your Majesty. Thus he spoke.
A sūtra states: "To those who are to be delivered by this body, he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for them.
The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed been manifested; however, I have not yet heard him preach the Dharma.

Zheng said, "Does Your Majesty behold this as a rare and auspicious sign and regard it with reverent faith? The Emperor replied, "I truly do believe it deeply. Thereupon, Zheng congratulated him, saying, "Your Majesty..."
Having descended and finished hearing the Dharma, the Emperor’s heart was filled with joy at such an unprecedented experience.
He issued an edict that every monastery throughout the realm should establish an image of Avalokiteśvara to express gratitude for this extraordinary grace. He further asked:
"Why is he called the Bestower of Fearlessness? The Song dynasty monk Guṇavarman—whose name means "Virtuous Merit"—was a native of Central India.
In the twelfth year of the Yuandi era, he went to Jianye and was held in high esteem by the Prince of Nanqiao, Xiao Yixuan.
When the Prince harbored rebellious intentions, [the Master] remonstrated with him until his tears flowed. Although the Prince did not listen, he did not dare to show anger.

During the defeat at Liangshan, [the Master] fell into the river; with single-minded devotion, he recited the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva while clutching a bamboo staff in his hand, looking back as he went.
The boy tugged at his robe, saying, "You are but a small child; how could you do such a thing?

Upon reaching the shore, [the Master] took off his *nāṃsa-vastra* (monastic robe) intending to reward him, but the boy suddenly vanished from sight. Alas! When the Bodhisattva appeared, Emperor Wenzong provided him with a sumptuous meal;
when the boy tugged at the robe, where did this *nāṃsa-vastra* of Guṇavarman come from?
From the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati [up to] the mind of *sambodhi*.
The Commentary says: That which is called the "jeweled necklace" of the gift of Dharma is not a worldly necklace;
it is an ornament for adornment. Akṣayamati, wishing to give it, said: "O virtuous one, out of compassion for us, please accept it."
This "necklace" (mālā) signifies the ultimate fulfillment of his vows.
When Avalokiteśvara immediately took pity upon the fourfold assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans, and accepted their necklace, he manifested the sign of his compassion.
This is as shown in the preceding text of the sutra, where Śākyamuni Buddha enters the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna and sits together with him upon the same seat.
That which is born yet possesses the characteristic of non-birth is the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, who long ago entered parinirvāṇa;

yet that he speaks of coming to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* represents the characteristic of being extinguished yet not extinguished. That which is born yet non-born, and extinguished yet not extinguished, is the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*), the very essence of one's own mind.
"Inexhaustible Intention" (*Akṣayamati*) refers to the Great Vow; furthermore, it is manifest therein.
The intention of the vow is Avalokiteśvara, who is Great Compassion; furthermore, he manifests the form of that compassion.
As for the *mālā* (necklace), it is an implement of adornment. Is not the purport of the sutra that the Dharma-body is adorned by compassionate vows?
Why is this so profoundly clear? Therefore, it says that upon receiving the *mālā*, it was divided into two parts, one part...
It is as follows: one portion is offered to Śākyamuni Buddha, and another portion is offered to the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna.
Master Wu-jin (Akṣayamati) comments: "The sound that surpasses the world" refers to the supramundane sound;
"viewing sentient beings with eyes of compassion" means observing them upon hearing that sound. Thus, Akṣayamati heard the discourse on Avalokiteśvara.
The Bodhisattva, by means of these causes and conditions, offered a jeweled necklace to Avalokiteśvara;

Avalokiteśvara, in accordance with the Buddha’s command, accepted it and divided it into two portions: one portion he presented to Śākyamuni Buddha, and the other portion he presented to the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna.
Thus, the merit of compassionately rescuing from suffering was attributed to the two Buddhas, while the merit of upholding the sutra need not be [attributed elsewhere].
This is further explained through words in the "Chapter on the Profound Sound Coming and Going," for the one who expounds it may speak or remain silent;
and in the "Chapter on the Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara," for the one who hears it is neither extinguished nor born.
When these two chapters complement one another, this sutra will be widely disseminated.
The Dharani Chapter, the Twenty-sixth of the Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma.
At that time, Bhaiṣajyarāja... [attained] the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Commentary says: An old sub-commentary states: "In the past, there was the son of a pauper who was intelligent but prone to much anger; he fled to another country."
Possessing such intelligence, he went to see the king of that country and deceived him, saying, "I am also a prince from a neighboring kingdom.
Having lost my father's favor, I have wandered in exile and now come to seek refuge with Your Majesty. May Your Majesty deign to show me compassion.
The king, fond of eloquence and hearing that he was also the son of a ruler, had him bathe.
Yiguan associated with his sons and grandsons for a long time and eventually gave him his daughter in marriage. The girl found it difficult to endure his frequent outbursts of anger.
Shortly thereafter, she heard that a guest had arrived from her husband’s home country; she sent someone to inquire about the family background of this "poor man's son" and told him:
"My husband is prone to anger; what can be done? The guest smiled silently and blessed her, saying: "Whenever he is about to become angry, you should explain the Dharma to him."
The verse says: "Do not wander idly through other lands to deceive all people; eating coarse food is but a constant matter, so why must you intentionally harbor anger?
When the son of a poor man spoke this verse to his wife, she immediately knelt before him and recited it.
Thereupon he remained silent and no longer felt angry. However, his wife and the others heard only the verse and did not understand its meaning, nor did they know it was a mantra.
This is what is called "secret silence," yet it is not merely silence. Furthermore, it is said that when a king has a desire, he simply calls for *saindhava*.
If he wishes to drink water, *saindhava* brings water and presents it to him; if he wishes to mount a horse, *saindhava* brings a horse and presents it to him.
None of the ministers or officials in the court are able to understand this.
The spell known only to a wise minister is likewise not so; how then can it be called a "spell" (*dhāraṇī*)?
It is said that *dhāraṇī* means "total retention. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu stated: "It takes mindfulness and wisdom as its essence;
through the application of the spiritual power of few, concise, and cryptic words devoid of [ordinary] meaning, its miraculous efficacy is unfathomable."
This is close to the truth. For instance, when Shi Gong acted for Fu Jian, he used incantations as a summons;
using the summons to command the dragon, the dragon descended into his bowl and rain followed immediately. The dragon is a being possessed of consciousness.
Similarly, when Fotudeng used incantations for Shi Le to bring about auspicious omens, blue lotuses would suddenly bloom in his bowl. These blue lotuses—
If one were without consciousness, could dragons be summoned by proclamation? Could lotuses be made to bloom by proclamation?

If one were to deliberate upon this matter with a mind of discursive thought, one would be either a fool or a madman. Alas! Is it not because of being without [discursive] mind and without [conceptual] principle that one can grasp the true nature of the myriad things?
Is this true only for the myriad things? It is also true for heaven and earth, the spirits, and the gods.
None can contravene it; and as for the Buddha propagating this sutra in an evil age, he declared that Bodhisattvas should protect and uphold it.

That the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Viśvāmitra, the Heavenly Kings Vaiśravaṇa and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the rākṣasī Pīlāmbā and others all vowed to guard it with mantras—is this not because it is rare?
Is it that the abbreviated and esoteric texts, devoid of conventional meaning, have been empowered by supernatural power?

Master Wujin (Inexhaustible) argued: "Dhāraṇī" is here translated as "Total Retention" (*saṃgraha*). These were all spoken by former Buddhas; their majestic spiritual efficacy is unfathomable, and thus they are called "divine.

Because they subdue all demons and allow one to know their origins, they are called "mantras."* *Note: This passage reflects the traditional Chinese Buddhist exegesis on the terms *dhāraṇī* and *mantra*. It distinguishes them based on their functions: *dhāraṇī* for retention and *mantra* for subduing malevolent forces.*
Bhaiṣajyarāja obtained it from sixty-two billion Ganges-sand Buddhas; Vīradatta Bodhisattva obtained it from as many Ganges-sand Buddhas;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King of the Devas, and the hosts of gandharvas obtained it from forty-two billion Buddhas;
Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Devas, the ten rākṣasīs, and Hārītī each obtained it from a Buddha.
As previously stated, for those who recite, uphold, and receive this sutra, there is the protection of mantras;
if it were not so, and if Māra were powerful while the Dharma were weak, how could it possibly endure long in the world?
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha.
At that time, the Buddha spoke... [up to] "the second is named Pure Eye.

The *Śāstra* says: According to the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*, because true wisdom has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and cannot know itself as being without nature, and because it is the nature of the absence of nature (*asvabhāvatā-svabhāva*) and cannot know itself as being without nature, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). — *Vajragarbha*.
The Bodhisattva said: "Because one does not comprehend the ultimate truth (paramārtha), it is termed ignorance (avidyā).

Since true wisdom is fundamentally without intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it cannot understand itself; therefore, the Buddhas must further manifest their appearance in the world to preach the Dharma and bring benefit and joy to humans and devas.
Although there are originally no sentient beings to be saved, since the former sages attained the Way and benefited the world, this is now made clear."
The essential wisdom that knows reality can only manifest when the conditions for realization are met. A question was asked: "Who serves as the condition for realization? It was said:

"Only the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the condition for sentient beings to attain Buddhahood. As stated in the following passage: "One should know that the spiritual friend is a great causal condition;
that is to say, they transform and guide others so that they may come to see the Buddha. Furthermore, regarding the spiritual friend—
To demonstrate and teach the benefits of the good, one should employ four methods to gather and transform all sentient beings, bringing them to full maturity before they can enter the Way.
These are: first, beneficial conduct; second, giving; third, kind speech; and fourth, collaborative action.
Because this chapter demonstrates these methods, it speaks of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Voice-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom.

Regarding beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*): there was a king named *Sudarśana*, which represents generosity (*dāna*). The king’s queen was named *Viśuddhaguṇā*, which represents pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).
They had two sons, one named *Viśuddhagarbha* and the other named *Viśuddhanetra*, which represent collaborative action (*samānārthatā*).
How is this known? It is known from the explicit meaning of the scriptural passage; that which is called beneficial conduct is as follows:
The practice of benefiting others is like clouds: they contain moisture through compassion to bring forth rain; their thunderous roar is wrathful to generate growth.
Therefore, it is said that the sound of the clouds and thunder spreads light to destroy darkness and causes blossoms to open so that fruit may be formed.
Thus, it is said that the "Wisdom of the Constellation-King Flower" refers to the Moon Deity (Candradeva). By this, one knows that the practice of benefiting others is like the clouds.

This is the Buddha Thunder-Sound Constellation King Flower Wisdom (Ghoṣadatta-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom). What is called "generosity" is the relinquishing of that which is most difficult to give up.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of rewards for giving: in the future, there will be great merit;
in the present, all excellences will converge upon one. Merit has the meaning of adornment, while the convergence of all excellences has the meaning of sovereignty. By this, it is known.
Generosity is King Miaozhuangyan. As for what is called "loving speech," because it is humble, gentle, and compliant, it is spoken of in relation to the Lady.
One loves others through virtue and speaks with harmonious beauty; therefore, loving speech is known as the Lady Jingde.
As for what is called "cooperative conduct," it is not that the virtuous act alone; they must necessarily [share their deeds] with others.

Because people are the same, they are called "two sons. Because they are profoundly hidden yet as empty as space, they are called "Treasury" (*kṣaya*); because they understand clearly and without delusion, they are called "Eye" (*cakṣus*).
From this we know that those who share the same purpose are the Pure Treasury and the Pure Eye; this explains their symbolic imagery.
As for the profound meaning, it is seen in the following passage from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*: "A virtuous friend is like..."
A virtuous and loyal wife is a spiritual friend like a kinsman; wealth is a spiritual friend like a merchant leader;
and a spiritual friend who guides one is like a son lying in his father’s lap. When a wife is virtuous and loyal, she loves her husband—is this not pleasant speech?
When wealth comes from kinsmen, it is never exhausted—is this not generosity? When led by a merchant leader—
"There must be something that benefits me; is this not the benefit of their conduct? When a son lies in his father's lap, it is the height of trust, yet they do not share the same tasks.
Thus, these two sons possess a subtle and profound countenance."
The Commentary says: "I wish to hear the profound meaning of the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu) being fulfilled.

It is said that these refer to "acting in concert" (samānārthatā), yet the Sūtra necessarily mentions "two sons," just as in the preceding passage where the Elder’s thoughts toward the impoverished son state: "He secretly dispatched two men who lacked majesty and power.
Furthermore, the Sūtra necessarily mentions those born into families with false views as "casting off precious and noble robes to don tattered and filthy garments."
Carrying a vessel for excrement is what is meant by "appearing as something fearsome.
Regarding the six *pāramitās*, these are the indelible practices of the Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles; the *sūtra* names them the "Six Perfections.

Yet this scripture alone, among the practices performed by Netra and Viśuddhanetra, adds the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) beyond the six perfections—is this not to transform beings through shared activity?

For a person, skillful means must always come first. Thus, after enumerating his names, he manifested eighteen transformations before his father, causing the father king’s mind to give rise to faith and understanding; this was the application of skillful means.
The sutra states that once the two sons had converted their father king and caused him to abandon false views, they then addressed their mother.
That those who seek to leave the household life together do so is indeed a skillful means (*upāya*) of acting in concert;
it is natural that once the task is accomplished through these means, they are abandoned. This is what is meant by "beneficial conduct" (*arthacaryā*).

The Sūtra must state that the Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* because he wished to guide King Subhavyūha and out of compassion for sentient beings; for there is nothing that precedes benefiting others.

Because they benefit one another through the Dharma, it is further said that when that Buddha preached the Dharma for the king, demonstrating, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, the king was filled with great joy.
He even proclaimed the king’s diligence among the fourfold assembly and bestowed upon him the prediction of his future Buddhahood. Finally, he told him:
"A spiritual friend is a great causal condition; therefore, they are developed, encouraged, and comforted."
All of these are acts for the benefit of others, specifically what is called "loving speech.
Although the sutra states that a mother told her son, "Your father has placed his faith in non-Buddhist paths and is deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma;
you must manifest supernatural transformations so that he may see them and surely develop faith," this was because she loved her husband most dearly. Nevertheless, she did not transform him herself.
That husband must have instructed his son to go and convert him; this is the intent of his words of affectionate speech.

As for what is called "giving," the sutra necessarily speaks of it as occurring at that time. When the father saw his son’s supernatural power was thus, he felt great joy, such as he had never experienced before;
these are words expressing his regret for having turned toward [the Dharma] so late. Thereupon, King Wonderful Adornment...

Together with his ministers and retinue, Queen Śuddhāśaya with the ladies of the inner palace, and the king’s two sons with forty-two thousand people, all went at once to the place where the Buddha was.
Among them, Queen Śuddhāśaya and the king’s two sons were those of right view; as the king now arrived at the Buddha’s presence together with them, he renounced [the kingdom].
The intent of returning from wrong views to the True Dharma is seen here. There are two kinds of giving:
namely, the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma. To abandon the Brahmanical teachings one has studied constitutes the giving of the Dharma;
to untie a pearl necklace worth hundreds of thousands from one's neck and scatter it over the Buddha constitutes the giving of material wealth. The sutra invariably states: "At that time..."
When King Subhavyūha and his queen offered pearl necklaces, this was an act of giving (*dāna*);
yet it also involved pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*). Is it not the case, then, that pleasant speech is also a category of the dharma of giving?
This is because one generates a virtuous mind through beautiful words and sincere intent. Thus, the Sūtra says: "The pearl necklaces transformed in mid-air into a four-pillared [pavilion]."
Regarding the jeweled terraces: practicing giving necessarily gives rise to the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. How is this known?
It is because the four pillars of the jeweled terrace serve as symbols for the four immeasurable minds;

as stated previously in the section on the *upāya-pāramitā*, it immediately follows with the mention of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path. Thus, the terrace [is so designated].
Regarding the "jeweled bed" therein, one should take the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) as the seat for these four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*);

the term "bed" is merely a variation of the word for "seat. As for the "spreading of hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial robes," this refers to protecting oneself deeply through the practice of patience (*kṣānti*).
A question is asked: Is it sufficient to employ giving (*dāna*) while being assisted and inspired by loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?
Furthermore, why is it that one is further instructed to contemplate the emptiness of phenomena and maintain patience? It is said: "The practice of giving is difficult;
if the mind dwells [upon it], one will fall back. When Śāriputra first wished to cultivate the six perfections, he resolved to give away all his internal and external possessions.
Suddenly, a Brahmin came and asked for his eyes. Śāriputra joyfully took them and gave them to him.
The Brahmin immediately threw it to the ground, saying, "I thought this was a precious jewel with lovely radiance;
I did not know it was merely a pellet of stinking blood. He then trampled it to pieces with his foot and departed. Thereupon Śāriputra thought to himself: "If it were of no use, let it be;
why go so far as to destroy it with one's foot? Because of this, he fell back for forty kalpas.

If one can contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) while maintaining patience, and further arouses the mind for giving through the assistance of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, this is called "giving without abiding in signs.
Therefore it is said that when the Buddha sat cross-legged and emitted great radiance, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells in phenomena with the mind while practicing giving, [it is not true giving]."

When a person enters darkness, they see nothing; if a Bodhisattva’s mind does not dwell on dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person with eyes who, when the light of the sun shines upon them, sees all manner of forms—this is the proof.
At that time, [the King] Cloud-Thunder Sound (up to the point where he) attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

The Commentary says: The Sūtra states that the king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother, along with his consort, two sons, and all his retinue, so that they might leave the household life and cultivate the Way within the Buddha-Dharma;
this refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), which are what all sentient beings require.
Because one employs skillful means to transform others into Buddhas by following their desires, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"First use desire to entice them, and later lead them into Buddha-wisdom. A mind of giving does not easily arise spontaneously through the practice of *samānārthatā* (common purpose);
even if it can arise spontaneously, it is due to the power of the guidance and habitual cultivation provided by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in past lives.
Because this was brought about by maturation, even endearing speech and praise could not assist in rousing his courage and vigor;

therefore, the Sūtra says that after the King had renounced the world, his two sons were "my spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*), who came to be born in my family for the sake of awakening my roots of goodness from past lives and benefiting me.
Thus, it was the ability of these two sons to practice giving [that served as the catalyst].
Using skillful means, his mother, Lady Pure Virtue, actually prompted him to ask:
"Regarding this praise of the Buddha by King Subhavyūha, why is it that among the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics,
he specifically extols the radiance of the *uṣṇīṣa* which illuminates his eyes, and the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows which reflects upon his mouth?"
It is said: This chapter also demonstrates the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions; therefore, the sutra says: "Is the King Subhūṣaṇa anyone else?
He is none other than the present Bodhisattva Padmaśrī. Is the Lady Viśuddhaguṇā anyone else? She is the present Bodhisattva Prabhāsaśrīlakṣaṇavyūha before the Buddha.
As for his two sons, they are the present Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata."
"Sa" refers to this: just as the light of the *uṣṇīṣa* reveals the summit of the head and its subtle, esoteric nature can be seen only by a Buddha, it is thus called the "eye.
The tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) reveals the meaning of the Middle Way;

because it is through causes, conditions, and karmic retribution that one is skillfully illustrated and well-guided, and because one cannot yet forget words, it is also called the "mouth. Question: In the preceding text, it was sometimes said that one has attained...

All sentient beings attained the Samādhi of the Language of All Beings; some said they had attained the Patience of the Non-arising of Dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), some said they had attained the Lotus Samādhi, some said they had attained the Samādhi of Manifesting Physical Bodies, and some said they had resolved their minds toward the peerless Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Yet, in this chapter alone, it is simply stated that eighty-four thousand people came from afar.
Why is it said that one merely attains the purity of the Dharma-eye by becoming free from dust and defilement among all phenomena?
It is because what is demonstrated here is the method of the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).

Since the four means of attraction are the skillful expedients (*upāya*) for guidance and assistance, those who attain them do no more than become free from dust and defilement and achieve the clarity of the Dharma-eye among all phenomena.
The Layman Wujin (Akṣayamati) argues: "How profound is the difficulty of believing and understanding the True Dharma!

Having demonstrated the retribution of sins and blessings, and having further shown the power of sovereign spiritual transformations, [the Buddha] cites the cause of King Bhaiṣajyarāja’s offering of his own body and life to clarify the fruit of such worship, thereby assembling a most wondrous and excellent retinue."
To arouse a sense of rarity and inspire vows among the beings of the evil realms and spirits, he recited mantras to solidify the power of their protective maintenance;
this may be called a most earnest and meticulous exhortation.

Yet, deeming this still insufficient, he further took the opportunity within the assembly for the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata to recount their past lives, thereby instructing the great multitude like thunder and clouds.
The Buddha Ghoṣadatta-guṇasāgaravairocana-jñāna was a Buddha of immeasurable and inconceivable kalpas past.
Ghana-svara-rāja is one whose virtue provides shade for all things and whose voice resounds throughout the ten directions.
Guṇarāja is one who planted roots of goodness in former lives and has attained supreme honor. Jñānakusuma is one who blossoms with wondrous wisdom to adorn the essence of his gnosis.
There was a king named Wondrous Adornment (*Su-vyūha*), who, though he studied the paths of non-Buddhists, was intelligent and easy to convert.
His queen was named Pure Virtue (*Viśuddha-guṇā*), who was pure and untainted, capable of providing guidance. They had two sons:
one named Pure Treasury (*Viśuddha-kośa*) and the other named Pure Eye (*Viśuddha-netra*). "Pure Treasury" refers to one who is pure and all-encompassing; "Pure Eye" refers to one who is pure...
Yet he was one who shone universally. The King studied non-Buddhist paths, while his two sons had left the household life.
These were those who, having received the Buddha’s entrustment in the past to protect and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, came as father and sons by the power of their vows.
Through the intimacy of their affection and skillful communication, they guided him back and shattered his heterodox mind and false views; thereafter, the father and the two...
The son, along with his ministers, subjects, retinue, and court ladies, were filled with joy at this reversal of fortune;
they realized that a Buddha is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower and resolved together to leave the household life, vowing to become Buddhas like the King of the Śāla Trees.
These two sons are none other than the present-day Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. Thus it was when the Buddha spoke the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment."
Is it not so that eighty-four thousand people have distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena?
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: "Exhortation by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva."
At that time, Samantabhadra... [up to] ...the *dhāraṇī*.

The Treatise says: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that from every single pore of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, worlds of all Buddhas and various bodhisattvas constantly emerge, filling the ten directions to transform sentient beings; because there is no fixed place of abiding, it is "universal" (*samanta*).
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla is difficult to see and difficult to know;

yet this sutra states that the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, with his sovereign supernormal powers, majestic virtue, and renown, comes from the east accompanied by immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable great bodhisattvas.
Thus, according to the sutra, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla would seem easy to know and easy to see.
Wherein lies the intent of this? It is said: Because Bodhisattvas possess the power of compassionate vows toward all sentient beings, there is none whom they abandon or neglect.
Even those who are most ignorant and dark may distinguish the general directions [of the path], and thus may be granted the Dharma;
it is not necessarily those of extraordinary brilliance or divine acumen. For example, even if a student does not recognize Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, or Avalokiteśvara...
Regarding the meaning of these sounds, he questioned his teacher. The teacher said: "Do you recognize the East?
It is the beginning from which the myriad things arise, like the growth of the myriad practices; this is the dwelling place of Samantabhadra. Furthermore, do you recognize the West?
It is where one pities and rescues all things because they are withered and slain by the autumn winds; this is the dwelling place of Avalokiteśvara. And so forth.
He said: "Do you recognize the northeast? The northeast is the position where all things reach their end and begin anew.
It is through wisdom that one becomes deluded, and through wisdom that one attains enlightenment; this is the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī.

Observing it from this perspective, all [the descriptions] speak of what is easily seen and easily known in order to encourage and inspire [the practitioner]. If one were to point toward the lofty and profound or manifest the subtle and mysterious..."
If [the teaching] is so subtle that one would turn back in awe at its precipice, how could one take delight in hearing it or wish to follow it?
Inferring from what is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding Samantabhadra having no fixed abode, and according to what is shown in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra*, it is said:
"When the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are perfected, one beholds the conduct of Samantabhadra. This is because within the ten stages, the samādhis and the perfections (*pāramitā*) increase twofold.
Entering doubly into immeasurable samādhis, one ultimately does not see the body of Samantabhadra, nor any of his spheres of activity;
how much less, then, can the merit within the Buddha-fruit—the constant practice of Samantabhadra’s conduct throughout all lands of the ten directions—be perceived?
Thus, the fruit is difficult to see and difficult to know. As the Sūtra says: "Whether this person is walking or..."
Whether standing and reciting this sutra, or even sitting and contemplating it, I shall mount the six-tusked White Elephant King and, together with the great bodhisattvas,
go to that place and manifest my body before that person. Why is it that bodhisattvas of the ten stages,
who have entered immeasurable samādhis, cannot see me, yet I appear before ordinary beings during their four modes of conduct?
If one can see him simply by reading, reciting, and upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* while in this world—ah, this too implies that he is easy to see and easy to know!
There was a Song dynasty monk named Puming who diligently and strictly recited and upheld the scripture without ceasing day or night;
whenever he reached this chapter, he would invariably see the Bodhisattva riding upon a white elephant king, accompanied by his retinue, their majestic radiance shining brilliantly.
"How could a Bodhisattva appearing before me deceive me? As for what was called the 'Dhāraṇī of the Revolving Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra,' it refers to the profound realm of all Buddhas;
it is like the whirlpool formed by the circling of flowing waves, which must reach the very depths.
It is also named the 'Samādhi of Revolving Back into the Ocean,' the king among immeasurable samādhis."
He then said, "Because I have seen his body, I have immediately attained it. How could this be so?

For the Buddha’s profound samādhi is something that the Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness and ten stages of sainthood cannot fathom; how then could one attain it simply by seeing Samantabhadra once?
This was spoken as an encouragement using easily understood language. The Sūtra says: "I, at the time of the King of Jewel Splendor and Virtue..."
When the Buddha heard from afar that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was being preached in this Sahā world, he had already heard it;
yet upon seeing the Buddha, the bodhisattvas who had come together earnestly entreated him, saying, "We pray that the Buddha will preach it for us.
This, moreover, concealed his vast and immeasurable power of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi*) and his knowledge and vision of hundreds of thousands of subtle and wondrous samādhis.
By the power of this, he displays signs of what has not yet been heard to encourage their aspiration.
All of these are the sublime practices performed by Samantabhadra; no bodhisattvas are able to know their intent, but the Buddha alone knows them.
Therefore, he declares: "Good sons and good daughters, there are four dharmas which, when accomplished after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata..."
When one attains this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, first, one is protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, one plants the roots of all virtues;
third, one enters the stage of those fixed in right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*); and fourth, one gives rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings.

Now, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas means that one’s aspiration delights in the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). Planting the roots of all virtues means that one gathers all wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*).
To enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is to never forget mindfulness;
to give rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings is to possess pure vows.

For a newly initiated bodhisattva, these four dharmas are as indispensable as food, drink, clothing, and medicine—how could one wait for the words of a Buddha to know this? One who is anxious to study [should understand this].
[The Master] thought that [the teachings] were easy to understand and easy to know, yet no one was willing to follow them; therefore, he explained them in detail.
A monk from India named Qiyu arrived in Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Hui.

After staying for a long time, as the city was falling into chaos and he was about to return to the West, the monk Zhu Faxing requested of him, saying: "I pray you, grant me a single word that I may practice throughout my life. Thereupon—
He assembled the monastics and the laity, ascended the seat, and said: "Guard your speech, restrain your body and mind, and take care not to commit any evil;
practice all that is good, and thus you shall attain deliverance from the world. Having finished speaking, he remained silent. Faxing said, "I wish to hear the Dharma I have not heard before.
[The Master] replied, "If this verse were such, even an eight-year-old child could recite it. Faxing laughed and said, "An eight-year-old can indeed recite it."
"If one is a hundred years old and does not practice, what benefit is there in reciting [the scriptures] without practicing?
Everyone knows to revere those who have attained the Way, yet they do not know that the Way is attained through practice itself. Thereupon, he pulled back his arm and departed directly.
Daoyu may truly be said to have known the essentials of transmitting the Dharma and to have grasped the underlying intent of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The Commentary says: When the Sūtra describes those who receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, transcribe, and correctly bring to mind [this teaching], it means that they personally see the Buddha and hear the Dharma;
that is to say, if one does not forget or lose mindfulness of this Sūtra, one sees the Buddha and sees the Dharma.
It is difficult enough to encounter a Buddha, let alone hear the sūtras from his own mouth;

it is even more difficult to receive the Buddha’s praise, to have him place his hand upon one’s head in blessing, or to be covered by his robe. Such is the ultimate extent of his affectionate regard, trust, compassion, and protective care.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the Bhikṣu Meghashiri said to the youth Sudhana: "I have attained the power of recollection."
The gate of the light of the wisdom of all Buddhas consists in ceasing the mind so that discursive thoughts do not arise;

the manifestation of right wisdom is called "recollection. Because this right wisdom is united with the signless, wondrous principle of all Buddhas, this manifest signless right wisdom universally illumines the five views—namely, the view of a self, the view of extremes, and the others—within the mind and its objects.
When all myriad objects are collectively extinguished and one perceives their void stillness, and when deluded karma has ceased, this is called "radiance.
Therefore, it is said that "recalling the wisdom-radiance gate of the Buddhas" means that seeing Śākyamuni Buddha is the convergence of the body;
hearing as if from his own mouth is the convergence of speech; and making offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha is the convergence of the mind.
"Ah! To be able to never forget mindfulness is to be in union with the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind; students should apply themselves to this with all their heart.
Having spoken thus, the person [from whom he had received the teaching] paid homage and departed.
The Commentary states: The general meaning of this section of the sutra is roughly like that of the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō-bon*);

it is, in fact, the Buddha’s final, pure, and clear instruction. He cautioned against being attached to the written texts of non-Buddhist scriptures because they act as a "leakage" (*āsrava*) for right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
It is, for example, like milk from near a city, whose flavor is diluted; thus [it cannot withstand] various evil objects.
Regarding the admonition in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* not to associate with [certain people], it is because they are superior conditions that obstruct the Path;

fearing that such conditions might cause deviation, the Buddha’s intention was solely to desire that you—dwelling among mountains and forests, practicing walking meditation and remaining in silent seclusion, wearing tattered robes and ragged patchwork, and subsisting on whatever gruel and rice comes your way—would find your mind naturally pure and your body naturally at ease. This is the Dharma of conformity.

The *Huā* (Flower) Samādhi is the essential gateway [to this teaching]. The Sūtra says: "If such a person’s mind is upright and honest, and they possess right mindfulness and the power of merit, how could they not believe?
Master Wujin (Inexhaustible) comments: "When the World-Honored One preached the Dharma, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were never absent."

When this Dharma assembly had concluded its preaching after all the immeasurable and boundless great Bodhisattvas from the ten directions had gathered, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva finally arrived from the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja in the east to listen and receive the teaching.
He then asked: "O sons and daughters of good family, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how can one obtain this sutra?"
He addressed [the assembly]: "After the parinirvāṇa of Tathāgata Samantabhadra, if one accomplishes four dharmas, one shall obtain this sutra.
First, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, planting the roots of all virtues; third, entering the stage of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma);
and fourth, generating the mind to rescue all sentient beings. If one accomplishes these, one will certainly obtain this sutra; thus, it need not await formal reception."
If one attains it by upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it, then by practicing these four dharmas, the sutra will manifest of itself without being sought.
This was the inquiry of Samantabhadra to the Buddha, intended to exhort future generations. The Buddha said:
"If the Lotus Sutra circulates in Jambudvīpa and there are those who uphold it, you should think: 'All of this is due to the majestic power of Samantabhadra.'"
As for the divine power in Jambudvīpa, this refers to our own world-system here.
Formerly, when the Great Monk Zhiyi was not yet proficient in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he dreamed that Samantabhadra, riding a six-tusked white elephant, came and rubbed his crown.
He subsequently realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Was this not a response manifested within Jambudvīpa?

Colophon for the Re-engraved Combined Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

The Chan Master Hong of the Song dynasty, Juefan, possessed a commentary on the *Lotus Sutra* that circulated in the world. Master Daguan spoke of it to me, saying that he had been working toward its reconstruction for ten years without success.
Among the writings of Juefan, I have already been able to peruse the *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha).

Among the various treatises on the realization of wisdom within the forests [of meditation], I have long admired those whose arguments are direct, incisive, and exhilarating, for they are uniquely capable of untying the knots and removing the fetters of sentient beings.
Yet, I had never seen this particular work and yearned for it with great intensity. One day, I visited Master Daguang at his quiet chamber at Lengyan;

he brought out the book and showed it to me, saying, "I obtained it from a monastery in Jingyan. My joy was so great that I nearly went mad, realizing that an unsurpassed treasure had finally come into my hands.
It has been re-illuminated in the world so that it may be read in its entirety.
Indeed, the World-Honored One appeared in the world to preach the Lotus Sutra, and the great disciples received their predictions of enlightenment because they awakened to the Lotus Sutra.

Yet, while "Lotus" is a metaphor, as for what constitutes the "Wondrous Dharma," there is not a single word within these seven fascicles of text that explicitly reveals it. I wish, therefore, to provide annotations alongside this work.

"Difficult, difficult! It is difficult! Jōgwan [Dōgen] states in this treatise that, for the most part, he has used his own realization to authenticate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, such that its horizontal and vertical expositions accord with his intent exactly as he wished;
yet, he has never uttered a single word to explicitly "break through" it.

Those who read this treatise should apply themselves with fierce vigor at the very point where nothing is explicitly broken through, and suddenly burst open the assembly on Vulture Peak as it stands in solemn majesty.
However, it was not until after the collection had been dispersed that I first came to believe that the Elder Juefan’s compassionate heart was truly too earnest.

Those bound by the formal teachings, seeing his unconventional critiques, might view him as a master of men against whom they must take up arms; yet, while he may have set aside their natural mechanisms to seek out their metaphysical "black and yellow" or "male and female" essences, how could one dare say he lacked them entirely?
At the end of each chapter, there is an appended commentary by Zhang Shangying, whose arguments are likewise direct.

I have completed the carving of the woodblocks for the *Juefan* (Model for Enlightenment), which is sufficient to serve as its wings and feathers. Master Daguang had already departed for the north ahead of schedule;
I imagine that he will feel great joy at seeing this book circulating thousands of miles away. At that time—
